title: Dom Casmurro
author: Machado de Assis
synopsis:
Dom Casmurro is a novel written by Machado de Assis, published in 1899 by Livraria Garnier. Written for publication as a book, which took place in 1900 – although dated the previous year, unlike The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas (1881) and Quincas Borba (1891), which were first written as serials –, it is regarded by critics as the third novel of Machado de Assis's "Realist Trilogy", alongside those other two, although the author himself never formulated this category.

Its protagonist is Bento Santiago, the narrator of the story which, told in the first person, sets out to "tie together the two ends of life", that is, to bring together accounts from his youth up to the days when he is writing the book. Between these two moments, Bento writes about his reminiscences of youth, his life at the seminary, his affair with Capitu and the jealousy that arises from that relationship, which becomes the central plot of the story.

Narrated from a first-person point of view, its main character is the 54-year-old Rio de Janeiro native Bento de Albuquerque Santiago, a solitary and well-established lawyer who, after having reproduced exactly, in Engenho Novo, the house in which he was raised "on the old Rua de Matacavalos" (today Rua do Riachuelo), intends to "tie together the two ends of life and restore adolescence in old age", that is, to recount in middle age his moments as a young man. In the first chapter, the author justifies the title: it is a tribute to a "train poet" who once pestered him with his verses and who called him "Dom Casmurro" for having, according to Bento, "closed his eyes three or four times" during the recitation. His neighbors, who found his "reclusive and quiet habits" strange, and also his close friends, popularized the nickname. To write the book he is inspired by medallions of Caesar, Augustus, Nero and Massinissa: Roman emperors who killed their adulterous wives.

In the chapters that follow Bento begins his reminiscences: he recounts the experiences he had when his mother, the widow D.

title: The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas
author: Machado de Assis
synopsis:
The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas is a novel written by Machado de Assis, initially developed as a serial, from March to December 1880, in the Revista Brasileira, and then published as a book the following year by the then Tipografia Nacional as Memorias Posthumas de Braz Cubas.

The book is marked by a caustic tone and a new style in Machado de Assis's work, as well as by boldness and thematic innovation on the national literary scene, which earned it puzzled reviews at the time.

Narrated in the first person, its author is Brás Cubas, a "deceased author", that is, a man who has already died and who wishes to write his autobiography. Born into a typical family of the 19th-century Rio de Janeiro elite, the dead man writes his posthumous memoirs from the grave, beginning with a "Dedicatória": To the worm that first gnawed the cold flesh of my corpse I dedicate these posthumous memoirs as a fond remembrance. After the dedication, in the next chapter, "Ao Leitor", the narrator himself explains the style of his book, while the following one, "Óbito do Autor", truly begins the narrative, explaining his funeral and then the cause of death, a pneumonia contracted while he was inventing the "Brás Cubas plaster", a medicinal panacea that was his last obsession and that would "guarantee him glory among men". In Chapter VII, "O Delírio", he narrates what preceded his death.

In Chapter IX, "Transição", the memoirs proper begin.

title: Quincas Borba
author: Machado de Assis
subjects: Language and languages, study and teaching
synopsis:
Quincas Borba is a novel written by Machado de Assis, developed at first as a serial in the magazine A Estação, between the years 1886 and 1891, and then, in 1892, published in definitive form by Livraria Garnier. In the process of adapting it from serial to book the author made a few minimal but significant changes.

Following The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas (1881), this book is considered by modern critics the second of Machado de Assis's realist trilogy, which the author was concerned with using to criticize the customs and philosophy of his time, although he does not remove Romantic residues from the plot.

"In Quincas Borba third-person narration is recovered in order to better objectify the birth, passion and death of a naive provincial. Rubião, the improvised heir to a great fortune, falls into the snares of an ambitious couple; the wife, the ambiguous Sofia, seeing him rich and exploitable, gives him hope, but cautiously refrains from fulfilling it upon perceiving in her admirer signs of growing madness. In long zigzags the fate of poor Rubião and the well-composed vileness of the world in which Sofia and her husband triumph take shape; and I know of no finer picture of the bourgeois society of the Second Reign than this one, composed in the manner of a mosaic of everyday attitudes and phrases. From that world the madman, the poor man, is expelled with methodical harshness, on the slopes of Barbacena, bear in their pathetic simplicity the seal of genius."

"In Quincas Borba, in which the motif of dissimulation already preludes D. Casmurro, Machado's art delights in the rhetoric of the implied. In this veiled style, metonymy reigns: the recording of effects suggests the causes, without making them explicit.

title: The Alienist
author: Machado de Assis
subjects: Language and languages, study and teaching
synopsis:
The Alienist is a humorous literary work by the Brazilian writer Machado de Assis. Many consider it a short story, but most critics and specialists consider it a novella because of its narrative structure.

Published in 1882, when it appears incorporated into the volume of short stories Papéis Avulsos, it had previously been published in A Estação (Rio de Janeiro), from October 15, 1881 to March 15, 1882.

The book tells the story of Dr. Bacamarte, an alienist (the term for a psychiatrist at the time) who creates the Casa Verde, a place for carrying out unprecedented studies of the human mind, but ends up losing himself in his own madness.

title: Esau and Jacob
author: Machado de Assis
synopsis:
Esau and Jacob is a novel by the Brazilian writer Machado de Assis, published in 1904 by the publisher Garnier. The author's penultimate novel, the work was written at the height of Machado's literary maturity, after Dom Casmurro, and is often singled out by critics as a refined synthesis of his narrative technique and of his ironic and relativist view of Brazilian society.

The novel stands out for the ambiguous construction of its narrative, for the psychological analysis of its characters and for its metaphorical representation of the political disputes of Brazil at the end of the nineteenth century.

The narrative revolves around the twin brothers Pedro and Paulo, sons of Natividade. From birth, the brothers have opposite personalities and live in constant rivalry.

Pedro is a monarchist and pursues a career in Medicine, while Paulo is a republican and studies Law. The opposition between them extends to their love lives, for both compete for the love of the same woman, Flora, who is unable to choose between them.

The conflict between the brothers, however, is never fully resolved, reinforcing the ambiguous and ironic character of the novel.

title: Counselor Ayres' Memorial
author: Machado de Assis
subjects: Language and languages, study and teaching
synopsis:
Counselor Ayres' Memorial is the last novel by the Brazilian writer Machado de Assis, written in 1907 and published in book form in 1908, the year of the author's death. The work takes the form of a diary, made up of entries written between 1888 and 1889 by the fictional character Conselheiro Aires, a retired diplomat who returns to Brazil after a long stay in Europe.

Unlike traditional novels, Counselor Ayres' Memorial does not have a linear plot, being structured as a succession of episodes, observations and reflections by the narrator, in an introspective and melancholy tone. The work is often associated with the final phase of Machado's output, marked by stylistic sobriety and ironic restraint.

title: The Hour of the Star
author: Clarice Lispector
synopsis:
The Hour of the Star is a literary novel by the Brazilian writer Clarice Lispector.

The novel tells the story of the typist from Alagoas, Macabéa, who migrates to Rio de Janeiro, her routine being narrated by a fictitious writer named Rodrigo S.M.

The novel recounts the misadventures of Macabéa, a dreamy and naive young woman, newly arrived in Rio de Janeiro from the Northeast, grappling with different values and a different culture. Macabéa leads a simple life without great excitement. She starts dating Olímpico de Jesus, who sees in her no chance of social advancement of any kind. That being so, he leaves her for Glória (Macabéa's co-worker), whose father was a butcher, which suggested to the ambitious Northeasterner the possibility of financial improvement.

Feeling constant pain, Macabéa goes to the doctor and receives a diagnosis of incipient tuberculosis, but tells no one. Glória notices her colleague's sadness and advises her to seek comfort from a fortune-teller. Madame Carlota predicts a happy future, in which she would meet a foreigner, a blond man whom she would marry. In a way, that is what happens: on leaving the fortune-teller's house, Macabéa is run over by a yellow Mercedes driven by a blond man and falls on the asphalt, where she dies.

title: The Passion According to G.H.
author: Clarice Lispector
synopsis:
The Passion According to G.H. is a novel by the Brazilian writer Clarice Lispector. The book was published in 1964.

The plot concerns a woman identified only by the initials G.H., who, after dismissing her maid and trying to clean the maid's room, recounts the loss of her individuality after having crushed a cockroach in the door of a wardrobe.

The following day she narrates her own powerlessness to write about the episode. The story is organized in chapters in systematic sequence – each one begins with the same sentence that closes the previous one. Interruption is thus an element of continuity, in a symbolic representation of what G.H.'s experience is.

title: Near to the Wild Heart
author: Clarice Lispector
synopsis: Near to the Wild Heart is Clarice Lispector's debut novel. Originally published in December 1943, the book is marked by the writer's introspective style. It received many positive reviews at the time, and was awarded the prize for best debut novel by the Fundação Graça Aranha, in October 1944.

title: Family Ties
author: Clarice Lispector
synopsis:
Family Ties is a book of short stories by the naturalized Brazilian writer Clarice Lispector, with its first edition by Editora Francisco Alves, in 1960.

Most of the protagonists of the stories are ordinary people shaken by an epiphany during their everyday activities (e.g.: shopping at the supermarket in "Amor", or a family gathering in "Feliz Aniversário"). The book seems to reflect the author's own experiences at the time. As the title itself suggests, the characters of Family Ties are for the most part housewives struggling to balance the demands of marriage and family with a less controllable, wild life.

This theme can be observed in the protagonist Ana of the story "Amor". In the story, Ana's orderly life collapses when she is confronted with a "wild" Jardim Botânico, in Rio de Janeiro. In their structure, the stories recall a later novel, The Passion According to G.H..

title: The Stream of Life
author: Clarice Lispector
synopsis: The Stream of Life is a book by the author Clarice Lispector, first published in 1973 by the publisher Artenova. Considered by the author herself to be a work of fiction, critics understand that the book has no defined literary genre, ranging across the genres of novel, essay and poetry. Like other works by the author, the book is characterized by stream of consciousness, being composed of a continuous flow of words with no division in the text other than the indications of the start of a new paragraph. It is considered that in this work Lispector freed herself from the limits of the typical narrative structure. The narrator of the work is a painter who reflects on various aspects of human existence.

title: Covert Joy
author: Clarice Lispector
synopsis:
Covert Joy is a collection of 25 short stories by the Brazilian writer Clarice Lispector, some of which had already been published previously. It was first published in 1971.

The stories address subjects such as childhood, adolescence and family, without failing to address the anguish of the soul.

As is common in the author's works, the description of settings and characters and the plot lose importance to the profound revelation of the characters (epiphany).

The story "Uma Amizade Sincera" is a first-person narrative about the beginning, deepening and end of a friendship between two people, from childhood to adulthood. This story was also published in the book "Onde Estivestes de Noite", under the title "Esvaziamento". "O Primeiro Beijo" narrates the emotions and sensations of the passage from childhood to adolescence.

In February 1977, the author spoke with the journalist Júlio Lerner about the story "O ovo e a galinha" in a televised interview for TV Cultura. Rejecting the label of "hermetic" sometimes attributed to her, Lispector said that she understands herself well, except in this story, which she does not understand, it being "a mystery" to her. In the same interview, she refers to this story as one of her "favorite children".

title: An Apprenticeship or The Book of Pleasures
editionTitle: Uma Aprendizagem ou O Livro dos Prazeres
author: Clarice Lispector
synopsis:
An Apprenticeship or The Book of Pleasures is the sixth novel by the Brazilian writer Clarice Lispector, published in 1969.

The book follows the love relationship between Loreley (Lóri), a primary school teacher, and Ulisses, a philosophy professor.

The tension between the two, who have different goals and desires, leads to a process of learning and self-discovery.

title: The Devil to Pay in the Backlands
author: João Guimarães Rosa
synopsis:
The Devil to Pay in the Backlands is an experimental modernist novel written by the Brazilian author João Guimarães Rosa and published by Livraria José Olympio Editora in 1956. Both the cover art and the illustrations of the first edition of The Devil to Pay in the Backlands are by Poty Lazzarotto. Initially conceived as one of the novellas of the book Corpo de Baile, released in that same year of 1956, it grew, gained autonomy and became one of the most important books of Brazilian literature and of Portuguese-language literature. In the same year, Rosa also released the novellas of Corpo de Baile and the revised fourth edition of Sagarana.

In 2006 the Museu da Língua Portuguesa held an exhibition on the work in its Temporary Exhibitions Hall, photos of which illustrate the article.

The story revolves around the hired gunman Riobaldo, also known as Tatarana or Urutu-Branco, the book's narrator-protagonist. There are two points in the work to which the narrator clings: Diadorim: another hired gunman with whom Riobaldo establishes a distinctive relationship, which sits on the border between friendship and the romantic relationship of a couple.

The pact with the devil: establishing an intertextual relationship with the story of Doctor Faust. The doubt as to whether or not the pact was actually sealed (after all, Lucifer does not make an appearance) troubles the narrator and leads him to profound questions such as the existence of the devil – and, consequently, of God. On the other hand, this pact can also be attributed to Exu, the first Orixá of Candomblé, of the Crossroads, which is in fact the place where the pact was made, as well as to other indigenous deities and deities of caboclo culture.

The narrative is constructed with the accents and ways of the backlands, a typical feature of the modern Brazilian novel written from the 1930s onward.

title: Sagarana
author: João Guimarães Rosa
synopsis:
Sagarana is a book of short stories published by João Guimarães Rosa in 1946, the first version of which he entered in the Concurso Humberto de Campos, held by the José Olympio bookshop, under the title Contos, in 1938, signing it with the pseudonym Viator. That submission was awarded second place in the contest, losing to Maria Perigosa, by Luís Jardim.

It is the first publication that the author did not later disown. The texts are a good example of the author's style, his innovative language and his themes, tied to the rural life of Minas Gerais. Guimarães Rosa skillfully combines and recombines the information of his surroundings, blurring places and landscapes, blending the real, the imaginary and the legendary in his work. It is a regionalist yet universalist book, since its stories are set in the backlands of Minas Gerais, yet within a context of universal existential questions.

title: The Third Bank of the River and Other Stories
author: João Guimarães Rosa
synopsis: The Third Bank of the River and Other Stories is a book of short stories by João Guimarães Rosa published in 1962 by Livraria José Olympio Editora and, since then, by various publishers. It contains 21 stories that take place, for the most part, in an unspecified rural setting, mirroring situations and themes both particular and universal.

title: Barren Lives
author: Graciliano Ramos
synopsis:
Barren Lives is an influential and important novel by the Brazilian writer Graciliano Ramos, written between 1937 and 1938, originally published in '38 by the legendary Livraria José Olympio Editora, now published by Editora Record, and considered by many to be the author's greatest work. Graciliano's fourth and last novel, narrated in the third person, Barren Lives deals with a family of drought migrants from the northeastern sertão conditioned to a subhuman life, faced with problems such as drought, destitution, hunger, social inequality, class struggles and, consequently, the kaleidoscope of feelings, thoughts, desires and emotions, mixed with the harshness and the climate of the semi-arid region, that their condition forces them to live through and to seek means of survival, thus expressing a still very strong artistic mirroring of political denunciation and of the historical and social situation.

As far as structure is concerned, the book has thirteen chapters, some of which can even be read in an order (a novel that can be taken apart) other than the one printed in the book. However, some chapters, such as the first, "Mudança", and the last, "Fuga", must be read in that order. These two chapters reinforce the idea that all the destitution surrounding the characters of Barren Lives represents a cycle in which, when least expected, the situation worsens and the family is forced to move on, again and again.

Graciliano's work can be considered a landmark for Brazilian literature, since it contains an implicit (and, in some cases, even explicit) social critique of all the poverty in the northeastern sertão, which affects a good portion of the population and which, in fact, ends up harming the whole country, preventing greater development. There is, therefore, an attempt to show this region's disconnection from the rest of the country (a poor Brazil within the whole of Brazil).

title: São Bernardo
author: Graciliano Ramos
synopsis:
S. Bernardo, also later published as São Bernardo, is a novel written by Graciliano Ramos, published in 1934 and belonging to the second phase of Brazilian modernism. It is with this novel that Graciliano Ramos gains critical recognition, and matures a drier style than that of the previous book, Angústia, which nevertheless brought him more popularity.

São Bernardo tells the story of a rural worker, a field hand with a hoe and no family who goes through poverty but rises unscrupulously and later acquires a critical consciousness (Antonio Candido defines the protagonist Paulo Honório as "a foundling"). The book, as Antonio Candido and João Luís Lafetá have shown, denounces the exploitative socioeconomic condition under capitalism and the large landed estate. In addition, significant Gothic elements have been noted in the narrative.

The work consists of the story of Paulo Honório, a simple but ambitious man who ends up becoming a great landowner in the backlands of Alagoas. He marries Madalena in order to obtain an heir. Unable to understand the humanitarian way in which his wife sees the world, he tries to nullify her with his authoritarianism.

title: Anguish
author: Graciliano Ramos
synopsis:
Anguish (1936) is the third novel published by Graciliano Ramos, after Caetés (1933) and São Bernardo (1934), and before Barren Lives (1938), one of the works most discussed by literary critics.

In 1936, Graciliano was working as Director of Public Instruction of Alagoas and had been receiving threats. A few months later, he would be dismissed. He then devotes himself solely to finishing Anguish, despite the tension and the financial difficulties. He is finally arrested on 3 March 1936, the same day on which he had handed over the manuscript of the novel to be typed. He would remain imprisoned for the following ten months – in Maceió, Recife and Rio de Janeiro – without ever having been heard, without a formal charge, without knowing the reasons for his imprisonment. The novel was published thanks to the help of friends, among them José Lins do Rego.

The work is written in the first person. The narrator, Luís da Silva, is a 35-year-old civil servant, solitary, disgusted with life, who ends up becoming involved with his neighbour, Marina. With existentialist traits, Luís mixes facts from the past and the present, narrating at a frenetic pace and making use of stream of consciousness.

The reader of Anguish will certainly be reminded of Crime and Punishment, by Dostoiévski, for in both works there is the anguish arising from a crime, the fear of being caught, the fever. But in Anguish the crime is the climax, whereas in Crime and Punishment it is the starting point of the plot, and in the end the character achieves redemption. Another marked influence is that of the Brazilian naturalists, especially Aluísio Azevedo, with regard to determinism and the animalization of man. The narrator does not want to be a rat, and fights against it; he frequently compares humans (himself included) to creatures (pigs, ants, cockroaches, rats) and uses verbs normally applicable to animals to describe human reactions.

title: Captains of the Sands
author: Jorge Amado
synopsis:
Captains of the Sands is a novel by the Brazilian writer Jorge Amado, written in 1937 and published in the same year. The work portrays the life of a group of abandoned minors who live on the streets of the city of Salvador, sheltering in a waterfront warehouse and surviving by means of petty theft. These youths, marginalized by society, are known as the "Captains of the Sands".

The novel is part of the so-called Novel of the 1930s, a phase of Brazilian modernism marked by the intensification of social engagement and by the critical representation of economic inequalities, social exclusion and urban violence, moving away from the formal experimentation predominant in the previous decade.

In the Brazil of the 1930s there was a vision of a "new" country, one that had not yet come into its own, as Antonio Candido de Mello e Souza recorded, with the authors of the time highlighting that which separated the nation from the rich countries.

Brazil was living through a turbulent moment, in which awareness was growing of the so-called class struggle, during Getúlio Vargas's rise to power; João Luiz Lafetá states that "The awareness of class struggle, albeit in a confused form, penetrates everywhere - literature included, and with a depth that will cause important transformations".

Social change was then being sought, in contrast to the previous literary moment, in which the country's qualities were extolled, present in the modernist movement; there is a certain disenchantment with reality, which literature begins to portray pessimistically, but doing so in an active, transformative way. In Lafetá's words, there came about the "pessimistic awareness of underdevelopment".

In this context, Amado's work can be described as "social and proletarian".

title: Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon
author: Jorge Amado
publisher: Distribuidora Record de Servicos de Imprensa S/A, Editora e Distribuidora de Livros
synopsis:
Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon is one of the most celebrated novels by the Brazilian writer Jorge Amado, published in 1958.

It represents a moment of change in the literary output of the author, who until then had addressed social themes. In this phase he writes a chronicle of customs, marked by popular types, powerful colonels and sensual women. "Critics point to Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon, which is set in Ilhéus, as the watershed of Amado's work. Besides Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon, the novels Dona Flor and Her Two Husbands, Tieta do Agreste and Teresa Batista cansada de guerra are representative of this period.

The book was completed in Petrópolis, Rio de Janeiro, in the month of May 1958. Its 1st edition was released by Livraria Martins Editora, São Paulo, 1958, with 453 pages, a cover by Clóvis Graciano and illustrations by Di Cavalcanti.

Such was its success that in December of the same year the 6th edition was released, which became part of the collection Obras Ilustradas de Jorge Amado as the fourteenth tome, volume XIX, and in one edition after another it reached the 50th edition in 1975.

That same year, an edition was published, outside the collection, under an agreement between Livraria Martins Editora and Distribuidora Record, Rio de Janeiro, the 51st edition, with a cover by Di Cavalcanti, keeping the earlier illustrations, this time with 363 pages, containing a portrait of the author by Carlos Bastos and a photo by Zélia Gattai.

title: Dona Flor and Her Two Husbands
editionTitle: Dona Flor e Seus Dois Maridos
author: Jorge Amado
synopsis:
Dona Flor and Her Two Husbands is one of the best-known novels by the Brazilian writer Jorge Amado, a member of the Academia Brasileira de Letras, who released it in June 1966, and it has been successfully adapted for cinema, theater and television.

Alternating extremely realistic words and descriptions of the bohemian life of 1940s Salvador with gentler passages about food and remedies, the book is an extensive and nostalgic panorama of the everyday life and the past of Bahian life.

The novel opens with the death of Vadinho, a bohemian, gambler and alcoholic who dies suddenly in the middle of street carnival, dressed as a baiana. He leaves a widow, Dona Flor, whom he exploited and who, despite her husband's dissolute life, was in love with him. The first part of the book recounts the excesses of Vadinho and of all the bohemian companions who surrounded him.

In contrast to this decadent environment of bad habits, described in detail by the author, in the second part of the book it is Dona Flor's quiet life that comes to be portrayed. It describes how she earns her living teaching cooking at the school she owns, "Sabor & Arte". Interspersed with the cooking lessons are the sighs of the widow for her dead husband, as she remembers, more and more constantly, Vadinho's qualities as an excellent lover and the few moments of luxury he had provided her when he won at gambling. At the same time, she is courted by a suitor, Teodoro, a quiet and religious pharmacist. The two end up getting married.

title: Sea of Death
author: Jorge Amado
synopsis:
Sea of Death is a novel by the Brazilian writer Jorge Amado, a member of the Brazilian Academy of Letters, published in 1936, "at the start of his career when he was only 24 years old. He was already intimate with the soul of the sea, with its mysteries and sorceries, secrets and enchantments, beliefs and superstitions."

It was one of Jorge Amado's best-selling books, with 1.5 million copies sold.

The book deals, "in a poetic prose of captivating rhythm", with the birth, life and death of the character Guma, which the author describes as a story told on the docks of Bahia, a legend, as he himself says at the end of the book: "so the men of the sea tell it".

The book also features Lívia, Guma's beloved, the couple's son and countless fishermen such as Mestre Manuel and his wife who sings to the sea (Maria Clara), all of it seasoned with the roguishness and the charms of Jorge Amado's one-of-a-kind Bahia.

In truth, the book makes countless references to other celebrated fishermen, and details the rich cosmology of the fishermen, which revolves around Iemanjá. Jorge Amado also describes in great detail the wretched way of life of the "people of the sea", with death always lurking, shipwrecks and loves.

The central story of the novel would later be adapted for television, in the telenovela Porto dos Milagres by Aguinaldo Silva.

title: Tent of Miracles
author: Jorge Amado
synopsis:
Tent of Miracles is a novel by the Brazilian writer Jorge Amado, published in 1969. This work also served as the basis for adaptations, in film and on television, in addition to earning translations into German, Arabic, Bulgarian, Spanish, Finnish, French, Hungarian, English, Italian, Russian and Turkish.

The action takes place in the Tent of Miracles, Lídio Corró's print shop in the Pelourinho in the capital of Bahia, Salvador. A land populated by Afro-Brazilians, who make up the majority of the local population, and who, notwithstanding the racial prejudice they suffer, never fail to show themselves combative in winning their place in society.

The Tent of Miracles serves as a meeting point for people connected to candomblé and to capoeira Angola. Candomblé forms the backdrop, and Pedro Archanjo is the mixed-race hero of this story. A mulatto with some schooling, he is protected by the professor at the Faculty of Medicine, Silva Virajá. "In this tent of invention and magic Jorge Amado gives his readers the vital measure of the importance of the black man as a formative element of Brazilian culture".

title: The Year Fifteen
author: Rachel de Queiroz
synopsis:
The Year Fifteen is the first and most popular novel by Rachel de Queiroz, published in 1930. The title refers to the great drought of 1915, which the writer lived through in her childhood. The book has 26 chapters and was written during a period of illness of the writer, at the age of 19. It is widely considered Rachel de Queiroz's masterpiece.

"Sometimes I look at my kids and my chest tightens. It's not just hunger, it's fear".

The plot unfolds on two planes, the first focusing on the cowhand Chico Bento and his family, the other on the romantic relationship between Vicente, a rough landowner and cattle rancher, and Conceição, his cultured cousin and a teacher in the capital.

Conceição is presented as a young woman who likes to read many books, including ones with feminist and socialist leanings, which her grandmother, Mãe Nácia - a representative of the old traditions - finds strange. Conceição used to spend the vacation period on the family farm, at Logradouro, near Quixadá. Although she was 22, she did not speak of thinking about getting married, but she always "took a fancy" to her cousin Vicente. He was the landowner who looked after the cattle, and he was rough and even wild.

title: The Memoir of Maria Moura
author: Rachel de Queiroz
synopsis:
The Memoir of Maria Moura is the last Brazilian novel written by Rachel de Queiroz, originally published in 1992.

The Memoir of Maria Moura is a polyphonic novel, narrated by different characters with their different points of view. The work anchors several parallel plots that intertwine as the novel unfolds, centering on the narrative of the title character, Maria Moura, and her transformation from "young mistress" of the house into the bandit chief of a gang during the 19th century.

The novel begins with the young woman finding her mother dead. Maria Moura comes to be raised by her stepfather, which creates a suffering and loneliness that lead the character to become the leader of a gang in the backlands.

The other plots are: the story of Father José Maria, who begins living as a fugitive after killing the husband of the woman he gets pregnant; and the love story between Marialva, a dreamy young woman oppressed by her own family, and Valentim, a knife thrower, member of a circus company.

title: Macunaíma
author: Mário de Andrade
synopsis:
Macunaíma, o herói sem nenhum caráter is a book published in 1928 by the Brazilian polymath Mário de Andrade, considered his masterpiece. Written in a short time, but the fruit of earlier research the author had been carrying out into the origins and particularities of Brazilian culture and the Brazilian people, it narrates the story of the Indigenous hero Macunaíma, from his birth in the jungle to his death and transfiguration, an eventful and adventurous trajectory in which he is helped by his brothers and other characters, in search of a magic stone, the muiraquitã, which he had received from his great love, Ci, the Mother of the Forest, but which had been lost and had ended up in the possession of Piaimã, a man-eating giant who lived as a wealthy bourgeois in São Paulo.

The work is difficult to classify within the system of literary genres, since its structure combines elements of many genres.

In the depths of the virgin forest was born Macunaíma, hero of our people. He was jet black and a son of the fear of the night. There was a moment when the silence was so great, listening to the murmuring of the Uraricoera, that the Tapanhumas Indian woman gave birth to an ugly child. That child is the one they called Macunaíma.

Even in his boyhood he did astonishing things. To begin with, he spent more than six years without speaking. If they urged him to speak he would exclaim:

— Oh! what laziness! ...

The book is divided into 17 chapters plus an epilogue. The hero's family consisted of his mother and two brothers, Maanape, a shaman, and Jiguê, a warrior, married to Sofará. While still a boy, by means of magic he sometimes turns into a man, and begins his sexual adventures, in secret, with Sofará, whose adultery is discovered and who is eventually abandoned by her husband. Jiguê turns up with a new wife, Iriqui, and kills a river dolphin to feed the village. The river dolphin was a sacred animal, and as punishment the toad Maraguigana, Father of the River Dolphin, sends a flood that destroys the crops and drives away the game. The tribe goes hungry.

title: The Slum
author: Aluísio Azevedo
synopsis:
The Slum is a novel by the Brazilian writer Aluísio Azevedo, published in 1890 and considered the principal work of Naturalism in Brazil. Set in Rio de Janeiro at the end of the 19th century, the novel portrays everyday life in a working-class lodging house — the tenement — and analyzes the social relations established there, laying bare mechanisms of economic exploitation, social determinism and moral degradation. Influenced by European Naturalism, especially the work of Émile Zola, The Slum presents a critical view of Brazilian urban society and remains one of the most studied novels in the national literature.

The work describes the social rise of the Portuguese merchant João Romão, owner of a shop, a quarry and a tenement, next to the townhouse of a wealthy fellow countryman, Commander Miranda. The rivalry between the two grows as the number of little houses in the tenement increases, rented for the most part by the quarry's workers, who also do their shopping at João Romão's store, and he thus begins to grow rich quickly. With an obsessive determination to become rich, João Romão saves every coin and exploits anyone at all whenever he has the chance, as he does with the runaway slave called Bertoleza, who helps him with the hard work and for whom he forged a document of manumission.

João Romão's dream is to acquire social prestige, like his countryman Miranda. The latter, as the shopkeeper grows richer, begins to consider the possibility of offering him the hand of his daughter, Zulmira; so a mutual friend, Botelho, acts as intermediary in the negotiations and everything is arranged. João Romão becomes engaged to Zulmira, thus reaching a higher rung on the social ladder.

title: The Sad End of Policarpo Quaresma
author: Lima Barreto
synopsis:
The Sad End of Policarpo Quaresma is a novel of Brazilian pre-modernism, considered by some to be the foremost representative of that movement. Written by Lima Barreto, it was first brought to the public in serial installments, published between August and October 1911 in the afternoon edition of the Jornal do Commercio of Rio de Janeiro. In 1915, also in Rio de Janeiro, the work was printed in book form for the first time, in an edition published by the author. Its central themes are: nationalism, bureaucracy, social and political criticism, utopia and failure. The setting is the end of the nineteenth century, the beginning of the Old Republic in Brazil (the government of Floriano Peixoto). Lima Barreto delivers a fierce critique of the corruption, militarism and false patriotism of the Brazilian elite.

Major Policarpo is a quixotic antihero, imbued with noble ideals, some bordering on the deranged (so much so that he spends a spell in the asylum).

The book is divided into three parts, each symbolizing a phase of the protagonist's dream and of his disappointment with Brazil.

The first part of the work unfolds in the city of Rio de Janeiro, shortly after the proclamation of the Brazilian republic.

Seeking political, economic and cultural solutions for Brazil, Policarpo spends much of his time buried in books, for which he is criticized by part of the neighborhood, who cannot accept that someone without an academic degree might own books – a critique of academicism, very present in Lima Barreto's work –, and who criticize him even more when he decides to learn to play an instrument frowned upon by the bourgeois Rio society of the time, the guitar, because he considers it a representative of the country's popular spirit.

And it is while learning the instrument that he meets the man who will be his great friend throughout the novel, the serenader Ricardo Coração dos Outros, hired to teach him. Soon, however, Policarpo becomes disenchanted with the guitar – and with folklore – and sets off in search of the genuinely national traditions: the indigenous ones.

title: Recollections of the Clerk Isaías Caminha
author: Lima Barreto
synopsis:
Recollections of the Clerk Isaías Caminha is the first novel by the Brazilian writer Lima Barreto. Autobiographical in reference, its central theme is racism and social subordination, and it is divided into two narrative cores: the protagonist's childhood and journey to Rio de Janeiro, marked by racial discrimination, and his later entry into Rio's journalistic milieu, portrayed satirically.

The narrative, in the first person and in a memoir-like tone, is divided into two relatively distinct parts. In the first, the young mixed-race man Isaías Caminha, raised by a humble mother and encouraged by his uncle Valentim, leaves a small town in the interior for Rio de Janeiro, dreaming of becoming a "doctor". Armed with a letter of introduction obtained through a local farmer, he faces the first episodes of racial discrimination already on the journey, and these are repeated and worsen on his arrival and during his first days in the capital, when his dreams of social advancement run up against color prejudice.

In the second part, the focus shifts from Isaías's personal trajectory to the newsroom of the fictional newspaper "O Globo", run by the powerful Loberant, where the protagonist rises from office boy to reporter. The work then becomes a biting satire of the behind-the-scenes world of journalism, of patronage in public jobs, of the bureaucracy and of the politics of the time, by means of a gallery of types such as the journalists Raul Gusmão and Gregoróvitch.

title: Iracema
author: José de Alencar
synopsis:
Iracema (originally, Iracema: Lenda do Ceará) is a Brazilian novel published in 1865 and written by José de Alencar that forms part of the author's Indianist trilogy. The other two novels belonging to the trilogy are The Guarani and Ubirajara.

In Iracema, Alencar created a mythological and poetic legend for the origins of his native land, Ceará, known as "the land where the jandaia sings". For this same reason, the full title of the work is "Iracema: Lenda do Ceará". The story begins with the meeting between the Indigenous woman Iracema, of the Tabajara people, and a blue-eyed white man named Martim. Iracema, the virgin of the honey lips, whose hair was blacker than the wing of the graúna, and longer than her palm-tree figure. (Chapter II) Frightened by the presence of the stranger, Iracema, who was resting beneath a tree and playing with a bird, shot an arrow at Martim, who, because of his upbringing and his principle of not attacking women, did not defend himself. Regretting having attacked him, Iracema rescued him and broke her arrow in half, a gesture that Alencar explains is a sign of truce and peace. Iracema then takes him to her village, where Martim meets the chief Araquém, Iracema's father. Welcomed with hospitality by the Tabajara, Martim is offered the hand of Araquém's daughters, but prefers the love of Iracema.

title: Senhora: Profile of a Woman
author: José de Alencar
synopsis:
Senhora: Profile of a Woman is an urban novel by the Brazilian writer José de Alencar, published in 1874, in serial form.

One of Alencar's last novels, released as a book in 1875, two years before the writer's death. Just as Iracema is the crowning achievement of Indianist fiction, Senhora is, together with Lucíola, one of the high points of his city-based, contemporary fiction. A novel with a happy ending, it is the final development — now in a key of greater psychological density — of the motif of the conflict between love and self-interest, present since the first books, notably A viuvinha.

Aurélia Camargo, the daughter of a poor seamstress and fatherless, after losing her brother fell in love with Fernando Seixas — an ambitious man — with whom she had a flirtation. He, however, breaks off the relationship, driven by the wish to marry a rich girl, Adelaide Amaral, and by the dowry he would be entitled to receive.

Some time later, Aurélia, by now motherless as well, receives a large inheritance from her grandfather and rises socially. She thus becomes a prominent figure at the society events of the time.

Torn between love and wounded pride, she charges her guardian and uncle, Lemos, with negotiating her marriage to Fernando for a dowry of one hundred contos de réis. The agreement reached includes, as one of its clauses, that the contracted party will not know the bride's identity until the eve of the wedding.

On discovering that his bride is Aurélia, Fernando is very happy, for, in truth, he never stopped loving her. The young woman, however, on the wedding night, makes it clear: she "bought him" to play the role of the husband that a woman in her social position must have.

title: The Guarani
author: José de Alencar
synopsis:
The Guarani (originally O Guarany: Romance Brasileiro) is a historical novel written by José de Alencar, initially developed as a serial. On 1 January 1857 the opening chapter of the novel is published in the Diário do Rio de Janeiro, to be published as a book at the end of that year, with minimal changes from what had been published in serial form.

The work made José de Alencar a recognized author. It has been republished by various publishers and is currently in the public domain.

The main facts that structure the story are: the devotion and fidelity of Peri (a term derived from the Old Tupi piripiri, a kind of rush), a Goitacá Indian, to Cecília de Mariz (who is frequently called Ceci, a term derived from the Old Tupi sasy, "his pain": in this case, Peri's pain at not seeing his love for Cecília returned); Isabel's love for Álvaro, and his love for Cecília; the accidental killing of an Aimoré Indian woman by Dom Diogo and the consequent uprising and attack of the Aimorés, all of this taking place alongside a rebellion by the men of Dom Antônio de Mariz, led by Loredano, an ambitious and unscrupulous man who wishes to plunder the house and abduct Cecília.

Álvaro, who already knew of Isabel's love for him and already loved her too, is wounded in the battle against the Aimorés. Isabel, seeing her beloved's body in her room, tries to kill herself by asphyxiation alongside Álvaro's body. When she sees that he is alive, she tries to save him, but he does not allow it and they die together.

title: Rebellion in the Backlands
author: Euclides da Cunha
synopsis:
Rebellion in the Backlands is a book by the Brazilian writer and journalist Euclides da Cunha, published in 1902. It is considered the first Brazilian work of book-length reportage.

The work was published and sold by the traditional Livraria Laemmert, which was located on Rua do Ouvidor, in the center of the São Paulo capital.

The book is divided into three parts: A terra, O homem and A luta.

In the first part the relief, soil, fauna, flora and climate of the Northeastern region are studied. Euclides da Cunha revealed that nothing surpasses the chief calamity of the backlands: drought. He also recorded that the great droughts of the Brazilian Northeast have followed a cycle of nine to twelve years, since the 18th century, in a cabalistic order.

Determinism held that man is the product of environment (geography), race (heredity) and historical moment (culture). The author analyzes the psychology of the backlands dweller and his customs; it is a description made by the sociologist and anthropologist Euclides da Cunha, who shows the inhabitant of the place, his relationship with the environment, his ethnological genesis, his behavior, beliefs and customs; but he then focuses on the figure of Antônio Conselheiro, the leader of Canudos. He presents his character, his past and accounts of what life and customs were like in Canudos, as reported by visitors and captured inhabitants.

title: The Athenaeum
author: Raul Pompeia
synopsis:
The Athenaeum is a novel by the Brazilian writer Raul Pompeia, considered the only example of an impressionist novel in Brazilian literature.

First published in 1888, the book tells the story of Sérgio, a boy who is sent to a renowned agricultural school in the city of Rio de Janeiro, called the Ateneu. Run by the headmaster Aristarco, the school maintains strict rules and the principles of the aristocracy of the time. The work criticizes Brazilian society at the end of the nineteenth century, taking as a metaphor the Ateneu, its reflection, a place where the strongest always wins.

The story is narrated by the main character, Sérgio, now an adult, in the first person and in a non-linear way. The book begins with Sérgio's first contacts with the Ateneu, the boarding school in which his father enrolls him, even before he goes through the admission interview with the strict, but apparently affable, headmaster of the establishment, Aristarco. Sérgio's entry into the Ateneu represents, for him, the passage to maturity, on account of his separation from his parents, above all from his mother's affection and protection. Before that, he had only attended a few classes at a family-run day school and had lessons with a tutor.

The Ateneu was an educational institution for the sons of wealthy families, although it admitted some pupils by way of charity. For that reason, its students represented "the cream of Brazilian youth", receiving pupils from various Brazilian states who were sent to the court and to Aristarco's establishment because of the educator's fame and of the books he sent to every corner of the country by way of advertising for his institution.

title: Memoirs of a Militia Sergeant
editionTitle: Memórias de um Sargento de Milícias
author: Manuel Antônio de Almeida
synopsis:
Memoirs of a Militia Sergeant is a novel by the Brazilian writer Manuel Antônio de Almeida. It was originally published in installments in the Correio Mercantil (Rio de Janeiro), always on Sundays in the supplement "Pacotilha", between June 27, 1852 and July 31, 1853, anonymously. The first edition in book form, by Tipografia Brasiliense, dates from 1854 (first volume) and 1855 (second volume), with the author identified only as "a Brazilian". The first non-anonymous edition, in which the author's name appears, only came out after his death, in 1863, also in two volumes, in the collection "Biblioteca Brasileira", edited by Quintino Bocaiuva, with Machado de Assis as proofreader.

The work stands out for its humorous tone and for its critical portrayal of the urban customs of Imperial Brazil, moving away from the idealism characteristic of the Romanticism that was dominant at the time.

The narrative follows the path of Leonardo, the son of rather unconventional parents, from birth to adulthood. Mischievous and undisciplined in childhood, Leonardo grows up caught up in scrapes, love affairs and intrigues, frequently benefiting from chance and from the protection of influential figures.

At the end of the narrative, in an ironic and hardly moralizing way, Leonardo attains the rank of militia sergeant, despite displaying no heroic virtues or exemplary behavior, which reinforces the novel's satirical tone.

"Cynical and unruly, the idler Leonardo is not a typical character of Romanticism. Always ready to relativize the values of his time, he more closely resembles the picaresque heroes who, in European literature, preceded him. He lives through a classic love triangle, but spends most of his time wandering the dark alleys of the underworld. The book therefore departs from many Romantic principles."

title: The Little Brunette
author: Joaquim Manuel de Macedo
synopsis:
The Little Brunette is a novel by the Brazilian writer Joaquim Manuel de Macedo (1820-1882), published in 1844. The work marks the beginning of the fiction of Brazilian romanticism and still enjoys great success today. It is considered the first typically national novel, as it portrays the habits of the bourgeois youth of nineteenth-century Rio de Janeiro, contemporary with the time of its publication.

Written in the same year in which the author graduates in medicine, the work brings him fame so intense that it leads him to give up his medical career to devote himself exclusively to literature and journalism.

Filipe, Leopoldo, Augusto and Fabrício, medical students, spend the holiday at the house of Filipe's grandmother, on the Ilha de Paquetá, in Rio de Janeiro. One of them bet that if he remained in love with a woman for more than fifteen days, he would write a novel telling the story of that passion. From then on, Augusto meets Carolina (the Moreninha), with whom he falls in love. The only obstacle to their union is the promise of fidelity made by the student to a girl he had met in childhood and whose whereabouts and identity he did not know. However, this obstacle is resolved at the end of the book, to the surprise of the readers and of the characters in the plot.

title: Dead Fire
author: José Lins do Rego
synopsis:
Dead Fire is the masterpiece of the writer José Lins do Rego, a book that shows, in strong and poetic language, the decline of the sugarcane mills. Literary critics place it within the second phase of Brazilian modernism.

Published in 1943, it is the last work of the most expressive of José Lins do Rego's cycles: the sugarcane cycle. Although it marks the end of the series, with the decline of the mill owners, the novel also marks its peak, its moment of transcendence, constituting a masterpiece of regionalist literature, neorealist in character.

"Dead Fire" by José Lins do Rego is a novel that narrates the decline of the sugar mills in the Brazilian Northeast, structured in three parts, each focused on a central character: Master José Amaro, the mill owner Lula de Holanda and Captain Vitorino Carneiro da Cunha. Each of the protagonists represents a different perspective on the decaying society of the time.

In the first part, we follow the story of José Amaro, a saddler and craftsman who is proud and resistant to modernization and to submission to the mill owners. He struggles to keep his dignity amid the growing devaluation of his craft, in contrast with the industrialization that was already making itself felt.

In the second part, the focus turns to Lula de Holanda, a mill owner who tries to maintain his position and power in society, even with the end of slavery and the economic changes that were undermining the sustainability of the traditional mills. Lula represents pride and the desperate attempt to remain relevant in a social and economic context that no longer fit the old molds.

title: Plantation Boy
author: José Lins do Rego
synopsis:
Plantation Boy is a Brazilian regionalist memoir-novel, the first work by José Lins do Rego, published in 1932. Paid for by the author, the book was acclaimed by Brazilian critics for portraying the decline of the sugarcane-growing Northeast.

Plantation Boy reveals, in simple language strongly marked by oral speech, the violence and contradictions of the patriarchal society of the Northeast, newly emerged from slavery, as seen through the eyes of a child.

The novel is made up of forty short chapters, which represent, at the same time, forty distinct scenes. Some of them expand on the basic theme of others. The book is written in the first person and recounts the experiences of Carlinhos, who at the age of four saw his father murder his mother. He then goes to live with his maternal grandfather on a sugar plantation. The novel is a semi-autobiographical narrative, in which the author recalls his childhood in the rural setting of the Brazilian Northeast.

The book portrays life on the plantation and Carlinhos's experiences as he grows up surrounded by the patriarchal culture of the Northeast, marked by social hierarchy and by the relationship between plantation owners and workers. Carlinhos's grandfather is an authoritarian but affectionate figure, who takes on the responsibility of raising him and introducing him to the world of the plantation.

Over the course of the book, Carlinhos comes face to face with the harsh reality of life on the plantation, encountering the inequality, prejudice and social conventions that pervade the workers' daily lives.

title: Time and the Wind
author: Erico Verissimo
synopsis:
Time and the Wind is a trilogy of historical novels by the Rio Grande do Sul writer Érico Veríssimo, published between 1949 and 1962, and considered by many to be the greatest work of 20th-century Brazilian literature. Made up of O Continente (1949), O Retrato (1951) and O Arquipélago (1961–1962), the trilogy narrates two centuries of the history of Rio Grande do Sul, from the founding of the Jesuit Missions and the arrival of the first settlers in the "Continente de São Pedro" in 1745 to the end of the Estado Novo in 1945, through the multigenerational saga of the Terra, Cambará and Amaral families in the fictional town of Santa Fé.

Over seven volumes and more than three thousand pages, Érico builds an epic panorama encompassing wars, revolutions, racial mixing, political transformations and the formation of a cultural identity.

The title sums up the work's philosophical project: the tension between time, which accumulates, settles and transforms, and the wind, which scatters, destroys and renews. Érico uses the family saga as a metaphor for gaucho and Brazilian identity itself, showing how character traits, vices and virtues are repeated and transformed from generation to generation. The idea of transience is reflected in the narrative itself: the heroes of the past had their importance, had their names marked in history, but are now part of a past that is becoming a specter. The device of the temporal zigzag in O Sobrado is not merely formal: it is the work's thesis materialized in narrative structure: the past returning in fragments ever closer to the present, until the two merge in the siege of the Sobrado.

One of the most important and least discussed aspects of the trilogy is the way Érico confronts two of the greatest myths of gaucho historical memory: that of the "whiteness of the gaucho" and that of the "scant use of slave labor in the southern past".

title: Incident in Antares
author: Erico Verissimo
synopsis:
Incident in Antares was the last novel written by Érico Veríssimo. Written in 1971, it makes use of the fantastic and the supernatural to address real themes (the so-called Fantastic Realism). The main themes Veríssimo writes about in this work are the violence of the military regime and the arrival of foreign industries in Brazil.

In the year 1963, on December 11, seven people die in Antares, a fictional town governed by corrupt politicians. As the gravediggers are on strike, the dead begin to wander through the town, prying into the private lives of relatives and friends. Because of their condition as dead people, they can do this without fearing reprisals.

title: Consider the Lilies of the Field
author: Erico Verissimo
synopsis:
Consider the Lilies of the Field is a novel by Érico Veríssimo, written in 1938. The title of the work was based on a passage from the Sermon on the Mount, also known as consider the lilies of the field.

The book tells the story of Eugênio Fontes, who, at great sacrifice, graduates in Medicine. At university, Eugênio falls in love with Olívia, but marries, out of self-interest, Eunice, a rich woman, the daughter of Vicente Cintra. With this story in the background, the author composes a panorama of human types forever caught up in the conflict of security versus happiness.

The first part of the novel begins with Eugênio traveling from his rural property in Santa Margarida, heading for the city, which is three hours away by car. The call came from a hospital where another doctor, Olívia, is dying. While he waits to arrive in the city, Eugênio, in successive flashbacks, revisits his past. He recalls his unhappy childhood, owing to the poverty of his tailor father, and the desire that had seized him to become a rich man and free the family from all the shames brought on by poverty. Thanks to his parents' sacrifice, he had been able to study at excellent schools, including a high-level boarding school called Columbia College. His parents, in order to pay for their son's boarding school, worked at the school, but Eugênio was ashamed of them.

title: The Girl in the Photograph
author: Lygia Fagundes Telles
synopsis:
The Girl in the Photograph is a novel by Lygia Fagundes Telles, written in 1973 and awarded the Prêmio Jabuti in 1974.

It displays a distinctive literary technique: the author uses several narrative points of view to tell the story of the 3 main characters, the friends Lorena, Lia and Ana Clara. The narration is at times in the first person, conveying directly the thoughts of one of them; at times in the third person, with their feelings, conflicts and impressions in free indirect speech. Lorena de Vaz Leme is the narrator who opens the text, and is also responsible for primarily leading six chapters, out of the book's twelve. This reveals that hers is the most present gaze in the work. Lorena is the intersection between the other two girls in the work.

Lia, Ana and Lorena are the main characters of the novel. Although very different, they share experiences and support one another. They live together in a boarding house run by nuns. Their conversations and thoughts reproduce the customs and topics of the 1970s: political radicalization; women's sexual liberation; experiments with hallucinogens; and musical tastes.

Lia de Melo Schultz is a social sciences student, but she suspends her enrollment at the university because of her absences. Her mother is from Bahia and her father is German, a former Nazi. She prefers reading Karl Marx and revolutionary subjects. Her friends call her Lião. She and Miguel, her boyfriend - a student leader imprisoned by the dictatorial regime - are to meet at the end of the novel, when he is going to be released, and they are going to be reunited in Algeria.

Ana Clara Conceição studied psychology, but did not finish the course. A drug user, she has a boyfriend who is a dealer. She suffered mistreatment in the past, when she lived with her mother on construction sites. Her nickname is Ana Turva. She dreams of a rich, conservative fiancé who will give her a "normal" life.

title: The Marble Dance
author: Lygia Fagundes Telles
synopsis:
The Marble Dance is a book by Lygia Fagundes Telles, published in 1954.

The story takes place roughly between the 1940s and 1950s, in São Paulo, and explores the psychological traits of the characters. The idea of the happy family, for example, is pursued by the protagonist Virginia, but this quest is almost always doomed to failure, since there is a recurring impression of characters trying to save their families from the threats of fragmentation and of emotional and financial decline.

In the work, Virgínia, the protagonist, lives through a difficult childhood with separated parents, being raised by her mother, Laura, and her neurologist, Daniel, who in fact, it is later discovered, is her real father. She visits the mansion of her mother's ex-husband, Dr. Natércio, whom everyone believes to be her father, but she cannot get along with her sisters Otávia and Bruna, who live with Dr. Natércio, or with their neighbors: Letícia, Afonso and Conrado (for whom she nurtures a passion).

Virgínia always compares Otávia, Bruna, Letícia, Afonso and Conrado to a fountain in the garden of Natércio's house, encircled by a ring of stone dwarfs dancing in a circle, for they, in the same way, never accept one more into the ring. With Laura's death, Virgínia is placed in a convent school, where she is somewhat "persecuted" by the nuns. Upon graduating, she returns to Dr. Natércio's mansion as a new person, adult and matured. Virgínia then discovers the many human weaknesses of the people whom, in childhood, she considered demigods, and before whom she once had a feeling of inferiority.

title: Before the Green Ball
author: Lygia Fagundes Telles
synopsis:
Before the Green Ball is a Brazilian work of short stories written by Lygia Fagundes Telles and originally published by Editora Bloch in 1970. It is considered one of the most significant publications by the author, who began the consolidation of her career in the 1970s. The book brings together realist contemporary short stories of an intimist character, reflecting characteristics of the third modernist generation and of Concretism.

Made up of eighteen short stories, written between 1949 and 1969, the book deals with themes such as adultery, marital dissatisfaction, madness and the demystification of family roles, with characters drawn from urban middle-class Brazilian families that hide dramas and conflicts.

title: Ancient Tillage
author: Raduan Nassar
synopsis:
Ancient Tillage is the first novel and the most famous work written by the Brazilian Raduan Nassar. It was first published in 1975 by Livraria José Olympio Editora and became better known through the release of its film version directed by Luiz Fernando Carvalho in 2001.

The novel tells the story of André, a young man from an archaic rural milieu who decides to abandon his large family in the countryside to go and live in a small town, fleeing the suffocating life of the farm, his father's moral rigidity, and his incestuous passion for his sister Ana. In this conflict of worldviews, which lies at the heart of the order of the farm, there unfold temporalities that put a strain on the protagonist's existence.

title: A Cup of Rage
author: Raduan Nassar
synopsis:
A Cup of Rage is a novella written by Raduan Nassar in 1970, but published only in 1978. The main character of A Cup of Rage narrates what happens on an ordinary morning, after a night of love, when the apparent harmony between him and his partner suddenly breaks down. The novella was highly praised by critics, being considered a contemporary classic, and won the APCA fiction prize.

Unlike Nassar's first novel, Ancient Tillage, in which the register leans toward the erudite, the prophetic and the archaic, the language of this novella is modern and edgy, full of slang. Even so, it retains the long sentences and the recreation of an expressive orality, which approaches the poetic as in Ancient Tillage.

title: Child of the Dark
author: Carolina Maria de Jesus
synopsis:
Child of the Dark: Diário de uma Favelada, better known as Child of the Dark, is an autobiographical book by the writer Carolina Maria de Jesus, first published in August 1960 by the bookshop and publisher Francisco Alves.

In the book, the author recounts her life in the Canindé favela, where she lived with her three children, whom she supported on her own by working as a collector of recyclable materials, predominantly paper.

The book reproduces the author's diaries, in which she narrates her day-to-day life in a poor community in the city of São Paulo, the former Favela do Canindé.

The diary describes her experiences in the period from 1955 to 1960, and the anguish of the favela's inhabitants, above all the routine of hunger, repeated daily. De Jesus supported herself by collecting paper in the streets. When she could not get paper, she and her children did not eat.

title: Death and Life of Severino
author: João Cabral de Melo Neto
synopsis:
Death and Life of Severino is a book of regionalist and modernist poetry by the Brazilian writer João Cabral de Melo Neto, written between 1954 and 1955 and published in 1955.

The work narrates the suffering faced by Severino, presenting a dramatic poem that recounts the harsh journey of a migrant from the backlands (a drought refugee) in search of an easier and more favorable life in the capital of Pernambuco.

title: The Rose of the People
author: Carlos Drummond de Andrade
synopsis: The Rose of the People is a Brazilian book of poetry, written by the modernist Carlos Drummond de Andrade between 1943 and 1945. It is the author's longest work, consisting of 55 poems, and is also his first mature work and the greatest expression of social and modernist lyricism. The work is regarded as a rendering of a dark era, reflecting a time that was not only individual but collective, in the country and in the world, in which the author captures the feeling, the pains and the agony of his time. In the title The Rose of the People, the rose represents the poetry (expression) of the people of that era.

title: Feeling of the World
author: Carlos Drummond de Andrade
synopsis: Feeling of the World is the third book of poems by Carlos Drummond de Andrade, published in 1940, written after Alguma poesia (1930) and Brejo das almas (1934). Drummond, considered by national critics to be one of the greatest Brazilian poets, shows in this work his most mature side, attentive to human frailties and anxieties.

title: Claro Enigma
author: Carlos Drummond de Andrade
synopsis: Claro Enigma is the seventh book of poems released by the Minas Gerais poet Carlos Drummond de Andrade. It was originally published by the publisher José Olympio in 1951. Claro Enigma is composed of 41 poems divided into six conceptual parts.

title: Libertinism
author: Manuel Bandeira
synopsis:
Libertinism is the fourth book of poetry by the Brazilian poet Manuel Bandeira, published in 1930. The work is considered one of the landmarks in the consolidation of Modernism in Brazil, bringing together poems that combine colloquialism, humour, eroticism and a lyricism marked by reflection on death, illness and everyday life.

The book deepens the break with traditional formal models and affirms a poetics based on expressive simplicity, formal freedom and the valuing of individual experience, central characteristics of the modernist poetry of the 1930s.

title: Ballads of the Minas Conspiracy
author: Cecília Meireles
synopsis:
Ballads of the Minas Conspiracy is a collection of poems by the Brazilian writer Cecília Meireles, published in 1953, which tells the history of Minas from the beginnings of colonization in the 17th century to the Inconfidência Mineira, a revolt that took place at the end of the 18th century in what was then the Captaincy of Minas Gerais.

In 85 "ballads", plus four "settings" and others serving as prologue and exodus, Cecília first evokes the enslavement of Africans in the central region of the plateau in episodes of the exploitation of gold and diamonds in the 18th century; then the center of the collection is devoted to the fate of the heroes of the so-called "Inconfidência Mineira" – Joaquim José da Silva Xavier, known as Tiradentes, Tomás Antônio Gonzaga, his fiancée and beloved Marília de Dirceu, as well as other historical figures implicated in the event, such as D. Maria I the Mad, at the time Queen of Portugal.

title: The Rogues' Trial
author: Ariano Suassuna
synopsis:
The Rogues' Trial is a play in the form of an auto, in three acts, written by the Brazilian author Ariano Suassuna in 1955. It was first staged in 1956, in Recife, in Pernambuco. The play was also staged in 1974, directed by João Cândido. On October 2, 1957 the play was published in book form by the publisher Agir in Rio de Janeiro.

It is a drama set in the Northeast region of Brazil, with elements of the cordel literature tradition, of the comedy genre and traces of Brazilian Catholic baroque, with a striking blend of popular culture and religious tradition.

title: The Romance of the Stone of the Kingdom
author: Ariano Suassuna
synopsis:
The Romance of the Stone of the Kingdom and the Prince of the Blood of the Go-and-Return is a novel by the Brazilian writer Ariano Suassuna, published in 1971.

The narrator-protagonist, Quaderna, is arrested in Taperoá for subversion, conducts his own defense before the magistrate and, to that end, recounts the history of his family, written in prison. He declares himself a descendant of legitimate Brazilian kings, brown-skinned and "mestizo", of the Stone of the Kingdom - unrelated to the "foreign and counterfeit emperors of the House of Bragança" - and tells of his involvement in the political, literary and philosophical struggles and disputes in his kingdom.

At the time of its release, the book was considered a landmark of Northeastern literature, following the cycle of the regional novel of 1930. The work has been adapted for film, theater and television.

title: The Wedding Dress
author: Nelson Rodrigues
publisher: Serviço Nacional de Teatro, Ministério da Educação e Cultura
synopsis:
The Wedding Dress is a Brazilian stage play, psychological in nature, written by Nelson Rodrigues and first staged in 1943.

In its set, the play presents three interwoven planes: the plane of reality, the plane of hallucination and the plane of memory.

It tells the story of Alaíde, a young woman who is run over by a car and who, while being operated on in hospital, recalls the conflict with her sister (Lúcia), whose boyfriend (Pedro) she took, and imagines her meeting with Madame Clessi, a madam murdered by her seventeen-year-old boyfriend decades earlier, in 1905.

title: A Time to Meet
author: Fernando Sabino
synopsis:
A Time to Meet is a novel written by Fernando Sabino.

In A Time to Meet, the protagonist Eduardo Marciano is on a genuine existential quest. Structured in two parts ("A procura" and "O encontro"), divided into three subparts (In "A procura": "O ponto de partida", "A geração espontânea", "O escolhido"; in "O encontro": "Movimentos simulados", "O afogado", "A viagem"), the novel traces a path through the protagonist's life. The work features precise themes - some of them characteristic of the autobiographical genre - such as: the cycle of childhood, school, sexual initiation, first romance, swimming, marriage, the friends Mauro and Hugo (representative of a generation), the new circles of friendship and of intellectual life, during the 1940s in Belo Horizonte and Rio de Janeiro.

title: Happy Old Year
author: Marcelo Rubens Paiva
synopsis:
Happy Old Year is a Brazilian novel by Marcelo Rubens Paiva, released in 1982.

It deals with the author's autobiographical experience: he recounts the accident that left him quadriplegic after a dive into a lake beside the Rodovia dos Bandeirantes, on December 14, 1979, when he accidentally hit his head on the bottom of the lake and lost the movement of his body. He is transferred from one hospital to another, facing reticent doctors. It shows the difficulty many people suffer in this situation and the willpower a man must have to rejoin society, facing his problems and fears.

During the military dictatorship, the narrator-protagonist tells of the social repression and the barring of citizens from any social participation that opposed the regime, as well as the invasion of his home by six military men who took away his father, the federal deputy Rubens Beyrodt Paiva, whom Marcelo Rubens Paiva would never see again.

During this period of recovery, Marcelo recounts with charisma and sincerity details of his childhood and his youth. He reveals his love affairs and portrays his musical career.

title: Zero
author: Ignácio de Loyola Brandão
synopsis:
Zero is a novel by Ignácio de Loyola Brandão originally published in 1974, in Italy, after having been rejected by several Brazilian publishers. Its first Brazilian edition came only a year later. In 1976, it was banned throughout the country by the Ministry of Justice, for being considered an offense against morality and decency. One of its main themes is repression and the desire for freedom, a subject that would be explored again in And Still the Earth, from 1981. Its historical backdrop is the Brazilian Military Dictatorship, the same period in which the book itself was written.

It was chosen by Revista Bravo, in 2009, as one of the 100 most significant works of Brazilian Literature.

A novel of a grotesque nature, in which Rosa and José, the protagonist couple, harbor a feeling of disdain for one another, in which, even as they disgust each other, they are hooked by an enormous desire on their nights of pleasure. Amid a social setting filled with freaks (who work in the town's circus), they give themselves over to a routine of slaps and kisses that can entertain only themselves.

title: And Still the Earth
author: Ignácio de Loyola Brandão
synopsis:
And Still the Earth is a Brazilian novel by Ignácio de Loyola Brandão originally published in 1981.

And Still the Earth began as a short story, O homem do furo na mão, and turned into a novel.

In São Paulo, in a not-too-distant future, Souza, a resident of an old building downtown, notices that he has a hole in his hand. In search of an answer to this unusual fact, Souza travels through the congested city, the traffic jams turned into scrapyards, a chaotic setting of a hypothetical São Paulo of tomorrow.

title: Sergeant Getúlio
author: João Ubaldo Ribeiro
synopsis:
Sergeant Getúlio is a novel by the Brazilian writer João Ubaldo Ribeiro, published in 1971. It is a regionalist work, which takes as its theme banditry in the backlands and which uses colloquial language full of regionalisms, some of the terms being the author's own creation.

João Ubaldo's second book, for which he received the 1972 Prêmio Jabuti as breakthrough author, it is considered a masterpiece, having already been translated into several languages and having received praise from writers such as Érico Veríssimo and Fernando Sabino. In an interview, the author declared:

Through his reminiscences the reader learns that he was of poor origins, that he had worked as a shoeshiner and market vendor, that he had murdered the wife who was cheating on him, that he had sought the protection of the politician Acrísio Nunes and that, for his loyalty to the boss, he had been awarded a sergeant's stripes.

To take the prisoner to his destination, Getúlio faces, with violence and cruelty, not only the prisoner's resistance, but also that of the latter's political allies, that of the police and, in the end, that of the hired gunmen answering to the same political boss as he does, since the original order is revoked after some time. Since the revocation was not heard from the boss's own mouth, but through a messenger, Getúlio believes he must ignore it. Thus he heads toward ruin, dragged down at once by his failure to understand how local politics works and by his undeniable qualities of courage and dedication. The novel ends abruptly, with the death of the title character in a confrontation with Acrísio Nunes's political allies.

title: An Invincible Memory
author: João Ubaldo Ribeiro
synopsis:
An Invincible Memory is a saga about the formation of Brazil by the Brazilian writer João Ubaldo Ribeiro, published in 1984. It is a historical novel of great scope, with a profusion of characters – heroes, antiheroes and villains, from both the ruling classes and the common people – spanning three centuries of Brazilian history (the 17th, 19th and 20th) and events such as the Dutch invasions, the War of Independence in Bahia, the Farroupilha Revolution in Rio Grande do Sul, the Paraguayan War, the War of Canudos, the abolition of slavery, the Proclamation of the Republic and the military dictatorship. It is divided into ten chapters which, in turn, are subdivided into sections introduced by the place and date of the episode narrated, for example, "Tuiuti Encampment, May 24, 1866" or "Vera Cruz de Itaparica, December 20, 1647".

The plot of An Invincible Memory stretches from 1647, a time of Dutch incursions into Bahia, to 1977, when the military regime was in force, in more or less chronological order, but with jumps in time. The Dutchman Heike Zernike (whom the Brazilians call Sinique), by seducing the eldest daughter of Caboco Capiroba, named Vu, begins the mixed-race lineage of the novel's characters, which will lead to Daê, also known as the little black girl Vevé or the slave Venância.

The "white" core, for its part, has as its first major character Perilo Ambrósio Góes Farinha, the prototype of the scoundrel, who appropriates his family's estate and fakes a wound in the War of Independence in order to be acclaimed a hero, which earns him the title of Baron of Pirapuama. A group of slaves conspires to poison him. His bookkeeper (accountant), the "mixed-race" Amleto Ferreira (who changes his name to Amleto Henrique Ferreira-Dutton), the son of an Englishman and a black woman, takes advantage of the baron's poor health (resulting from the poisoning attempt) to divert part of his fortune and get rich.

title: The Voices of the Dead
author: Autran Dourado
synopsis:
The Voices of the Dead is a novel by the Brazilian writer Autran Dourado, published in 1967. Listed in the UNESCO Collection of Representative Works and regarded as his major work, alongside O Risco do Bordado, it is probably the author's best-known book.
