The author structures the narrative in the form of a baroque opera. The work also explores formal features of architecture in the description of the residence of the Honório Cota family. The action takes place in the mythical town of Duas Pontes, also the setting of other works by Dourado.

title: Chronicle of the Murdered House
author: Lúcio Cardoso
publisher: ALLCA XX, Université Paris X, Centre de recherches latino-américaines
synopsis:
Chronicle of the Murdered House is an epistolary book by Lúcio Cardoso published in Brazil in 1959. It is considered the author's most important book.

Chronicle of the Murdered House (1959) is considered the masterpiece of the novelist, poet and playwright Lúcio Cardoso (1912-1968). Told through letters, it is a dense story, full of jealousy, resentment and perversion, set on an old country estate in the interior of Minas Gerais, which receives a visit from a woman.

In the story of the decline of the Meneses family, kinships, extramarital affairs, violent acts, forbidden loves and incestuous relationships come to light.

The scholar Mario Carelli (1951-1994) states that Cardoso's "human and artistic journey" "flows into" this novel. Considered the peak of the trajectory begun with Maleita (1934), the novel fits the regionalist trends of the time of its release. Crônica explores the psychological-existential path of Luz no Subsolo (1936), characterized by Carelli as an "enthralling rough draft". This same characteristic can be seen in the novella Mãos Vazias (1938) and in the trilogy made up of Inácio (1944), O Enfeitiçado (1954), as well as in the unpublished book Baltazar. All of these books served as a kind of laboratory for the creation of the Crônica.

title: The Vampire of Curitiba
author: Dalton Trevisan
synopsis:
The Vampire of Curitiba is a novel written by Dalton Trevisan and published in 1965 by the publisher Civilização Brasileira. The book is divided into 15 chapters that present the character Nelsinho (also called the "hero") through different phases of life, with his troubled relationship with women as the connecting thread.

The chapters, almost all set in Curitiba, are steeped in suspense and enigmas. In brief accounts, the narrator reveals the everyday reality of human degradation in direct language. The Vampire of Curitiba takes us into the day-to-day life of Nelsinho, the "vampire" proper, a Curitiba native obsessed with sex, who wanders the provincial capital in pursuit of his "victims", walking along obtuse paths while opening the reader's eyes to the vision of a decadent city, in which he not only hides but blends in.

Curitiba, scoured by Nelsinho, who is first seduced by the arms and legs of a sensual billboard girl and, in the end, plunges to the lowest circle of hell, to the room of a brothel beside a prostitute. Downhill toward his savage satisfaction. This is the image of the vampire that the book offers; not the classic one thirsting for blood, but a slave to licentiousness and urban loneliness.

title: Happy New Year
author: Rubem Fonseca
synopsis:
Happy New Year is a book of short stories by the Brazilian writer Rubem Fonseca, published in 1975. The book became an immediate best-seller, but its narratives of sex, violence and conflict between social classes led to the work being banned by the censors of the military regime.

Happy New Year

The narrator, Pereba and Zequinha are hungry. There is a stash of weapons that they are keeping for Lambreta but, because of their hunger, the three decide to rob a New Year's party at some mansion. The plan succeeds and, as things unfold, they end up killing a lady and her daughter, the owners of the house, and also a man who told them to take whatever they wanted ("to them all of that was crumbs"); Zequinha rapes a girl. At the end of the story, the three toast to a happy new year.

Corações Solitários

The narrator is a former crime reporter who starts working at a newspaper aimed at a female readership, Mulher. His job is to answer letters from women readers, under the pseudonym Dr. Nathanael Lessa; however, according to Peçanha, no real woman writes to the newspaper, so the narrator himself makes up the letters. Later he also begins writing the scripts for the photo-novels, under the pseudonym Clarice Simone, basing them on classic literature.

title: Crimes of August
author: Rubem Fonseca
synopsis:
Crimes of August is a historical novel by Rubem Fonseca published in 1990 in Brazil.

The book has as its backdrop the events that culminated in the suicide of Getúlio Vargas, in August 1954. Blending fiction and reality, it tells the story of the murder of a businessman and the investigations, whose clues led the investigator Mattos to the Catete palace and could incriminate people close to the president and linked to the country's political crisis.

title: Turbulence
author: Chico Buarque
synopsis:
Turbulence is the first novel by Chico Buarque; it was written in Rio de Janeiro, finished in Paris in 1990 and published on 7 August 1991 by the publisher Companhia das Letras.

Narrated in the first person, the story alternates between different times and states of consciousness to present a character who oscillates between time and wakefulness.

title: Budapest
author: Chico Buarque
synopsis:
Budapest is Chico Buarque's third novel, released in 2003 by the publisher Companhia das Letras. The book tells the story of a ghostwriter who lives between Rio de Janeiro and Hungary.

It received a film adaptation in 2009, directed by Walter Carvalho.

In Budapest the narrator José Costa is a ghostwriter, a person who specializes in writing letters, articles, speeches or books for third parties, on condition of remaining anonymous. Costa writes the texts at Cunha & Costa Agência Cultural, a firm in which he is a partner with his college friend Álvaro Cunha, the latter specializing in promoting José Costa's work.

On the way back from a congress of anonymous authors, Costa is forced to make an unplanned stopover in the city of the novel's title, which sets off a series of events that form the center of the plot: married to the television news presenter Vanda, Costa meets Kriska in Hungary, who nicknames him Zsoze Kósta and with whom he learns Hungarian - according to the narrator, "the only language in the world that, according to wagging tongues, the devil respects". Amid the various comings and goings between Budapest and Rio de Janeiro, the plot alternates between his bewitchment by the Hungarian language and his fascination with seeing his writings published by others, as well as his romantic involvement with Vanda and Kriska.

title: Spilt Milk
author: Chico Buarque
synopsis:
Spilt Milk is the fourth novel by Chico Buarque, released on March 28, 2009 by the publisher Companhia das Letras.

A very old man lies in a hospital bed. A member of a traditional Brazilian family, he unspools, in a monologue addressed to his daughter, to the nurses and to anyone who cares to listen, the history of his lineage from his Portuguese ancestors, by way of a baron of the Empire and a senator of the First Republic, down to his descendant, a strapping young man of present-day Rio de Janeiro. A family saga characterized by social and economic decline, set against the backdrop of the history of Brazil over the last two centuries. The view the author offers us of Brazilian society is extremely pessimistic: cronyism, class and race prejudice, machismo, opportunism, corruption, the destruction of nature, delinquency.

The family saga marked by decline is an established genre in the modern Western novel.

The old man's disjointed speech, while serving a function of verisimilitude, creates doubts and suspense that hold the reader.

title: The Brothers
author: Milton Hatoum
synopsis:
The Brothers is a Brazilian novel written by Milton Hatoum and released in 2000 by the publisher Companhia das Letras. The book, winner of the Jabuti prize in 2001, is the second novel published by the author.

The book narrates the story of the troubled relationship between two brothers from a family of Lebanese descent living in Manaus. It is a novel whose plot presents situations of jealousy, resentment, envy, desire, pride and death, psychological tones that mark the progression of the narrative. The fight between brothers, the rivalry in love, added to a series of pertinent political and social discussions, is one of the merits of Milton Hatoum's novel.

The main characters are Halim (father), Zana (mother), Yaqub (the elder son, of the twins), Omar (the younger, of the twins), Rânia (daughter), Domingas (maid) and Nael (the maid's son, the narrator).

The story is told from the point of view of Nael, who narrates temporary moves forward and backward in order to delve into one of the characters or emphasize certain defining events in the lives of the family members, always explaining some facts and leaving many others in doubt.

title: City of God
author: Paulo Lins
synopsis:
City of God is a novel written by Paulo Lins and published in 1997 by Companhia das Letras. It paints a panorama of the social transformations undergone by the City of God housing project: from the petty crime of the 1960s to the situation of widespread violence and domination by drug trafficking in the 1990s. To redefine the situation of the place where he grew up, Lins uses the term "neofavela", in contrast to the old favela, the one of samba circles and romantic street hustling.

The book is based on real events. It is divided into three parts, respectively: A história de inferninho; A história de Pardalzinho; A história de Zé Pequeno.

title: There Were Many Horses
author: Luiz Ruffato
synopsis:
There Were Many Horses is a 2001 Brazilian postmodernist novel by Luiz Ruffato. In 70 chapter-fragments, the book narrates scenes involving various characters on a single day in the city of São Paulo, May 9, 2000, in various textual genres: third-person narrative, newspaper notes, radio announcements, horoscope, stream of consciousness, etc.

The title of the book refers to a verse by Cecília Meirelles in Ballads of the Minas Conspiracy: "They were many horses/but no one knows their names anymore/their coat, their origin..."

For Thiago Lopes Schifner and Mariana Figueiró Klafke, despite the fragmentary text, the novel does not amount to a collection of mini short stories. There is, in their view, a thread running through the narrative, in a polyphony of voices that composes a setting in which the city is the protagonist. For the critic Eloésio Paulo, in There Were Many Horses, Ruffato masterfully uses the juxtaposition of the characters' exterior landscape (the environment) and interior (psychological) landscape, alternating the narratives among narrators who express themselves through different forms (such as hagiography, the cake recipe, the weather forecast and newspaper advertisements) in relation to the metropolis.

In most of the chapters, the characters are anonymous, lost people, lower-class workers or those on the margins of society, the city's "many horses", revealing its most degenerate face.

title: Crooked Plow
author: Itamar Vieira Junior
synopsis:
Crooked Plow is a 2019 Brazilian novel written by the Bahian author Itamar Vieira Junior. It tells the story of two sisters, Bibiana and Belonísia, marked by a childhood accident, who live in conditions of contemporary slave labor on a farm in the backlands of the Chapada Diamantina. The novel was originally published in Portugal, by the publisher Leya, after winning the prize of the same name. In Brazil, it is published by the publisher Todavia. In addition to the Prêmio Leya, it also won important competitions such as the Prêmio Jabuti 2020 and the Prêmio Oceanos 2020. In 2022, it was reported that the work will be adapted by HBO Max. With direction by Heitor Dhalia and a screenplay by Luh Maza, Maria Shu and Viviane Ferreira, the work is intended to be told over at least three seasons. It will be the theme of the samba school Unidos de Vila Isabel at the Rio de Janeiro Carnival in 2027.

In the depths of the Bahian backlands, the sisters Bibiana and Belonísia find an old and mysterious knife in the suitcase kept under their grandmother's bed. An accident then occurs. And their lives will be forever linked — to the point that one needs to be the voice of the other. In a masterfully handled plot and with melodious prose, the novel tells a story of life and death, of struggle and redemption.

title: Ponciá Vicêncio
author: Conceição Evaristo
synopsis:
Ponciá Vicêncio is a Brazilian novel by Conceição Evaristo first published in 2003, though it has since gone through several editions. In literary criticism, it is considered a circular novel that makes a significant connection between story, narrative space and time, which are linked by the memory of the character Ponciá, in such a way that a web is created at certain moments. Because Conceição does this so beautifully, the reader is captivated by the character.

The work presents an "identity memory of Ponciá's grandfather and establishes a dialogue between the past and the present, between remembrance and lived experience, between the real and the imaginary", as Maria José Somerlate Barbosa comments at the end of the book.

title: Alleys of Memory
author: Conceição Evaristo
synopsis:
Becos da memória is a book by Conceição Evaristo that had its first edition in 2006, from Mazza Editora. The second edition, in 2013, came from Editora Mulheres. In 2016, it was translated into French by Editora Anacaona. From Pallas Editora, the third edition was made available to the public in 2017.

In the international cataloguing-in-publication data (CIP), the following are listed: 1. Brazilian literature; 2. Brazilian literature - Black writers; 3. Brazilian novel.

title: A Defect of Color
author: Ana Maria Gonçalves
synopsis:
A Defect of Color is a metafictional novel by the Brazilian writer Ana Maria Gonçalves (Ibiá, Minas Gerais), published in 2006.

The work ranked seventh on the list of the 200 most important books for understanding Brazil, released by Folha de S.Paulo in 2022, as part of the project "200 years, 200 books".

The book tells the life story of Kehinde, an elderly, formerly enslaved African woman who lived in Brazil for most of the 19th century. It begins with the protagonist returning to Africa, after having been enslaved and having lived through traumatic experiences in Brazil. Her main purpose is the search for a son, lost decades earlier. Over the course of the journey, she reflects on her life, from her childhood in the Kingdom of Dahomey (present-day Benin), her capture at the age of eight, trafficking, and enslavement on Itaparica Island, Bahia, and how this resulted in countless acts of violence, her life as an adult in Bahia, how she obtained her letter of manumission and her return to Africa as a successful businesswoman, living amid a community of people formerly enslaved in Brazil who returned to Benin and Nigeria.

title: The Dark Side of Skin
author: Jeferson Tenório
synopsis:
The Dark Side of Skin is a novel by Jeferson Tenório, published in 2020 and winner of the Prêmio Jabuti in 2021. The book addresses themes such as racism and police violence.

The narrator Pedro reconstructs the life of his family from the memories of his father, the teacher Henrique, who was killed during a police stop. With a narrative that is sensitive in its treatment of a relationship between father and son, Tenório lays bare the features of a country marked by racism, by a precarious education system and by the fetishization and sexualization of Black bodies.

title: The Invisible Life of Euridice Gusmao
editionTitle: A Vida Invisível de Eurídice Gusmão
author: Martha Batalha

title: Phenotypes
author: Paulo Scott
synopsis:
Phenotypes is a 2019 Brazilian novel written by Paulo Scott. The work deals with race relations in Brazil from the perspective of two Black brothers with different skin tones. Federico, light-skinned, is a social scientist and anti-racist activist; Lourenço, dark-skinned, treats racism as normal and tries to play down the prejudice he suffers.

The novel, narrated in the first person by Federico, alternates between two moments: the present (2016), in which he takes part in a ministerial commission in Brasília discussing third-party racial verification criteria for racial quotas in public universities, and the past (1984), during the narrator's adolescence in the Partenon neighborhood of Porto Alegre, a formative year in which he acquired racial consciousness.

title: Resistance
author: Julián Fuks
synopsis:
Resistance is a Brazilian novel written by Julián Fuks and published in 2015 by the publisher Companhia das Letras.

The book tells the story of a family of Argentine intellectuals who came to Brazil after the military coup in Argentina in 1976 and adopt a child and, later, have other, biological children. The complexity of this relationship is analyzed by Sebástian, the younger brother, who, from his understanding of his parents' story and of his adopted brother's feelings, seeks to rewrite this family plot.

title: Blood-Drenched Beard
author: Daniel Galera
synopsis:
Blood-Drenched Beard is a novel by the Brazilian writer Daniel Galera published in 2012. The novel was chosen as "the best book of the year" by the jury of the Prêmio São Paulo de Literatura 2013.

In Blood-Drenched Beard, an omniscient third-person narrator follows the protagonist, who is never named at any point, a physical education teacher who lives in Garopaba, in Santa Catarina. The protagonist has a neurological condition that prevents him from recognizing faces, including his own. He searches for clues to the disappearance of his grandfather Gaudério, a mysterious figure and something of a local myth.

title: Nine Nights
author: Bernardo Carvalho
synopsis: Nine Nights is the sixth novel by the writer Bernardo Carvalho, which received the 2003 Prêmio Portugal Telecom (now Prêmio Oceanos) and the Prêmio Machado de Assis for best novel of 2023, awarded by the Biblioteca Nacional. It is considered one of the leading novels of contemporary Brazilian fiction.

title: The Smell of the Drain
author: Lourenço Mutarelli
synopsis:
The Smell of the Drain is the debut novel of the cartoonist Lourenço Mutarelli, published in 2002 by Devir and later reissued in 2011 by Companhia das Letras.

The book was written in 5 days, during a trip his wife and son took over a Carnival holiday, and it took 10 days for him to correct the problems found by his wife, Lucimar Mutarelli. The book is dedicated to Férrez.

The protagonist is a man of about 40, the owner of a shop that buys and sells antiques, who struggles against the eternal bad smell coming from the bathroom drain.

The book paints a portrait of the human soul in a cynical and humorous way. It was adapted for the cinema in 2007 under the same title, with Selton Mello as the main protagonist.

title: Whatever Happened to Dulce Veiga?
author: Caio Fernando Abreu
synopsis:
Whatever Happened to Dulce Veiga? is a novel by the Brazilian writer, journalist and playwright Caio Fernando Abreu. Published in 1990, it was the second and last of the novels by the author, who is known mainly for his output of short stories and chronicles.

In 2008, it served as the basis for the screenplay of the film of the same name by the Brazilian director Guilherme de Almeida Prado, starring Maitê Proença as Dulce Veiga and Eriberto Leão as the protagonist-narrator.

Set in the São Paulo of the 1980s, the book tells the story of a washed-up journalist who becomes obsessed with finding and telling the story of the singer Dulce Veiga, a rising star who mysteriously disappeared from the public eye in the 1950s.

On this journey in search of the singer and of himself, which takes him deep into São Paulo and Brazil, the nameless narrator-protagonist comes across a series of semi-mystical characters who inhabit the night and the invisible corners of the city.

title: What Is This, Comrade?
author: Fernando Gabeira
synopsis:
What Is This, Comrade? is a book written by the Brazilian journalist, writer and politician Fernando Gabeira, in 1979, after his return to Brazil from exile. It recounts his experience in the armed struggle against the Brazilian military dictatorship in the 1960s, the kidnapping of the American ambassador Charles Elbrick, his imprisonment and subsequent exile in Europe during the 1970s.

Narrated in the first person, the book was a great sales success at the time of its release, with more than 250,000 copies sold in forty editions to date. It was made into a film in 1997 by the filmmaker Bruno Barreto, competing for the Oscar for best foreign film that year.

title: Bagagem
author: Adélia Prado
synopsis:
Bagagem is the debut book, consisting of a collection of poetry, by the Brazilian writer Adélia Prado.

Written in 1976, when the author was already forty years old, the book was well reviewed by Carlos Drummond de Andrade, who recommended its publication.

title: At Your Feet
author: Ana Cristina Cesar
synopsis:
At Your Feet is the last book of poetry by the Brazilian poet Ana Cristina Cesar, who belonged to the so-called mimeograph generation.

It was originally published by the publisher Brasiliense in 1982, one year before its author's suicide.

title: My Sweet Orange Tree
author: José Mauro de Vasconcelos
synopsis:
My Sweet Orange Tree or O My Sweet Orange Tree is a novel for children and young adults, written by José Mauro de Vasconcelos and published in 1968. It has been translated into 52 languages and published in nineteen countries, adopted in schools and adapted for cinema, television and theater.

This book portrays the story of a six-year-old boy named Zezé, who belonged to a very poor and large family. His mother worked in a factory and his father was unemployed. They went through many hardships, so the older sisters looked after the younger children and Zezé, in turn, looked after his younger brother, Luís.

title: The Nutty Boy
author: Ziraldo
synopsis:
The Nutty Boy is a Brazilian comic book series created by the illustrator and cartoonist Ziraldo. The magazine was based on the children's book of the same name published in 1980, which became a phenomenon during the 1990s and 2000s. The comics were published by Abril and Globo, from 1989 to 2007.

The book The Nutty Boy, published in 1980, achieved great publishing success, with more than 2.5 million copies sold by 2005. The work's popularity gave rise to various adaptations, including films, television series, stage plays, operas and the comic book magazine based on the character.

Maluquinho is a cheerful boy, full of imagination, who loves getting up to mischief and having adventures with his friends. One of his quirks is wearing a big pot on his head, which sets him apart from the others. The stories blend a sometimes naive humor (albeit with a certain scatology typical of childhood) with a certain taste of nostalgia.

title: A Bolsa Amarela
author: Lygia Bojunga
synopsis:
A Bolsa Amarela is a book for children and young readers by the Brazilian writer Lygia Bojunga. It was originally written in 1976 and tells the story of Raquel, a ten-year-old girl who, in the days of the military dictatorship, and because of her family's disapproval, finds herself prevented from fulfilling the three wishes she keeps in the yellow bag: to grow up, to be a boy and to be a writer.

Repressed by her family, Raquel hides her wishes in a yellow bag, and through it she discovers friends who help her find a new way of being in the world. Feminism is one of its themes.

title: Reinações de Narizinho
author: Monteiro Lobato
synopsis:
Reinações de Narizinho is a fantasy and children's book by the Brazilian writer Monteiro Lobato. Published in 1931, it is the book that serves as the springboard for the series that would be set at the Sítio do Picapau Amarelo. It is a classic of literature, and to this day serves as inspiration for many children's authors, such as Ana Maria Machado, Ruth Rocha, Pedro Bandeira and many others.

The book is made up of several short stories, previously published, arranged in chapters. Some stories are entirely original, while other stories are combinations using already familiar stories and characters, such as the visit from the characters of the Mundo das Maravilhas, including the princesses Snow White, Cinderella and Aladdin.

title: Urupês
author: Monteiro Lobato
synopsis:
Urupês is a collection of short stories and chronicles by the Brazilian writer Monteiro Lobato, considered his masterpiece and originally published in 1918. It inaugurates in Brazilian literature a regionalism that is critical and more realistic than the one practiced earlier, during Romanticism.

The chronicle that gives the book its title offers a disparaging view of the Brazilian backwoodsman, called by the author a "maker of deserts", a stereotype contrary to the romantic view of the modernist authors. Urupês is a name that comes from the Tupi language (urupé) and designates a mushroom (Pycnoporus sanguineus) that grows on pieces of wood. Lobato chose this name to refer to the country folk because they live hidden in the woods like mushrooms. ("Amid Brazilian nature, the backwoodsman is the gloomy urupê of rotten wood, dozing silently in the recesses of the hollows.")

OS FAROLEIROS (1917) - After reading a story by Rudyard Kipling about lighthouse keepers ("The Disturber of Traffic"), Eduardo has the chance to visit a lighthouse, and there he will witness a sinister drama signed by "a name greater than Shakespeare's": "Life".

O ENGRAÇADO ARREPENDIDO (1917) - Francisco Teixeira de Souza Pontes, a jokester, who "knew by heart the Enciclopédia do riso e da galhofa", when he finally decides to become a serious man, no one takes him seriously. All that is left for him is to make a major die laughing in order to get his job at the federal tax office.

A COLCHA DE RETALHOS (1915) - For fourteen years a grandmother has been sewing a quilt from the scraps left over from her granddaughter's dresses, to serve in the future as a wedding dress. But the plan goes wrong.

A VINGANÇA DA PEROBA (1916) - Two small farmers, Nunes and Pedro Porunga, live in constant conflict. One day Nunes cuts down the peroba tree that separates their properties in order to build a water-powered pestle mill, infuriating his neighbor.

title: Roots of Brazil
author: Sérgio Buarque de Holanda
synopsis:
Roots of Brazil is a book by the Brazilian historian Sérgio Buarque de Holanda. Written as an essay, it was originally published by Editora José Olympio, in 1936, and was subsequently reissued several times over the course of the twentieth century, and it is considered one of the most important classics of Brazilian historiography and sociology. The work has also been translated and published in Italian (1954), Spanish (1955) and Japanese (1971, 1976), as well as in German, French and English.

Published in 1936, Roots of Brazil addresses central aspects of the history of Brazilian culture. The text consists of a macro-interpretation of the process by which Brazilian society was formed. Its central thesis is that the personalist legacy of the colonial experience constituted an obstacle to be overcome for the establishment of political democracy in Brazil.

Holanda's conceptions of what a modern nation would be, which are imprinted in Roots of Brazil, owe a vast debt to his stay in Berlin, as an international correspondent, between 1929 and 1930. It was at that moment that Holanda developed his heuristic instrument for analysing Brazil. The activities he pursued in what was then the Weimar Republic went far beyond the life of a newspaper correspondent, as he attended Friedrich Meinecke's classes at the University of Berlin and deepened his studies of various German thinkers such as Ernst Kantorowicz, Leopold von Ranke, Carl Schmitt. His stay in Berlin was so important that Holanda came back from there with a set of texts written by him called "teoria da América", a notebook written during his Berlin sojourn of about 400 pages. In it Holanda sketched out a comparative sociology, of Weberian inspiration, focused on the colonization of America in its Portuguese, Spanish and English undertakings. From that manuscript, two chapters were published in Roots of Brazil.

title: The Brazilian People
author: Darcy Ribeiro
synopsis:
The Brazilian People: a Formação e o Sentido do Brasil is a work by the Brazilian anthropologist Darcy Ribeiro, released in 1995, which addresses the history of the formation of the Brazilian people. The book deals with the cultural matrices and the mechanisms of ethnic and cultural formation of the Brazilian people.

In the preface to the first edition, from 1995, Darcy Ribeiro states that writing this book "was the greatest challenge" he ever set himself. It took him 30 years to write it. According to Darcy, the book unifies an empirically based theory of social classes in Brazil and Latin America; a typology of the forms of exercising power and of political activism; and a theory of culture.

The book has 5 parts: (I) The New World; (II) Ethnic Gestation; (III) Sociocultural Process; (IV) The Brazils in History; (V) The National Destiny.

Each of the sections is structured with the following chapters:

(I) The New World

Ethnic matrices

The island of Brazil

The Tupi matrix

Lusitanity

The clash of worlds

The opposing views

Mismatched reasons

Salvationism

The civilizing process

Germinal peoples

The baroque and the gothic

Historical updating

(II) Ethnic Gestation

A breeding ground of people

Cunhadismo

The general government

Indigenous captivity

Mills for grinding down people

The Brazilindians

The Afro-Brazilians

The Neo-Brazilians

The Brazilians

Being and consciousness

Seeds and wombs

De-Indianization

The prodigious increase

The Black stock

(III) Sociocultural Process

Adventure and routine

The wars of Brazil

The Brazil enterprise

Assessment

Chaotic urbanization

Cities and towns

Industrialization and urbanization

Urban decay

Class, color and prejudice

Class and power

Social distance

Class and race

Assimilation or segregation

Race and color

Whites versus Blacks

Immigrants

title: Pedagogy of the Oppressed
author: Paulo Freire
synopsis:
Pedagogy of the Oppressed is the best-known work of the Brazilian educator Paulo Freire. It is regarded by the author himself as a continuation of his first book, Educação Como Prática da Liberdade.

Freire argues that traditional education, which he calls banking education, is oppressive and does not allow learners to develop in a critical and reflective way. Instead, he proposes a dialogic education, that is, one grounded in dialogue. Such education, unlike the banking kind, is based on the active participation of learners in the learning process and on critical reflection on the reality in which they live. The dialogue begins as early as the choice of program content, that is, of the curriculum to be delivered in the culture circles (places where dialogue and literacy teaching take place).

Written in the form of an essay, it is divided into four chapters:

Justification of the pedagogy of the oppressed

The "banking" concept of education as an instrument of oppression. Its presuppositions, its critique

Dialogicity: the essence of education as the practice of freedom

The theory of antidialogical action

title: Ideas to Postpone the End of the World
editionTitle: Ideias para Adiar o Fim do Mundo
author: Ailton Krenak
synopsis:
Ideas to Postpone the End of the World is a book by the Brazilian environmentalist, philosopher and indigenous leader Ailton Krenak. The book is written in a dialogic tone, using essays, reflections and anecdotes, and brings together two lectures and an interview given by the indigenous writer in Portugal in 2017 and 2019. It was first published in Brazilian Portuguese by the publisher Companhia das Letras in São Paulo in 2019. The book is divided into three parts, namely "Ideas to Postpone the End of the World", "Do sonho e da terra" and "A humanidade que pensamos ser". Presenting the worldview of an indigenous people, which is opposed to the excessive exploitation of nature, the author considers the future of the planet and, therefore, of humanity, trying to present ways of slowing the destruction of life. For this reason it is a work that offers reflections on the present and on the future as a possibility not yet opened.

The book focuses on the concept of the relationship between humanity and nature, and on the need to find a sustainable balance for the future of the planet. The book describes the indigenous perception of contemporary problems, reflects critically on the idea of humanity as something separate from nature and proposes to discuss the challenges and potential of modernity in understanding past and contemporary problems in order to create a fairer and more sustainable world. According to the Brazilian indigenous leader, only by rejecting the idea that human beings are superior to other forms of life will we be able to value our lives again and, at the same time, have the possibility of re-establishing a proper relationship with the planet.

The title, according to Krenak, is a provocation and a starting point for reflection on the "myth of sustainability, invented by corporations to justify the assault they make on our idea of nature".

title: The Falling Sky
author: Davi Kopenawa
synopsis:
The Falling Sky: Palavra de um Xamã Yanomami is a book organized by the French anthropologist Bruce Albert from the recorded words of the Yanomami shaman Davi Kopenawa, in an "ethnographic pact", in which the Shaman asked the anthropologist to be his voice to the world. It was originally published in French, in 2010, by the publisher Plon in the Terre Humaine collection. Soon afterwards, in 2013, it was published in English, by Harvard University Press. Finally, it was published in Brazil, in 2015, by the publisher Companhia das Letras.

The work, filled with shamanic visions and ethnographic reflections on white people, presents a complex and informative universe that questions the concepts of progress and development, subjective terms with multiple meanings, championed by those whom the Yanomami call the "people of merchandise".

title: Holocausto Brasileiro
author: Daniela Arbex
synopsis:
Holocausto Brasileiro is a book of investigative reportage by the journalist Daniela Arbex, released in 2013, which exposes the mistreatment that took place at the Hospital Colônia de Barbacena, based on testimony from survivors, former employees and people directly involved in the routine of the largest asylum in Brazil. The Colônia was responsible for the deaths of 60 thousand people and went so far as to raise at least 600 thousand reais from the sale of bodies.

In the preface, the name "Holocausto Brasileiro" is justified:

title: Lockdown: Inside Brazil's Most Dangerous Prison
author: Drauzio Varella
subjects: Penitenciária do Estado de São Paulo
synopsis:
Lockdown: Inside Brazil's Most Dangerous Prison (1999) is a book by the oncologist, professor and writer Drauzio Varella.

In the best-seller, the author recounts his experience as a volunteer doctor, starting in 1989, at the Casa de Detenção de São Paulo, where he provides health care, especially in the prevention of AIDS. He tells what he heard from the prisoners or what he witnessed and ends with an account of the 1992 massacre, when one hundred and eleven inmates were killed in "Pavilhão 9". The author records that, according to the prisoners, there were more than "...250 dead, counting those who left wounded and never returned".

title: The Alchemist
author: Paulo Coelho
synopsis:
The Alchemist is a bestseller by the Brazilian writer Paulo Coelho, originally published in 1988, in Portuguese.

An allegorical novel, The Alchemist follows a young Andalusian shepherd on his journey to Egypt, after he has a recurring dream of finding treasure there.

The Alchemist follows the journey of an Andalusian shepherd named Santiago. Believing a recurring dream to be prophetic, he decides to travel to a Romani fortune teller in a nearby town to discover its meaning. The woman interprets the dream as a prophecy telling the boy that there is a treasure at the pyramids in Egypt.

Early in his journey, he meets an old king, whose name was Melquisedeque, who tells him to sell his sheep in order to travel to Egypt and introduces the idea of a Personal Legend. Your Personal Legend is what you have always wanted to accomplish. Everyone, when they are young, knows what their "Personal Legend" is. He adds that "when you want something, the whole universe conspires to help you achieve it". This is the central theme of the book.

Along the way, the boy meets an Englishman who has come in search of an Alchemist and continues his travels with him. They travel across the Sahara and during their journey, Santiago meets and falls in love with a beautiful Arab woman named Fátima, who lives with her clan near an oasis.

title: Veronika Decides to Die
author: Paulo Coelho
synopsis:
Veronika Decides to Die is a book by the Brazilian writer Paulo Coelho, released in 1998 and adapted for the cinema in 2009, with the actress Sarah Michelle Gellar in the leading role.

The book was reissued by the Paralela imprint of the publisher Companhia das Letras in 2017. It is the story of a young woman who decides to commit suicide — even though everyone around her believed she had a perfect life.

"On November 11, 1997, Veronika decided that the moment to kill herself had — at last! — arrived". Thus begins Veronika Decides to Die, a novel that narrates a young woman's struggle against (and for) her life.

In the author's own words, the Veronika of the book is he himself, committed three times to psychiatric hospitals, from which he drew elements for this hard-hitting account of acceptance and madness.

title: The Lusiads
author: Luís de Camões

title: Message
author: Fernando Pessoa
synopsis:
Message is the only book published in his lifetime by the Portuguese poet Fernando Pessoa, if we discount the poems published in English. Made up of 44 poems, it was described by the poet as a "small book of poems". Published in 1934 by Parceria António Maria Pereira, the book was awarded in the same year the Prémio Antero de Quental, in the category of "poem or standalone poetry", by the National Secretariat of Information, headed by António Ferro, the young editor of Orpheu, a quarterly literary magazine, of which two issues came out in 1915.

It is a Portuguese Modernist work that carries at its core an emphasis on the lyrical self, is full of polyphony and has notable intertextuality with the work The Lusiads by Luís de Camões.

It is a book that revisits and, to a large extent, creates a mythology of Portugal's heroic past, full of symbols, Sebastianist, and which was later partly incorporated into the official ideology of the Salazarist dictatorship.

It is divided into three parts (tripartite structure), with a preliminary note preceding them. All of them, including the preliminary note, have epigraphs in Latin. The first, Brasão, uses the various components of the arms of Portugal to revisit some figures from the country's history. The second, Mar Português, turns to the age of the great voyages of discovery, knocking on the door of figures such as Infante D. Henrique, Vasco da Gama and Fernão de Magalhães, but not limiting itself to them. The third, O Encoberto, is the most markedly symbolic and Sebastianist part, also returning to speak of other figures from Portugal's history. The term "O Encoberto" is a designation for the former king of Portugal D. Sebastião, which demonstrates Sebastianism.

title: The Book of Disquiet
author: Fernando Pessoa
synopsis:
O The Book of Disquiet is one of the greatest works of Fernando Pessoa. It is signed by the semi-heteronym Bernardo Soares. It is a fragmentary book, always under study by Pessoa scholars, who hold disparate interpretations about how to organize the book.

"I was born in a time when the majority of young people had lost their belief in God, for the same reason that their elders had had it – without knowing why."

title: Blindness
author: José Saramago
synopsis:
Blindness is a novel by the Portuguese writer José Saramago, published in 1995, and translated into several languages. The work tells the story of the epidemic of white blindness that spreads through a city, causing a great collapse in people's lives and shaking social structures. The novel became one of the author's most famous and renowned, along with Baltasar and Blimunda and The Gospel According to Jesus Christ, and was, without a doubt, one of the main reasons for his being chosen for the Nobel prize in literature in 1998.

The blindness begins in a single man, during his usual routine. While he is sitting in his car at the traffic light, this man has an attack of blindness, and it is there, with the people who rush to his aid, that a successive chain of blindness forms…

A blindness, white, like a sea of milk and never before known, spreads rapidly in the form of an epidemic. The government decides to act, and the infected people are placed in a quarantine with limited resources that will gradually reveal the primitive traits of the human being.

The force of the epidemic does not diminish with the measures taken by the government and soon the world becomes blind, where only one woman, mysteriously and secretly, will keep her sight, facing all the horrors that will be caused, visually witnessing all the feelings that unfold in the work: power, obedience, greed, affection, desire, shame; dominators, dominated, subjugators and subjugated.

title: Baltasar and Blimunda
author: José Saramago
synopsis:
Baltasar and Blimunda is an internationally acclaimed novel by José Saramago, first published in October 1982. The action takes place in the early 18th century, during the reign of D. João V and the Inquisition. This absolutist king, thanks to the large quantity of gold and diamonds coming from colonial Brazil, ordered the construction of the magnanimous Palácio Nacional de Mafra, better known as the Convento de Mafra, as the result of a promise he made to secure the succession to the throne.

Through the close relationship between fictional and historical narration, the novel criticizes the exploitation of the poor by the rich, which gives rise to war between individuals, and the corruption inherent in human nature - with a special focus on religious corruption. It also reveals the theme of the solitary individual who struggles against authority, recurrent in Saramago's works.

In this work, Saramago portrays the personality of King D. João V and also narrates the lives of several anonymous workers who contributed to the quixotic construction of the Convento de Mafra. Among those workers was Baltasar, and the novel focuses, among other things, on his great love for Blimunda, a woman endowed with the strange power of seeing inside people.

The two meet a priest, Bartolomeu de Gusmão, who went down in history as a pioneer of aviation.

The trio begins building a flying machine, the Passarola, which rises towards the Sun, since the Sun attracts the wills, which are trapped inside the Passarola. Blimunda, by seeing inside people, collects their wills, described by the author as open clouds or closed clouds.

After the Passarola's first flight, Bartolomeu flees to Spain, pursued by the Inquisition. Blimunda and Baltasar go on hiding and maintaining the Passarola, which was concealed by bushes at Monte Junto.

title: The Gospel According to Jesus Christ
author: José Saramago
synopsis:
The Gospel According to Jesus Christ (1991) is a novel by José Saramago which, with a modern and critical view of religion, retells the biblical story of the life of Jesus Christ.

The book tells a fictionalized and humanized story of the life of Jesus and alludes to a possible relationship of his with Mary Magdalene (in the book, it was with her that Jesus "came to know the love of the flesh and in it recognized himself as a man"). By adopting this perspective, of the humanization of Christ, far removed from the traditional representation of the Gospel, Saramago argues that the historical propaganda of the crucifixion of Jesus, "a strong jolt, something capable of shocking sensibilities and sweeping away feelings", resulted in the imposition of "an endless history of iron and blood, of fire and ashes, an infinite sea of suffering and tears", in keeping with his worldview, according to which "it is because of God and in God's name that everything has been permitted and justified, especially the most horrendous and cruel", and that, "deep down, the problem is not a God who does not exist, but the religion that proclaims Him. I denounce religions, all religions, as harmful to humanity. These are harsh words, but they must be said".

title: Death with Interruptions
author: José Saramago
synopsis:
Death with Interruptions is a book by the Portuguese writer José Saramago published in 2005. Its opening sentence "The following day, no one died" is the starting point for a wide-ranging digression on life, death, love and the meaning, or lack of it, of our existence.

True to his style and even more sarcastic and ironic, Saramago goes beyond existential reflections, delivering a harsh critique of modern society (the country in the work is fictitious) as he recounts the reactions of the Church, the Government, the Clergy, the reporters, the philosophers, the economists, the funeral homes, boarding houses, hospitals, insurance companies, the families with a dying person at home, the maphia, etc.

The work can be divided into three parts. The first is the intermittence of death, a panoramic view of events from January 1st onward, when no one died any longer in that country. Here the paradoxes of death's absence are addressed, along with conflicts, discussions and solutions to the problem of those who neither die nor can return to living, the dying.

In the seventh chapter there is a letter sent by death to a television station, so that the news of her return may be made public. However, the return will take place under new rules: "from midnight tonight people will go back to dying just as they used to, without notable protest (...) I offered a small sample of what living forever would be like for them (...) from now on everyone will be warned equally and will have a period of one week to put in order what still remains of their life". For each person whose dreaded hour of departure with no return was drawing near, that seven-day period would be preceded by the receipt of a letter, written by death, announcing to them the "termination of this temporary contract we call life".

title: The Year of the Death of Ricardo Reis
editionTitle: O Ano da Morte de Ricardo Reis
author: José Saramago
synopsis:
The Year of the Death of Ricardo Reis is a novel written in 1984 by José Saramago whose protagonist is Ricardo Reis, the heteronym of Fernando Pessoa. In this work Saramago continues the biography of Ricardo Reis after the death of his creator, Fernando Pessoa.

"Here the sea ends and the land begins. It is raining over the pale city, the waters of the river run muddy with clay, the floodplains are under water."

Thus begins this dense book, which draws the reader in from beginning to end, while also taking a journey through the history of Portugal.

The character who lends his name to the work returns to Lisbon on December 29, 1935, after an absence of 16 years, and settles there, observing and witnessing the unfolding of a tragic year, through which the reader is led to feel the somber climate in which fascism asserts itself in society, with a dark future foreseen in the history of Portugal, Spain and Europe.

title: Seeing
author: José Saramago
synopsis:
Seeing is a novel by José Saramago published in 2004. The novel forms a pair with Blindness and Saramago does not hide his allegorical intent, playing a game of light and dark as he delves into contemporary impasses.

In some country or other, on a rainy day, few voters, after great floods, turned out to vote during the morning. The electoral authorities, worried, went so far as to suppose there would be a gigantic abstention. In the afternoon, almost at the close of voting, hundreds of thousands of voters turned up at the polling places. Miles-long queues formed, and everything seemed normal. But, to the despair of the electoral authorities, almost seventy percent of the votes were blank. A catastrophe. Evidently the institutions, political parties and authorities had lost credibility with the population. The blank vote had been an innocent demonstration, an outpouring, indignation at the debacle wrought by politicians belonging to the parties of the right, the left and the middle. Politicians from different parties, but identical in their conduct, enjoying privileges that were an affront to the population. The voters were tired, outraged.

The rulers, feeling threatened, set about acting in the name of order, spying, lying, torturing, blowing things up, driving people to despair.

title: The Stone Raft
author: José Saramago
synopsis:
The Stone Raft is a novel by José Saramago. It tells the fictional story of the geographical separation of the Iberian Peninsula from the rest of the European continent. This work, translated into more than twenty languages, was adapted for the cinema in 2002 by George Sluizer. The work is written in a singular format, in which the dialogue is incorporated into the narrative, omitting dashes, exclamation marks and question marks.

The geographical separation is an allusion to what Saramago saw happening in the face of the unification of Europe, in which the Iberian countries were set aside, drifting without identifying culturally, socially or economically with the rest of the continent.

Joana Carda: On scratching the ground (on Portuguese soil, mind you) with an elm stick (wych elm or elm), she feels she shares the blame for the separation of the Iberian Peninsula from the rest of Europe. The line is permanent; when disturbed, it immediately remakes itself.

Maria Guavaira: She found in her house, on the coast of Galicia, a blue woolen sock that never finishes unraveling, forming an enormous ball of yarn (described as a cloud).

Joaquim Sassa: The character claims to have performed a superhuman feat, throwing a stone into the sea on a beach in the city of Porto; a stone which, by its mass and the distance it traveled, makes the act impossible for Joaquim's physique.

José Anaiço: Followed by a flock of starlings during the early part of the book, for no apparent reason or immediate connection with the other cases, or with the splitting of Europe, the character reveals his purpose only as the plot unfolds.

Pedro Orce: A pharmacist, over 60 years old. He feels a continuous vibration coming from the ground, as if he could perceive the oscillations caused by the movement of Spain and Portugal.

title: The Maias
author: Eça de Queirós
synopsis:
The Maias is one of the best-known works by the Portuguese writer Eça de Queiroz, published by Livraria Lello & Irmão in Porto, in 1888. The work concerns the story of a family (Maia) over three generations, then focusing on the last one with the love story between Carlos da Maia and Maria Eduarda.

It all begins with the description of the house – "O Ramalhete" - Lisbon, which nevertheless has nothing fresh or rustic about it. Its name comes from a panel of tiles with a bunch of sunflowers, set where the coat of arms should have been.

Afonso da Maia, the master of the house, married Maria Eduarda Runa, and from this marriage came only one son - Pedro da Maia. Pedro da Maia, who had a typically romantic upbringing, was very attached to his mother and after her death was inconsolable, recovering only when he met a woman named Maria Monforte, whom he married, even though Afonso did not approve. From this marriage came two children: Carlos Eduardo and Maria Eduarda. Some time later, Maria Monforte falls in love with Tancredo (a Neapolitan prince, an Italian whom Pedro accidentally wounds in a hunting accident and takes into his home) and runs away with him to Italy, taking her daughter, Maria Eduarda, with her. When he learns of this, Pedro, devastated, goes with Carlos to the house of his father, Afonso, where he commits suicide.

title: Cousin Bazilio
author: Eça de Queirós
synopsis:
Cousin Bazilio is a novel by Eça de Queiroz. Published in 1878, it is an analysis of the urban bourgeois family in the nineteenth century.

The author, who had already criticized the provinces in The Crime of Father Amaro, now turns to the city in order to probe and analyze the same ills, this time in the capital: to do so, he focuses on a bourgeois home that is seemingly happy and perfect, but built on foundations that are false and equally rotten. The creation of these characters reveals and underscores Cousin Bazilio's commitment to its time: the work is meant to function as a weapon of social combat. The bourgeoisie — the main consumer of novels at that time — was supposed to see itself in the novel and find its flaws objectively analyzed there, so that it could thus change its behavior.

Jorge, a successful engineer and ministry official, and Luísa, a romantic and dreamy young woman, play the typical bourgeois middle-class couple of nineteenth-century Lisbon society. Married and happy, they lack only a child to complete the joy of the "engineer's home", as the couple's residence was called by the poor neighbors.

There is a group of friends who frequent Jorge and Luísa's home: D. Felicidade, the pious churchgoer who suffers from bouts of gas and is head over heels in love with the Conselheiro; Sebastião, Jorge's close friend; Conselheiro Acácio, the well-read one; Ernestinho; and the maids Joana — forward and flirtatious — and Juliana – resentful, envious, spiteful and bitter, responsible for the novel's conflict.

While she cultivates a formal and happy union with Jorge, Luísa still maintains a friendship with a former schoolmate, Leopoldina — called "Pão e Queijo" for her continual infidelities and adulteries. Luísa's happiness and security come under threat when Jorge has to travel to the Alentejo for work.

title: The Crime of Father Amaro
author: Eça de Queirós
synopsis:
The Crime of Father Amaro is one of the works by the Portuguese writer Eça de Queirós most widely circulated throughout the world. It is a controversial work, which provoked protests from the Catholic Church when it was published in 1875, in Portugal.

This work is one more human and social document of the country and of its time, written with the mastery of Eça de Queirós. It is also the first artistic achievement of Portuguese realism.

It deals with the romance between Father Amaro and the young Amélia, which arises in an environment in which the very role of religion is the subject of great debate and each person's morality is put to the test. While the tragic love story unfolds, secondary characters engage in thought-provoking debates about the role of faith.

Eça de Queirós is said to have taken advantage of being appointed administrator of the municipality of Leiria to get to know and study there, for six months, what would be the setting of The Crime of Father Amaro, a work that more than a hundred years later continues to hold the interest of different generations.

An orphan, the young Amaro comes under the protection of the Marchioness of Alegros, the employer of his late parents. The marchioness intends Amaro to follow an ecclesiastical career, despite the lack of vocation in the young man, who from an early age showed a voluptuous temperament. Resignedly, Amaro is ordained a priest and, against his will, goes to exercise the priesthood in a small provincial backwater. Through the influence of the marchioness's daughter, Amaro manages to be transferred to Leiria.

title: The City and the Mountains
author: Eça de Queirós
synopsis:
The City and the Mountains is a novel by Eça de Queiroz, published in 1901, belonging to the writer's final phase, in which he moves away from realism and abandons the heavy criticism he used to level at the Portuguese society of the time. The title itself already gives an indication of the plot. In this book, Queiroz draws a comparison between the civilized, hectic life of Paris and the calm, quiet life in the mountain town of Tormes.

One day, Jacinto, bored with urban life, informs Zé Fernandes of his departure for Portugal, on the pretext of transferring the mortal remains of his grandparents, moving the comforts of the palace there. However, the servant Grilo gets lost with the luggage, which, by mistake, was sent to Alba de Tormes, Spain. Thus the supercivilized Jacinto arrives in Tormes with only the clothes on his back.

In close contact with nature, Jacinto is renewed, at first lyrically, in an attitude of enchantment; at this stage of the narrative the greatest contrast between the cities and the mountains is shown, and the author describes every detail of that region of the Douro. Later becoming part of the productive life of the countryside, he applies his technical and scientific knowledge to the concrete situation of Tormes; he plans to build cheese dairies, plant crops, etc. Without breaking completely with the values of "civilization", Jacinto adapts what he can to the countryside. In this way the mountains are modernized.

Up to this part of the narrative Jacinto sees the mountains as a perfect and ideal place.

title: Doomed Love
author: Camilo Castelo Branco
synopsis:
Doomed Love is a novella by the Portuguese writer Camilo Castelo Branco, written in 1861 and published in 1862. It is considered the writer's principal work, and one of the most important of the Romantic period in Portugal. It mainly portrays the story of the forbidden love between Simão Botelho and Teresa de Albuquerque. It was subtitled by the author Memórias duma Família.

When the work was written, in 1861, Camilo Castelo Branco was imprisoned in the Cadeia da Relação, in Porto, for the crime of adultery, which he had committed with Ana Plácido.

Doomed Love was written over a period of fifteen days, during the author's stay in jail. While he was imprisoned, he also wrote the works O Romance de Um Homem Rico and part of Doze Casamentos Felizes.

The first edition of the book was published in 1862, the year in which he also published the works Memórias do Cárcere, Coisas Espantosas and Coração, Cabeça e Estômago. However, the periodical Revolução de Setembro of January 1 of that year reported that the work was already in circulation, so it must in fact have been published in 1861, although the official date is 1862, the date shown on the title page of the book.

In 1864, Camilo Castelo Branco wrote the work Amor de Salvação, which was intended in part to serve as a counterpoint to the book Doomed Love.

title: Sleepwalking Land
author: Mia Couto
synopsis:
Sleepwalking Land is a novel written by Mia Couto and published in 1992.

The work was published in Portugal by Editorial Caminho in 1993. It won the Prêmio Nacional de Ficção da Associação dos Escritores Moçambicanos (1995) and was considered one of the twelve best African books of the 20th century by a jury set up by the Zimbabwe Book Fair. It was reissued in Brazil by Companhia das Letras – it is a mise en abyme novel, written in a poetic prose reminiscent of Guimarães Rosa. Couto also draws on the resources of animist realism and of traditional African narrative art to compose this beautiful fable.

Muidinga is a boy who suffered from amnesia and was rescued by Tuahir, an old man who spends his time teaching Muidinga everything about the world all over again. They are fleeing the conflicts of the Civil War in Mozambique.

A bus that had been set on fire becomes the shelter of Tuahir and Muidinga, who are fleeing the devastating Civil War raging everywhere in Mozambique. The vehicle is full of burned bodies. But there is also another body by the roadside, and next to this body Muidinga finds the "notebooks of Kindzu", the long diary of the dead man in question. Among other things, Kindzu tells of his father, who was a fisherman and suffered from sleepwalking and alcoholism. In addition, Kindzu mentions the problems of the lack of resources that his family suffered, the death of his father, the carnal relationship he has with Farida and the beginning of the war. Kindzu goes on recounting moments of his life in his diary. Likewise, he fled the Civil War in the country.

title: The Last Flight of the Flamingo
author: Mia Couto

title: The Book of Chameleons
author: José Eduardo Agualusa
synopsis:
The Book of Chameleons is a novel by the Angolan writer José Eduardo Agualusa, first published in 2004 by the publisher Don Quixote. The book, divided into 32 chapters, is a critique of the political and social situation of Angola in a post-colonial context, and has as its protagonist Félix Ventura, a man who sells illustrious, albeit false, pasts to those who want them.

The Book of Chameleons portrays the life of Félix Ventura, an albino man, a native of Angola, whose strange profession consists of devising honorable fictitious pasts. Prominent among his clients are businessmen, politicians, generals, as well as a large part of the Angolan bourgeoisie. They have every social recognition in the present and assuredly in the future as well, but they need a past that gives them prestige and, therefore, illustrious lineages; it is in this false genealogy that the basis of the book's social and political critique of Angolan society lies.

One day, a foreigner turns up at Félix's door, in Luanda (where all the action takes place), confessing to him that he needs not only a genealogy but also a new Angolan identity, without offering any justification for this. Although intrigued, the protagonist grants the request, thus creating the individual who would come to be called José Buchmann, a professional photographer who devotes himself to capturing the destruction of the city brought about by the effects of the war.

title: A General Theory of Oblivion
author: José Eduardo Agualusa
synopsis:
A General Theory of Oblivion is a 2012 novel by the Angolan author José Eduardo Agualusa.

The novel tells the story of a Portuguese woman who moves to Angola with her sister and locks herself in her apartment as the country stands on the brink of independence. She tries to keep away from the outside world for three decades, until she meets a young man who tells her about the radical changes that have taken place in the country over the years that have passed. The book is based on real-life events.

The novel is set in Luanda, on the eve of and just after Angola's independence from Portugal. The war for independence left the area in a tumultuous and dangerous state for more than twelve years. In addition, the tensions among the anti-colonial forces (financed by the Soviet Union) indicate that there may be continued violence and terror after independence is achieved.

The novel revolves around Ludo, a Portuguese woman living in the Angolan capital. Amid all the violence and chaos caused by the clashes between the anti-colonial movement and the Portuguese authorities, she decides to isolate herself from society, shutting herself in her penthouse apartment. She provides for herself by growing vegetables and luring pigeons into the apartment through a window. She burns her furniture for warmth. The story is told from her perspective over the course of thirty years. The only information she receives about the outside world and the political situation it faces comes from the news on the radio, or from listening in on the neighbors' conversations.

title: Mayombe
author: Pepetela
synopsis:
Mayombe is a novel by the Angolan writer Pepetela originally published in 1980. It was written between 1970 and 1971, when the author was a guerrilla fighter in the People's Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), and deals with the daily life of the Angolan revolutionaries in the colonial war against the Portuguese forces. In the year of its publication, Mayombe earned its author the Prémio Nacional de Literatura de Angola, and, in 2016, the book joined the list of required reading of the Fundação Universitária para o Vestibular, of the University of São Paulo, making Pepetela the first African author to be included in the list of works.

The plot takes place between the Mayombe forest, in the Cabinda region, in Angola, and the city of Dolisie, in the Republic of the Congo. In the forest are the MPLA guerrillas, who are called by code names, most notably Comandante Sem Medo, Comissário Político João, Chefe das Operações, Teoria (a teacher), Lutamos, Milagre and Mundo Novo. Among them, disputes motivated by tribalism are constant. In the city, André and Ondina stand out. The latter becomes important because of her relationship with the Comissário.

The guerrillas are in the forest, looking for a place where civilians from Cabinda extract timber for the colonialists. Teoria is injured, but they carry on with the plan. When they find the workers, the only Portuguese man manages to escape, spared by Sem Medo. They keep the prisoners until the following day, presenting the MPLA's ideology to them. On releasing them, the guerrillas realize that a hundred-escudo note has been stolen from one of the workers. The workers leave and, later, Sem Medo notices that the thief was the guerrilla Ingratidão do Tuga, who would be tried at the base.

title: The Land at the End of the World
author: António Lobo Antunes
synopsis:
The Land at the End of the World is a book by António Lobo Antunes first published in 1979.

It is the author's second book and in 1987 earned him a prize from the French embassy in Lisbon.

"What I liked best about the Zoo was the skating rink under the trees and the very upright black instructor gliding backwards over the concrete in slow ellipses without moving so much as a muscle, surrounded by girls in short skirts and white boots, who, if they spoke, surely possessed voices as gauzy as those that announce the departure of planes in airports, cotton syllables that dissolve in the ears the way threads of candy do in the shell of the tongue."

So begins this testimony about the horrors he witnessed during the two years he was stationed in the former Portuguese colony.

It portrays Lobo Antunes's personal experience as a field doctor sent to Angola in the Portuguese Colonial War. Throughout the book, the reader, who even takes on the dimension of the main character's female "interlocutor", encounters a degraded Angola, in the midst of the colonial war, that "unbelievable absurdity of war".

title: The First Wife: A Tale of Polygamy
author: Paulina Chiziane
synopsis:
Niketche. Uma História de Poligamia is a novel published in 2002 by the Mozambican writer Paulina Chiziane. It won the first Prémio José Craveirinha de Literatura, established by the AEMO (Associação Escritores Moçambicanos), in 2003, jointly with Mia Couto.

The title of the book refers to a traditional dance practiced in the north of Mozambique. A dance that the writer herself defines as the dance of the sun and the moon, dance of the wind and the rain (...) that immobilizes the body and makes the soul fly (p. 160).

Written after Balada de Amor Ao vento, the novel represents and belongs to a sequence of novels on the theme of polygamy. The female protagonists represent the cultural plurality of Mozambique's geographical identities, while the sole male protagonist represents the Nation as a whole. Rami is the name of Tony's first wife. After her husband's repeated absences, Rami decides to investigate the reality of her marriage. Thus begins a journey of stripping away masks that leads to an encounter with the manifold regional realities of womanhood in Mozambique.

title: Jerusalem
author: Gonçalo M. Tavares
synopsis:
Jerusalem is the third novel in the series O Reino by the Portuguese writer Gonçalo M. Tavares, published in 2005 by the publisher Círculo de Leitores.

It is the winner of the Ler Millennium bcp prize and of the 4th edition of the Prémio Literário José Saramago, in 2004. It is currently published by Editorial Caminho.

title: New Portuguese Letters
author: Maria Isabel Barreno
synopsis:
New Portuguese Letters (NCP) is a literary work written jointly by Maria Isabel Barreno, Maria Teresa Horta and Maria Velho da Costa, between 1971 and 1972.

The book revealed the existence of acute discriminatory situations in a Portugal under the Estado Novo regime — among them, dictatorial repression and the condition of women (marriage, motherhood, sexuality). The NCP also denounced the injustices committed in the colonies and the reality of the Portuguese as colonialists in Africa.

title: Aparição
author: Vergílio Ferreira
synopsis: Aparição is a Portuguese feature film directed by Fernando Vendrell and adapted from the novel of the same name by Vergílio Ferreira, and it features Jaime Freitas, Victoria Guerra and João Cachola as Alberto, Sofia and Carolino. It premiered on March 22, 2018.

title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
author: Gabriel García Márquez
synopsis:
One Hundred Years of Solitude (in Spanish, Cien Años de Soledad) is a novel by the Colombian writer Gabriel García Márquez, winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982. It is considered one of the most important works of Colombian and South American literature and one of the most widely read and translated in the whole world. During the 4th International Congress of the Spanish Language, held in Cartagena, Colombia, in March 2007, One Hundred Years of Solitude was considered the second most important work in all of Spanish-language literature, behind only Don Quixote de la Mancha. Drawing on the style known as magical realism and on the historical novel, One Hundred Years of Solitude has captivated millions of readers and still attracts thousands of fans to the enduring literature of Gabriel García Márquez.

Considered one of the best books of Spanish-language literature ever written, its story takes place in a remote, fictional village in America called Macondo. This small settlement was founded by the Buendía–Iguarána family.

The first generation of this peculiar family is made up of José Arcadio Buendía and Úrsula Iguarán. This couple had three children: José Arcadio, who was a strong, virile and hardworking boy; Aureliano, who contrasts inwardly with his older brother in that he was philosophical, calm and terribly introverted; and finally Amaranta, the typical housewife of a 19th-century middle-class family. They will be joined by Rebeca, who was sent from José Arcadio and Úrsula's former village, with neither father nor mother.

The story unfolds around this generation and their children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren and great-great-grandchildren, with the particularity that all the generations were accompanied by Úrsula (who lived to between 115 and 122 years of age).

title: Love in the Time of Cholera
editionTitle: O Amor nos Tempos do Cólera
author: Gabriel García Márquez
synopsis:
El amor en los tiempos del cólera (Brazil: Amor nos Tempos do Cólera / Portugal: O Amor nos Tempos de Cólera) is a book by the Colombian writer Gabriel García Márquez published in 1985. The book is a novel in the fantastic realism genre, set in the 19th century in Latin America, which deals with a love triangle that lasted for more than fifty years.

The novel tells the story of Florentino's love for Fermina, which spans more than 53 years with almost no contact. They met through Florentino's job as a telegraph operator, when he delivered correspondence to Lorenzo (Fermina's father). The two spent two years sending letters to each other, until Florentino decided to send a letter with a marriage proposal, even without any physical contact and with almost no time spent together up to that point; in doubt, Fermina waited 4 months without giving an answer, and was pressed by a more than symbolic piece of correspondence containing a note asking her to accept or forget the proposal; she accepted, but imposed the condition that they wait two more years before getting married, but 4 months before the appointed date came the intervention of Lorenzo, who had discovered the relationship between the two through a nun at his daughter's school.

Lorenzo took measures such as sending Fermina's aunt away, since she had been covering up the affair, and taking his daughter away with him to another city. There followed two more years of correspondence hidden from Lorenzo.

title: Chronicle of a Death Foretold
author: Gabriel García Márquez
synopsis:
Chronicle of a Death Foretold (original title in Spanish: Crónica de una muerte anunciada) is a book by Gabriel García Márquez published in 1981. The work tells, in the form of a journalistic reconstruction, the story of the murder of Santiago Nasar by the two Vicario brothers.

The book is a non-linear narrative, told by an anonymous narrator in the form of recollections. The book subverts the traditional detective narrative by revealing, right at the outset, points central to the crime: the real focus of the book is the reason that led the entire town to let the crime happen, without serious attempts to save or even warn the victim, even though it was known everywhere that the murder was going to happen very soon.

Beginning on the morning of Santiago Nasar's death, the book is divided into an account of the events immediately preceding the crime, followed by background on several characters central to the plot (Angela Vicario, Bayardo San Román, and the Vicario twins), a detailed description of Santiago Nasar's autopsy, and finally, an account of the crime itself.

title: No One Writes to the Colonel
author: Gabriel García Márquez
synopsis:
No One Writes to the Colonel (El coronel no tiene quien le escriba) was one of the first short stories written by Gabriel García Márquez, published at the end of 1961.

The Colonel was one of the many officers of the revolution, and so he spends years waiting for the arrival of a letter that would announce his long-awaited pension. While he waits, his life goes by. His wife has a respiratory illness and the two live in extreme poverty. His son dies and leaves as an inheritance a fighting cock, which becomes the only hope - besides the long-awaited letter - of paying his debts and getting food for the family.

The action takes place between October and December 1956. At the beginning of the story the Colonel goes to the funeral of a musician who was the same age as his son. This death had the particularity of being the first natural death in recent years. Since their son had died, the Colonel, his wife and the rooster had survived on the money from the sewing machine of the son, who was a tailor. With the money about to run out, the Colonel tries to sell the only possession he had left, a wall clock, but shame prevents him from admitting that he is out of money and he ends up not selling it. Then he comes to the conclusion that he has to sell the rooster. D. Sabas, the rich man of the village, offers him 900 pesos for the rooster. On the day the cockfighting training sessions begin, his rooster has a spectacular victory, which convinces the Colonel that he could make more money by keeping the rooster than the price offered by D. Sabas. But there are still 45 days to go before the cockfights begin...

The Colonel had attained his rank in the war, at the age of twenty.

title: Ficciones
author: Jorge Luis Borges
synopsis:
Ficciones (original title in Spanish, Ficciones) is a collection of short stories by the Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges, considered by specialist critics to be one of the masterpieces of twentieth-century Latin American literature.

In 1961 this work won the Prémio Internacional de Literatura, awarded by publishers from France, the USA, England, Germany, Italy and Spain.

Part One: O Jardim de Caminhos que se Bifurcam (1941)

Prologue

Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius

A Aproximação a Almotásim

Pierre Menard, Autor do Quixote

As Ruínas Circulares

A Loteria em Babilônia

Exame da Obra de Herbert Quain

A Biblioteca de Babel

O Jardim de Caminhos que se Bifurcam

Part Two: Artifícios (1944)

Prologue

Funes, o Memorioso

A Forma da Espada

Tema do Traidor e do Herói

A Morte e a Bússola

O Milagre Secreto

Três Versões de Judas

O Fim

A Seita da Fênix

O Sul

title: The Aleph
author: Jorge Luis Borges
synopsis:
The Aleph (in the original, El Aleph) is a book of short stories by Jorge Luis Borges, published in 1949 and containing, among others, the story that gives the book its name. The writer addresses various paradoxical points such as immortality, identity, the double, eternity, time, pride, the human condition and its beliefs, with a high degree of creativity and superior writing, of an extremely high cultural level, subjecting the reader to an intricate labyrinth of ideas and reflections.

Borges's literature makes demands on the reader and challenges them. His writing, full of allusions and symbolism, introduces the reader to a labyrinth of words that harks back to the whole of literary construction.

title: Hopscotch
author: Julio Cortázar
synopsis:
Hopscotch (in Spanish, Rayuela) is a novel published in 1963 by the Argentine writer Julio Cortázar, and is considered his principal work.

The book narrates the story of Horacio Oliveira, an Argentine exile and the protagonist of the plot, and his relationship with a Uruguayan woman known as "la Maga". The narrative involves the active participation of the reader and offers multiple possibilities of reading and interpretation. The work is often classified as an "anti-novel", although Cortázar himself preferred to define it as a "counter-novel". With it, the author took a leap into the void, moving away from the controlled safety of the fantastic short stories that marked the beginning of his career to embark on a search without discoveries, made of unanswered questions.

Although the style varies considerably over the course of the novel, Cortázar himself stated that the work "is, in some way, the experience of a lifetime and the attempt to put it into writing".

On May 30, 1962, Cortázar sent a letter to his friend and editor at Sudamericana, Francisco Porrúa, informing him that the manuscript of Rayuela had been sent by air to the editor Julián Urgoiti.

title: Bestiary
author: Julio Cortázar
synopsis:
Bestiario is the first book of short stories by the Argentine writer Julio Cortázar, first published in 1951, by the publisher Sudamericana. Since its publication, the author has stood as one of the most outstanding short story writers in the Spanish language, and of Argentina, in the 20th century, one who renewed the fantastic genre. All the stories in this book belong to that genre, and, in Cortázar's own words, were written as self-therapies of a psychoanalytic kind. On this subject, the author said: "I wrote those stories while having neurotic symptoms that bothered me". Among the stories, "Casa tomada" stands out, which is seen as an allegory of the political and social context of Argentina during the emergence of Peronism in the 1940s.

Bestiary is a work of significant importance for two distinct reasons.

Bestiario is made up of eight stories: Casa tomada, Carta a uma senhorita em Paris, Distante, Ônibus, Cefaleia, Circe, As portas do céu and Bestiary.
