It tells the story of two siblings (Irene and the narrator himself), who have always lived in an old house belonging to their family, to whose upkeep and care they have devoted their lives. Neither of them married, on the pretext of looking after the house, and they are greatly troubled by the idea that one day, when they die, distant cousins will tear it down to put up a new building, or sell it to get rich. After a detailed description of the house and of the meticulous habits the two of them keep, the narrator relates that they must progressively abandon different parts of the house, because of some indistinct noises. Little by little the house is 'taken over' by these invisible, ghostly intruders. In the end, the whole house is left in the hands of the strangers and the siblings decide to leave; on their way out they throw the key into the sewer drain, in the hope that no one will ever enter the 'taken over' house.

title: Pedro Páramo
author: Juan Rulfo
synopsis:
Pedro Páramo is the only novel by the Mexican writer Juan Rulfo, published in 1955. It is Rulfo's second book, following El llano en llamas.

The work is considered one of the best and most influential novels in Spanish American literature, having received praise from writers such as Jorge Luís Borges, Gabriel García Márquez, Carlos Fuentes, Octavio Paz, Günter Grass and Susan Sontag. Although critics promptly recognized the qualities of the book, which received that year's Prêmio Xavier Villaurrutia, its reception by the public was weak: of the 2000 copies of the first edition, only 1000 were sold.

Juan Preciado, after his mother's death, returns to the town of Comala to look for his father, Pedro Páramo. As soon as he arrives, he learns that the man had already died years earlier. In Comala he comes into contact with various residents, all of them in some way connected to his late father, owner of the Meia Lua ranch, the largest in the region. Many of them, in fact, are his illegitimate children.

Little by little, small contradictions and absurdities follow one another: ghosts are heard, the boundaries between the real and the supernatural, sleep and wakefulness, past and present are blurred, until one understands that everyone, including the various narrators, who alternate, is dead. Although they are not aware of their own condition, the inhabitants of the place perceive that the others are dead. They are condemned to wander eternally because they committed sins (suicide, incest, murder, etc.) that were not absolved by the priest at the hour of death. One exception is Toríbio Alderete, murdered by Pedro Páramo and left unburied precisely so that his soul would have no rest.

title: The House of the Spirits
author: Isabel Allende
synopsis:
The House of the Spirits is the first and most famous novel by the Chilean writer Isabel Allende. It was originally released in 1982 in the city of Buenos Aires by Editorial Sudamericana.

Classified as magical realism, this historical novel incorporates implausible and strange things into the ordinary. Narrated from the perspective of its protagonists, the events of the plot deal with love, family, death, spirits, social classes, revolution, politics, ideologies and the fantastic.

The narrative centres on the life of the Trueba family and follows three of its generations through the female characters who embody the place of mother, daughter and granddaughter, spanning almost the whole of the twentieth century.

The drama takes place in an unnamed, fictitious country, though one with deliberate and explicit similarities to Chile, especially in its socioeconomic make-up and political upheavals, such as the large landed estates and the military coup of 1973. In addition, the writer drew on the history of her own family, to which she added fictitious events and characters, which give the story great richness and drama.

There are three protagonists, the three generations of women who are the basis for following the generational succession of the narrative; all with difficult lives and striking, traumatic events: Clara, the "clairvoyant", her daughter Blanca and the granddaughter Alba, who is the alter ego of Isabel herself. These women, feminine and strong, courageously face the passions, the family dramas and the turbulent events of their times.

title: The Savage Detectives
author: Roberto Bolaño
synopsis:
The Savage Detectives (in Spanish: Los detectives salvajes) is a book in the novel genre published in 1998, written by the Chilean writer Roberto Bolaño. The author won the Prémio Rómulo Gallegos for this same work.

We have to live life, that is all there is to it, simply. The one who said that was a drunk I met the other day as I was leaving the bar La Mala Senda. Literature is worth nothing.

The Savage Detectives is narrated in the first person by many narrators and structured in three parts. The first, entitled "Mexicanos perdidos no México", consists of the diary of the young poet Juan García Madero, aged 17, who narrates the final months of 1975 in Mexico City. Newly admitted to the group of the visceral realists - an avant-garde literary movement founded by the poets Arturo Belano and Ulises Lima -, García Madero drops out of university and plunges into the group's bohemian life, without ever understanding all of the movement's purposes.

The second part, "The Savage Detectives", takes up about two thirds of the novel and is the most formally ambitious. Constructed as a series of testimonies gathered between 1976 and 1996 in countries of North America, Europe, the Middle East and Africa, it brings together more than forty narrators who, at different moments in their lives, crossed paths with Belano and Lima.

author: Roberto Bolaño
subjects: National Book Critics Circle Award Winner
synopsis:
2666 is a posthumous novel written by the Chilean novelist Roberto Bolaño (1953-2003). The book, released in 2004, was written with the author aware of his failing health and was published a year after his death. Bolaño left clear instructions on how the book should be delivered to the public: as five different novels, one publication per year. Even so, the book was published in a single volume, owing to the magnitude of the work as a whole.

The novel is divided into five parts:

title: The Time of the Hero
author: Mario Vargas Llosa
synopsis:
La ciudad y los perros (A cidade e os cães in Portugal, in Brazil Batismo de Fogo) is the first novel by the Peruvian writer Mario Vargas Llosa, winner of the 2010 Nobel Prize in Literature.

The work, released in 1963, narrates the daily life of the students of the Colégio Militar Leoncio Prado, in Lima. The book has had multiple editions in dozens of languages and received the Prêmio da Crítica in Spain. It was also included in the list of the 100 best Spanish-language novels of the twentieth century by the newspaper El Mundo.

title: The Feast of the Goat
author: Mario Vargas Llosa
synopsis:
La fiesta del chivo (Brazil: The Feast of the Goat / Portugal: A festa do chibo), from 2000, is a novel by the Spanish-Peruvian writer Mario Vargas Llosa, winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2010. The book is set in the Dominican Republic and portrays the assassination of the Dominican dictator Rafael Leónidas Trujillo and its aftermath, from two points of view, a generation apart: during and immediately after the assassination itself, in May 1961, and thirty-five years later. Throughout, there is also a broad reflection on the heyday of the dictatorship, in the 1950s, and its significance for the island and its inhabitants.

The novel follows three interwoven narrative lines.

title: Like Water for Chocolate
author: Laura Esquivel
synopsis:
Like Water for Chocolate is a novel by the Mexican writer Laura Esquivel. It was used as the basis for the film of the same name. It accompanies the stories with 12 traditional Mexican recipes, one for each month.

Almost 30 years after the publication of this work, the author Laura Esquível published the sequel El diario de Tita.

title: The Invention of Morel
author: Adolfo Bioy Casares
synopsis:
La invención de Morel is a novel by the Argentine writer Adolfo Bioy Casares.

The book tells the story of a fugitive who hides on an apparently deserted island. Little by little, the character begins to discover the island's curious inhabitants, falling in love with a young woman. Later, he discovers the truth about the inhabitants, the story of the ghost ship found near the island, and the invention of the scientist Morel.

title: Open Veins of Latin America
editionTitle: As Veias Abertas da América Latina
author: Eduardo Galeano
synopsis:
Open Veins of Latin America (in Spanish: Las venas abiertas de América Latina) is a book by the Uruguayan writer and journalist Eduardo Galeano.

In the book, from 1971, Galeano analyzes the history of Latin America from the period of European colonization to the contemporary age, arguing against the economic exploitation and political domination of the continent, first by Europeans and their descendants and, later, by the United States. The exploitation of the continent was accompanied by the constant shedding of indigenous blood. Because it exposed events of great impact for the understanding of the continent's history, the book was banned in Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Uruguay during those countries' military dictatorships. Years later, the author would state that "it was meant to be a book of political economy, but I did not have the necessary training and preparation" when writing it, later affirming that he did not regret having written it and that it was already "a stage in the past".

title: Things We Lost in the Fire
editionTitle: As Coisas que Perdemos no Fogo
author: Mariana Enriquez

title: Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair
editionTitle: Vinte Poemas de Amor e uma Canção Desesperada
author: Pablo Neruda
synopsis:
Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair (in Spanish: Veinte poemas de amor y una canción desesperada) is a book of poetry by the Chilean poet Pablo Neruda, in which the eroticism of poetry that celebrates the female body intersects with Neruda's love of nature. In these poems, the two planes frequently intersect, with a certain identification between the female body and the natural world (the landscapes, the earth, the sea...).

Neruda wrote these poems when he was about twenty years old, but they are among the most celebrated of his work. The book was published on June 15, 1924.

title: Crime and Punishment
author: Fiódor Dostoiévski
synopsis:
Crime and Punishment (in Russian, Преступление и наказание, Prestuplênie i nakazánie) is a novel by the writer Fiódor Dostoiévski, published in the literary magazine O Mensageiro Russo in twelve monthly installments over the course of 1866. It was later published in a single volume. It is Dostoiévski's second novel written after his ten-year exile in Siberia. Crime and Punishment is considered the first great novel of his "mature" period of writing. The novel is often cited as one of the greatest works of world literature.

The novel is based on a view of religion and existentialism with a predominant focus on the idea of attaining salvation through suffering, to which the author adds some questions concerning socialism and nihilism.

The main character, despite being a former law student, is an extremely poor man who lives in anguish under the shadow of doing something important. He divides individuals into ordinary and extraordinary, in an attempt to explain the breaking of rules for the sake of human progress. Following this precept, the character plans and carries out, amid a struggle with his conscience, the killing of a moneylender.

Before fleeing the scene of the crime, however, Raskólnikov also commits, against his will, driven only by the surprise of the situation, the murder of Lizavieta, the old moneylender's sister, for she had turned up at the place unexpectedly.

Raskólnikov steals some jewels, but never gets to enjoy this gain and, feeling remorseful, buries them under a stone.

After this event and its outcomes, the novel recounts in great detail the psychological dramas suffered by the perpetrator of the homicide.

title: Notes from Underground
author: Fiódor Dostoiévski
synopsis:
Notas do Subterrâneo (BR) (also translated as Notes from Underground or Notas do Subsolo) or Cadernos do Subterrâneo (PT) (in pre-reform Russian orthography: Записки изъ подполья and in post-reform orthography: Записки из подполья, transliterated: Zapíski iz pódpol'ia) is a novella by Fiódor Dostoiévski, published in 1864.

For Walter Kaufmann, this work makes Dostoiévski the chief forerunner of existentialism. It presents itself as an excerpt from the memoirs of a retired civil servant living in Saint Petersburg. The book, of about 150 pages (depending on the edition), is divided into two parts: the first, entitled "O Subterrâneo", contains 11 chapters, and the second part, "A Propósito da Neve Derretida", has 10 chapters.

title: The Idiot
author: Fiódor Dostoiévski
synopsis:
The Idiot (in Russian: Идиот, transl. Idiot) is one of Fiódor Dostoiévski's major novels. The novel was begun on 14 September 1867 in Geneva and was completed on 25 January 1869 in Florence. It was initially published in serial form, and not as a book, by the magazine O mensageiro russo, its first part having been published in March 1868 and its final chapters in February 1869.

At the time the novel was being written, Dostoiévski was in a very precarious physical and emotional state: his epileptic fits were constant, his debts were high and he was losing the little he had at gambling; moreover, he was under heavy pressure from his publishers and, as if that were not enough, his daughter Sônia was born and died prematurely.

Prince Míchkin is 26 years old when he returns to Petersburg, after spending several years in a sanatorium in Switzerland to treat his epilepsy. The plot then unfolds, its central theme resting on the problem of the pure, superior individual who, in a corrupt society, ends up being for everyone else an idiot, a misfit.

The hero of the novel, the humanist and epileptic Míchkin, is a blend of Christ and Don Quixote, whose boundless compassion will collide with the worldly dissoluteness of Rogójin and the maddening beauty of Nastácia Filíppovna. His goodness and the impact of his sincerity will reveal to the reader in tragic fashion how, in a world obsessed with money, power and conquests, the sanatorium ends up being the only place for a saint.

title: Anna Karenina
author: Liev Tolstói
synopsis:
Anna Karenina (Анна Каренина), or Ana Karênina, in some translations (Anna Karénina, in direct transliteration into the Latin alphabet), or Anna Karenina, according to the most recent Portuguese-language edition (published in Brazil by the publisher Cosac & Naify, in 2010), is a novel by the Russian writer Liev Tolstói. The story began to be published in the magazine Ruskii Véstnik (The Russian Messenger), between January 1875 and April 1877, but its ending was never published there owing to a disagreement between Tolstói and his editor, Mikhaíl Katkov, over the novel's ending. Therefore, the first complete edition of the text appeared in book form later in 1877.

It is one of the most outstanding works of literary realism. For Tolstói, it was his first true novel, and he regards his work War and Peace as more than a novel.

The plot revolves around the extramarital affair of the character who gives the work its title, an aristocrat of Tsarist Russia who, despite seeming to have everything (beauty, wealth, popularity and a beloved son), feels empty until she meets the impetuous officer Count Vronsky, with whom she begins a love affair. The story begins with Anna arriving at the home of her brother, Stepan, who is in a difficult situation with his wife, Dolly, and Anna sets about intervening in the situation, which is in some way a reflection of her own situation.

The officer Vronsky is willing to marry Anna Karenina as soon as she divorces her husband Alexey Karenin, a senior civil servant, but she is vulnerable to the pressures of Russian society, to her own insecurities and to Karenin's indecision. Although she and Vronsky flee to Italy, they find it hard to make friends. Back in Russia, she becomes increasingly anxious and isolated, while Vronsky carries on with his social life.

title: War and Peace
author: Liev Tolstói
synopsis:
War and Peace (in Russian: Война и мир) is a historical novel written by the Russian author Liev Tolstói and published between 1865 and 1869 in Russkii Vestnik, a periodical of the time. It is one of the most voluminous works in the history of world literature. The book narrates the history of Russia in the time of Napoleon Bonaparte (notably the Napoleonic wars in Russia). The richness and realism of its details, as well as its numerous psychological descriptions, mean that it is considered one of the greatest books in the History of Literature.

In the book Tolstói develops a fatalistic theory of History, in which free will would have no more than minor importance and in which all events would simply obey an irrefutable historical determinism.

The vastness of the work makes it difficult to summarize clearly and concisely. In addition, the author threads his narrative with many personal reflections that tend to break the rhythm of the reading. The action is set between 1805 and 1820, although, in reality, the essence of the work is concentrated in certain key moments: the War of the Third Coalition (1805), the Peace of Tilsit (1807) and finally the Russian Campaign (1812). However, it would be wrong to believe that "War and Peace" deals only with Franco-Russian relations of the period. Besides the battles of Schoengraben, Austerlitz and Borodino, Tolstói describes with great care and precision the thousands of nobles of tsarist Russia, addressing various themes then in vogue: the question of the serfs, secret societies and war. The characters of "War and Peace" are so abundant and richly detailed that it is hard to find a "hero" in the work, although Pierre Bézoukhov is the most recurrent character.

title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
author: Liev Tolstói
synopsis:
The Death of Ivan Ilyich (in Russian: Смерть Ивана Ильича, Smert' Ivana Ilyicha) is a novella by Liev Tolstói, first published in 1886. Considered one of the masterpieces of literature, it was written shortly after his religious conversion of the late 1870s, and in it the old writer criticizes family-centered conventions and social appearances, the superficiality and hypocrisy of high society.

"Generally ranked among the finest examples of the novella", The Death of Ivan Ilyich tells the story of a high court judge and his suffering and death from a terminal illness in nineteenth-century Russia.

The book begins by narrating the wake. It then goes back in time to show how Ivan Ilitch, a respected judge, meets his wife, whom he marries for money and for her beauty. After being offered the chance to become a judge in another city, Ivan Ilitch buys an apartment for himself, his wife and the son and daughter they have. Ivan moves first and starts the work of decorating the apartment the way he liked, but he falls and injures himself in the region of the kidney. At this point, Ivan Ilitch believes he has contracted an illness - which, however, is never diagnosed at any moment -, one that always revolves around a diseased kidney or intestine. Then the great lever of the narrative emerges: the continuation of life or death.

As time passes, the injury worsens, until the character reaches the point of no longer being able to leave the house: when he tries to go to work, he is no longer capable of performing his duties properly. Confined to the family environment, he comes to believe that a lie is being lived in his home, and that his family hides him from his friends.

title: The Master and Margarita
author: Mikhail Bulgákov
synopsis:
Мастер и Маргарита (in Russian; in Brazil: The Master and Margarita / in Portugal: Margarita e o Mestre) is a novel written by the Russian Mikhail Bulgákov (Михаил Афанасьевич Булгаков). The book has many plots, which are centred on a visit by the devil to Moscow in the early 1920s, at the height of the Stalinist era.

The Moscow of 1929 is visited by the devil, under the name of Woland (Воланд). In his retinue are Koroviev (Коровьев) or Fagote (Фагот, like the musical instrument, the bassoon), the enormous black cat Beemote or Behemot (Бегемот, in Russian, means both the biblical creature and hippopotamus), Azazello (Азазелло), Abadon (Абадонна) and the witch Hella (Гелла).

The epigraph is taken from Fausto, by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, which influences the whole book, and reads:

— "... but who are you, after all?"

— "I am part of the force that always wills evil, but always does good."

The book begins with the conversation between the chairman of MASSOLIT (a Soviet-style abbreviation for Moscow literary society, which can also be interpreted as literature for the masses), Mikhail Aleksandrovic Berlioz (Михаил Александрович Берлиоз) and the poet Ivan Nikolaevitch Poniriev (Иван Николаевич Понырев), who goes by the nickname Bezdomni (Бездомный, in Russian, means "homeless") about an anti-religious poem written by Biezdmomni.

title: Dead Souls
author: Nikolai Gógol
synopsis:
Dead Souls (in Russian: Мёртвые души) is a book by Nikolai Gogol, published in 1842. Although he supposedly finished the second part of the trilogy, Gogol destroyed it a few days before he died. The work, even without having been concluded, is commonly considered complete in its current form and represents an important milestone in Russian Literature.

The book follows the character Pável Ivánovitch Tchítchicov, a bureaucrat removed from public service for dishonesty, in his wanderings through the Russian countryside, in search of fortune. His contacts with the authorities of the small towns and with the landowners serve for the author to present a critical and scathing view of the semi-feudal system existing at the time, with the serfs living under a regime of slavery.

title: Madame Bovary
author: Gustave Flaubert

title: The Red and the Black
author: Stendhal
synopsis:
Le Rouge et le Noir (The Red and the Black, in French), subtitled Chronique du XIX siécle ("Chronicle of the 19th Century"), is a psychological historical novel in two volumes by the French writer Stendhal, published in 1830. It is often cited as the first realist novel, although it is imbued with a romantic sensibility and, unlike realist literature in general (Balzac in particular), is sparing in its descriptions of physical settings and people, preferring to delve into their psychological processes and taking the focus of the omniscient narrator to an extreme. The action takes place in France at the time of the Restoration, before the Revolution of 1830, supposedly between 1826 and 1830, and deals with a young man's attempts to rise in life, despite his plebeian birth, through a combination of talent, hard work, deceit and hypocrisy, only to find himself betrayed by his own passions.

The Red and the Black is the story of Julien Sorel, the ambitious son of a carpenter, in the fictional village of Verrières, in Franche-Comté.

The novel is made up of two parts: the first takes place in the provinces, as tutor to the Rênal children and then at the seminary in Besançon, the second in Paris as secretary to the Marquis de La Mole.

The first book introduces Julien Sorel, who preferred to spend his time reading or dreaming of the glory of Napoleão's army rather than working as a carpenter in his father's yard alongside his brothers. Julien Sorel ends up becoming an acolyte of the parish priest Chélan, who later secures him a position as tutor to the children of the mayor of Verrières, Mr. de Rênal.

Sorel, who appears to be a pious and austere cleric, in reality has little interest in the Bible beyond its literary value and the way he can use memorized passages to impress important people (passages which, incidentally, he learned in Latin).

After his arrival at the Rênal home, Julien Sorel falls in love with Mrs. de Rênal (a shy and naive woman). Mrs.

title: Les Misérables
author: Victor Hugo
synopsis:
Les Misérables (Les Misérables) is a novel by Victor Hugo published in 1862 that has given rise to many adaptations, in film and many other media. In this emblematic novel of French literature, which describes the lives of poor people in Paris and in provincial France in the nineteenth century, the author focuses more particularly on the fate of the convict Jean Valjean.

The novel sets out Hugo's political philosophy, portraying social inequality and the resulting misery and, on the other hand, work as performing a beneficial function for the individual and for society. It also portrays the conflict in the relationship with the State, whether through the arbitrary action of the policeman or through the attitude of the revolutionary obsessed with justice.

The story takes place in nineteenth-century France between two great battles: the Battle of Waterloo (1815) and the riots of June 1832. From this follows, over five volumes, the life of Jean Valjean, a convict set free, until his death. Around him revolve a number of people who lend their names to the different volumes of the novel, bearing witness to the misery of that century, the wretched poverty of: Fantine, Cosette, Marius Pontmercy, but also Thénardier (including Éponine and Gavroche) and Inspector Javert. The book portrays nineteenth-century French society and shows the socioeconomic panorama of the poorest part of the population.

In this volume two destinies are intertwined: that of Fantine and that of Jean Valjean.

Jean Valjean, having served 19 years in the galleys (five for stealing a loaf of bread for his sister and her seven children, who were starving, and fourteen more for numerous escape attempts), has just been released. Valjean is shunned by everyone he meets for being an ex-convict, and is turned out of every inn.

title: The Count of Monte Cristo
author: Alexandre Dumas
synopsis:
The Count of Monte Cristo (from the French: Le Comte de Monte-Cristo) is a French adventure novel written by Alexandre Dumas (père), in collaboration with Auguste Maquet, completed in 1844. Initially published as a serial from 1844 to 1846. Loosely based on the life of Pierre Picaud, the work tells the story of the promising sailor Edmond Dantès, unjustly imprisoned for a crime he did not commit. In prison, he befriends a learned abbé, who shows him the way to an immense and ancient fortune, which Edmond uses, disguised as the Count of Monte Cristo, to take revenge on those who betrayed him.

Together with Os Três Mosqueteiros, it is considered one of Dumas's most popular works, and it is frequently included in lists of the best-selling books of all time.

"A novel of Destiny. Victim and avenger, Edmond Dantès, the central character, himself embodies destiny.

The story of a good man who is robbed of his freedom and his love. In captivity he strikes up a friendship with Abbé Faria, who offers him help to escape.

A man who will return covered in riches, a merciless avenger, beyond all human or divine law."

Edmond Dantès, a bold but naive 19-year-old sailor, is arrested on a false charge of being a spy for Napoleon Bonaparte, in 1815, for having gone to the island of Elba and received a letter from him in his exile. In truth, he was the victim of a plot among three interested parties:

the judge de Villefort, son of the addressee of Napoleon's letter, who, even while attesting to his innocence, wanted to silence him;

his friend, Danglars, who coveted the post of captain of the ship, since Dantès had been given the post on merit;

Fernand Mondego, a Catalan interested in Mercédès (Dantès's fiancée), who envied Dantès for being the object of her love, and who became the future husband of the Catalan woman (who, however, never forgot him).

title: In Search of Lost Time
author: Marcel Proust
synopsis:
In Search of Lost Time (from the French À la recherche du temps perdu) is a novelistic work by Marcel Proust written between 1908-1909 and 1922, published between 1913 and 1927 in seven volumes, the last three posthumously.

The seven volumes that make up the work are (the Portuguese titles are those of the Portuguese edition from Relógio d'Água, published between 2003 and 2005 in a translation by Pedro Tamen):

Du côté de chez Swann (Do Lado de Swann, 1913)

À l'ombre des jeunes filles en fleurs (À sombra das raparigas em flor, 1919, received the Goncourt prize for that year)

Le Côté de Guermantes (O caminho de Guermantes, published in 2 volumes in 1920 and 1921)

Sodome et Gomorrhe (Sodoma e Gomorra, published in 2 volumes in 1921-1922)

La Prisonnière (A prisioneira, published posthumously in 1923)

Albertine disparue (A Fugitiva - Albertine desaparecida, published posthumously in 1927) (original title: La Fugitive)

Le Temps retrouvé (O tempo reencontrado, published posthumously in 1927)

For its ambitions (to reach the substance of time in order to escape its law, so as to try to grasp, through writing, the essence of a reality hidden in the unconscious "recreated by our thought"), its disproportion (nearly 3500 pages in the pocket collection), and its influence on literary works and on the research to come (

title: The Stranger
author: Albert Camus
synopsis:
L'Étranger (French: ) is a 1942 novella by the French author Albert Camus. Its theme and outlook are often cited as examples of Camus's philosophy, absurdism coupled with existentialism, although Camus personally rejected the latter label.

The title character is Meursault, an indifferent French settler in Algeria described as "a citizen of France domiciled in North Africa, a man of the Mediterranean, an homme du midi, yet one who hardly partakes of the traditional Mediterranean culture". Weeks after his mother's funeral, he kills an Arab man in French Algiers, who was involved in a conflict with one of Meursault's neighbors. Meursault is tried and sentenced to death. The story is divided into two parts, presenting Meursault's first-person narrative view before and after the murder, respectively.

Meursault learns of the death of his mother, who lives in a nursing home in the countryside. He takes time off work to attend the funeral, but shows none of the signs of mourning or grief that the people around him expect from someone in his situation. When asked if he wishes to see the body, he declines, and he smokes and drinks coffee at the vigil beside his mother's coffin the night before the burial. Most of his comments to the reader at this point are about his observations of the elderly attendees of the vigil and the funeral, which take place on an unbearably hot day.

Back in Algiers, Meursault meets Marie, a former secretary at his firm. The two become reacquainted, go swimming, watch a comedy film and begin a sexual relationship. All of this happens the day after his mother's funeral.

Over the next few days, Meursault helps Raymond Sintès, a neighbor and friend who is rumored to be a pimp (procurer) but says he works in a warehouse, to take revenge on a Moorish girlfriend whom he suspects of accepting gifts and money from another man.

title: The Plague
author: Albert Camus
synopsis:
The Plague (La Peste), the magnum opus of Albert Camus, is a novel published in 1947, considered a classic of existentialist and absurdist literature. The book tells the story of workers who discover solidarity during a plague that ravages the city of Oran in Algeria, and it can be interpreted as a metaphor for the horrors of the Second World War.

Camus drew inspiration from the cholera epidemic that wiped out a large proportion of Oran's population in 1849, but set the novel in the 1940s. Oran and its surroundings were struck by epidemics several times before Camus published his novel. According to an academic study, Oran was overrun by the bubonic plague in 1556 and 1678, but all the later outbreaks had a much smaller impact than the one described in the novel.

title: Nausea
author: Jean-Paul Sartre
synopsis:
Nausea (in the original French, La nausée) is an existentialist novel by the philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre, published in 1938 and written when Sartre was teaching at the lycée in Le Havre. It is one of Sartre's best-known works.

This book begins in the form of a diary, and follows the day-to-day life of the historian Antoine Roquentin.

title: The Little Prince
author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
synopsis:
Le Petit Prince (French pronunciation: ) (Portugal: O Principezinho; Brazil: The Little Prince) is a novella by the French writer and aristocrat aviator Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, originally published in English and French in April 1943 in the United States.

During the Second World War, Saint-Exupéry was exiled to North America. Amid personal upheavals and failing health, he produced almost half of the works for which he would be remembered, including the tale of loneliness, friendship, love and loss, in the form of a young prince who fell to Earth. A memoir written by the author recounted his aviation experiences in the Sahara desert, and it is thought that he used these experiences as the basis for the novella.

The story begins with the narrator describing his recollections, in which at the age of 6 he made a drawing of a boa constrictor that had swallowed an elephant. When he asked the adults what they saw in his drawing, they all thought the boy had drawn a hat. Whenever he corrected people about his drawing, he was always told that he needed a more serious and mature hobby. The narrator then laments the lack of creativity shown by adults.

Without encouragement and disappointed by the reactions, he gives up on a career as a painter and becomes an aviator. During a flight, his plane breaks down in the Sahara desert. On waking, after the accident, he comes across a boy whom the author describes as having golden hair and a yellow scarf, who asks him to draw a sheep. The narrator then shows him his old drawing of the elephant inside a boa constrictor and, to his surprise, the boy interprets it correctly, although he is dissatisfied because he still wanted the drawing of a sheep.

title: The Metamorphosis
author: Franz Kafka
synopsis:
The Metamorphosis (in German: Die Verwandlung) is a novella of fantastic literature, fiction and existentialist themes written by Franz Kafka in 1912 and first published in 1915. Considered one of the most important works of twentieth-century literature, the narrative became a landmark of the so-called "Kafkaesque" style, characterized by the presence of the absurd, alienation, psychological oppression and the feeling of estrangement in the face of reality.

The work tells the story of Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman who supports his family financially and lives trapped in an exhausting routine of work and responsibilities. One day, Gregor wakes up inexplicably transformed into a monstrous insect, an event that triggers a profound change in his relationship with his family and with society.

In this work, Kafka describes a traveling salesman by the name of Gregor Samsa, who gives up his own wishes and desires in order to support his family and pay off his parents' debt. One morning, Gregor wakes up metamorphosed into a monstrous insect. Kafka describes this insect as something resembling a giant cockroach. In its first moments, the book describes Gregor's initial difficulties in his new form. An irony present in this passage of the book is that Gregor is not worried about his transformation, but rather about the fact that he is late for work.

When Gregor, after much difficulty, manages to open the door, everyone is frightened, including the manager, who runs off. His father advances on him, forcing him back into his room. After this episode, he is dismissed, his family rejects him and his only company is himself. Only at certain moments does his sister show some compassion for him.

As the story unfolds, the author narrates the anguish of Gregor, who, unable to do anything, hears his family discussing among themselves how to support themselves, since their only source of income was gone.

title: The Trial
author: Franz Kafka
synopsis:
The Trial (in the original German, Der Prozess) is a novel by the Czech writer Franz Kafka, which tells the story of Josef K., who wakes up one morning and is prosecuted and subjected to a long and incomprehensible trial for an unspecified crime.

According to Max Brod, a personal friend of Kafka, the book remained unfinished as it was when Kafka handed him the manuscripts, in 1920. After his death, Brod edited The Trial into what he judged to be a coherent novel and published it in 1925.

On the morning of his thirtieth birthday, Josef K., the chief clerk of a bank, is unexpectedly arrested by two unidentified agents from an unspecified agency, for an unspecified crime. However, Josef is not imprisoned, but left "free" and instructed to await directions from the Committee of Affairs. His landlady, Frau Grubach, tries to console Josef about the trial, but insinuates that the proceedings may be related to an immoral relationship with his neighbor Fräulein Bürstner. Josef visits Bürstner to vent his worries and then kisses her.

A few days later, Josef discovers that Fräulein Montag, a lodger from another room, has moved into Fräulein Bürstner's room. He suspects that this maneuver is intended to keep him away from Bürstner. Josef is ordered to appear at the court's address the following Sunday, without being told the time or the exact room. After a period of exploring, Josef finds the court in the attic.

title: The Castle
author: Franz Kafka
synopsis: The Castle (Das Schloss in the original) is a novel by Franz Kafka, written over about six months in 1922, but released only posthumously. The book consists of the story of a land surveyor called K. (the same surname as the protagonist of the book The Trial) who is summoned by a count from an unspecified place to render his services. However, try as he might, he cannot get into the castle, remaining in the village outside the castle throughout the narration. The monologues in the book are numerous (the book has more than 400 pages) and the characters often contradict themselves or offer varied interpretations of the same fact, which creates an atmosphere of confusion or of a simple lack of information (for example, the second letter from the castle official, Klamm, addressed to the land surveyor K).

title: The Magic Mountain
author: Thomas Mann
synopsis:
The Magic Mountain (in the original German Der Zauberberg) is a book written by Thomas Mann in 1924. One of the most influential novels of 20th-century world literature, it was important to Mann's winning of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929. It is a classic example of the literature that Germans classify as Bildungsroman or, in the term used in Portuguese, a novel of formation.

About the work, Malcolm Bradbury writes:

Sometimes described as a book without a plot, the work deals with the story of a young student of naval engineering, a German from Hamburg, named Hans Castorp. He visits his cousin Joachim Ziemssen at a sanatorium for the treatment of respiratory diseases located in Davos, in the Swiss Alps, shortly before the start of the First World War. Despite being sent to the sanatorium only for a visit and to treat anemia, Hans Castorp gradually shows signs of having pulmonary tuberculosis and ends up extending his visit to the sanatorium for months and years, as his departure is always postponed because of the illness.

During this period, Castorp, little by little, distances himself from life "in the flatland" and gains what he calls freedom from normal life. He detaches himself from time, career and family and is drawn to illness, introspection and death. At the same time, he matures and comes into deeper contact with politics, art, culture, religion, philosophy, human frailty (including death and suicide), the subjective nature of time (one of the most important themes of the work) and love.

title: Death in Venice
author: Thomas Mann
synopsis:
Death in Venice (in the original German, Der Tod in Venedig) is a novella written by Thomas Mann and first published in 1912.

In A Death in Venice, Thomas Mann offers complex and profound writing, in which almost every paragraph can be read in several ways. By contrast, the plot is practically nonexistent: a middle-aged man travels to Venice, falls platonically in love with an extremely attractive young Polish boy and dies without ever having exchanged a single word with him.

During a walk in Munich, Gustav von Aschenbach — an established author whose work is known for its discipline and formal perfection — encounters a strange fellow who leaves him somewhat shaken, and he decides to break with his routine and set off on a journey. First he goes to Pula, on the Austro-Hungarian coast, but then decides to continue on to Venice. At his Venetian hotel on the Lido, he comes across an adolescent of extreme beauty, from a Polish family: the young Tadzio. The hot and humid weather affects the health of Aschenbach, who decides to leave, but on the way to the station he begins to regret it, and when he discovers that his luggage has been sent to the wrong train and that he will have to wait for its return, he is pleased to be able to remain near Tadzio. Although he watches Tadzio obsessively, he never dares to speak to him; at most they exchange a furtive, fleeting glance with one another.

title: Steppenwolf
author: Hermann Hesse
synopsis:
Brazil: Steppenwolf / Portugal: O Lobo das Estepes (in the original, Der Steppenwolf) is a book by Hermann Hesse, published in 1927. It is considered one of the best of Hesse's books and one of the most representative novels of German literature.

It was the first of Hesse's books to be translated into Portuguese and published in Brazil, as early as 1935, during the author's lifetime, in a version by Augusto de Souza for the publisher Cultura Brasileira, of São Paulo (Coleção literatura moderna). Another translation, by Ivo Barroso, was published by the publisher Civilização Brasileira in 1968 and successively reissued by other publishers.

The book tells the story of Harry Haller, an outsider, a fifty-year-old misanthrope, alcoholic and intellectualized, anguished and seeing no way out of his tormented condition, who calls himself a "steppe wolf". But some unexpected and fantastic incidents lead him slowly, yet decisively, to awaken from his long sleep: he meets Hermínia, Maria and the musician Pablo. And then the story unfolds in a surprising way.

The character of Harry Haller was inspired by the Swiss sculptor Hermann Haller, a friend of Hermann Hesse.

title: Siddhartha
author: Hermann Hesse
synopsis:
Siddharta is a novel written by Hermann Hesse, one of the greatest German writers. Winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1946. It was first published in 1922 and recounts a passage from his life and thought during his stay in India in 1910, inspired by the traditional account of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha.

The book is essentially about the search for spiritual fullness, and the attainment of states in which the human mind is absolutely complete and whole.

Siddharta is a promising young man who lives in a Brahmin village. Talented, slender, eager for knowledge, Siddharta was adored by everyone. He was advanced in the Brahmin teachings and everyone saw a brilliant future in him. One sensed in him a sage, a priest, a prince among the Brahmins. And the one who adored him most was his friend Govinda.

But for himself, Siddharta had no joy. For himself he was not a source of pleasure. He harbored discontent deep within him. He felt that the love he received from everyone would not always have the strength to gladden him. He also felt that he had already absorbed the main Brahmin teachings, but they were not enough.

He questioned the validity of the rituals: "The ablutions, beneficial as they might be, were only water; they did not take the sin away from him; they did not quench the thirst of the spirit; they did not relieve the anguish of the heart. Excellent were the sacrifices and the invocations of the gods - but what good did all that do him? Did the sacrifices bring happiness? And as for the gods: was it really Prajapati who created the world? And not the Átman? He, the only one, the indivisible?"...

title: Demian
author: Hermann Hesse
synopsis:
Demian is a coming-of-age novel written by Hermann Hesse, winner of the 1946 Nobel Prize in Literature. Considered by many critics to be Hesse's major work, Demian shows the influence that Nietzsche's writings had on him and the application of his knowledge of psychoanalysis in crafting the ethical drama and the enormous mental confusion of a young man who becomes aware of the fragility of morality, the family and the State. Demian was first published under the pseudonym "Emil Sinclair", the name of the story's narrator, but Hesse later revealed that he was the author.

The book tells the story of a young man - Emil Sinclair, protagonist and narrator - raised by very pious parents, who suddenly finds himself in a world quite different from the one preached by his parents and grandparents. Tormented by the lack of answers to the questions he asks about his existence, he begins to seek his answers through introspection. Torn between the ideal world and the real one, with their interpretations (a bright, paternal world, associated with his parents' ideas and their home, and a dark, cold world, outside his parents' home and with values foreign to theirs), Sinclair experiences both, through confrontation with his own conceptions, in an attempt to find his true personality. Traveling this dangerous path, influenced by Max Demian, a precocious and captivating classmate, Sinclair tastes crime, friendship and uncertainty - surprises that give rise to the discoveries of his adolescent life. Sinclair then rebels against social conventions and discovers not only the sweet taste of independence but also his power to do good or evil.

title: The Sorrows of Young Werther
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
synopsis:
The Sorrows of Young Werther, or in the original German Die Leiden des jungen Werthers (1774), is a novel by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe. A founding landmark of Romanticism, considered by many to be a masterpiece of world literature, it is one of the author's first works, autobiographical in tone — although Goethe took care that names and places were changed and, naturally, some fictitious parts added, such as the ending.

In this book, the supposed Werther sends letters, over a long period, to the narrator, who, in footnotes, states that names and places have been changed.

Werther is marked by a deep, stormy and ill-fated passion. Werther sees his feelings returned but suffers from the impossibility of consummating them, for the object of his love, the young Charlotte, had been promised to another man. There are strong indications that the work contains autobiographical details, for Goethe had a relationship of close friendship with Charlotte von Stein, who was married to another man. For Werther, life has meaning only with his beloved. With every gesture, every dance and even amid slaps, Werther falls more and more in love with her.

title: Faust
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
synopsis:
Faust (in German: Faust) is a tragic poem by the German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, divided into two parts. It is written as a play with rhymed dialogue, intended more to be read than to be staged. It is considered one of the great masterpieces of German literature.

The creation of the work occupied Goethe's entire life, though not continuously. The first version was composed in 1775, but it was only a sketch known as Urfaust (Proto-Faust). Another sketch was made in 1791, titled Faust, ein Fragment (Faust, um fragmento), and it too was never published.

title: Pride and Prejudice
author: Jane Austen
synopsis:
Pride and Prejudice (br/pt: Pride and Prejudice) is a novel by the British writer Jane Austen. First published in 1813, although it had been completed in 1797, before the author turned 21, in Steventon, Hampshire, where Jane lived with her parents. Originally called First Impressions, it was never published under that title; when revising her writings, Jane retitled the work and published it as Pride and Prejudice. Austen may have had in mind the final chapter of Fanny Burney's novel Cecilia, called "Pride and Prejudice".

The story shows the way the character Elizabeth Bennet deals with problems related to education, culture, morals and marriage in the aristocratic society of early 19th-century England.

At the beginning of the novel, Mr. Bingley, a young and healthy gentleman, rents a country estate called Netherfield, near the Bennets. He arrives in town accompanied by his sisters, Caroline Bingley and Louisa Hurst, his brother-in-law, Mr. Hurst, and a friend, Mr. Darcy. While Bingley is well received by the community, Darcy keeps a more distant and distrustful attitude toward the country people. Bingley and Jane Bennet begin a relationship, despite the inappropriate and embarrassing interference of Mrs. Bennet and the opposition of Bingley's sisters, who consider Jane socially inferior. Meanwhile, Elizabeth is "wounded" by Darcy's rejection at a local dance, and decides to counter Darcy's indifference with her sharpness and wit.

Elizabeth, for her part, begins a friendship with Mr. Wickham, an officer who is on hostile terms with Darcy. Wickham tells her that he was mistreated by him, and this becomes one of the reasons why Elizabeth hates Darcy. Ironically, but without her knowing it, Darcy gradually begins to take an interest in Elizabeth.

During this period Mr.

title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Brontë
synopsis:
Jane Eyre is a novel by the British writer Charlotte Brontë published in 1847. The book, which had as its subtitle a biography, was originally released in London, by the publisher Smith, Elder & Co., Cornhill, on October 16, 1847, in 3 volumes. Nowadays the novel is sold in a single volume. Jane Eyre was written by Brontë under the pseudonym Currer Bell.

The novel is considered a landmark of the Bildungsroman genre, which characterizes the so-called "coming-of-age novels": following the journey of a protagonist throughout her life. It presents several elements of Gothic literature, such as the setting of the story, the buildings, the mystery surrounding the plot, made up of secrets from the past, and the tragic events that surround these characters.

Jane Eyre is the fictional autobiography of the main character. The narrative follows the character Jane Eyre from childhood to adulthood. Over the course of her journey, she lives in several houses that were important to the development of her personality and her moral values. At first, Jane is introduced as a ten-year-old girl, wild and disobedient, who lives in the mansion of Gateshead Hall under the guardianship of her aunt. After a confrontation with her, Jane is sent to a school, Lowood, where she experiences her first moments of happiness. Her education is strict and she goes through several transformations during the eight years she lives at the institution. Having graduated and after working for two years as a teacher at the same school, Jane decides to follow other paths, accepting a position as governess to young Adèle, at the house of Thornfield Hall, which belongs to Mr. Edward Rochester. It is at Thornfield Hall that the story reaches its climax. Jane will be confronted by ethical and moral dilemmas and will have to make decisions based on everything she has lived through and matured from in the previous years.

title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë
synopsis:
Wuthering Heights (translated into Portuguese as Wuthering Heights, O Monte dos Vendavais or also Colina dos Vendavais), released in 1847, was the only novel by the British writer Emily Brontë. Now considered a classic of English literature, it received harsh criticism in the 19th century.

It has had several adaptations for television and film, one of them directed by the British filmmaker A. V. Bramble. In music, it gave rise to an album by the band Genesis: Wind and Wuthering: the album's title is an allusion to Wuthering Heights, and the track "Afterglow" to the characters Heathcliff and Catherine. It also inspired a hit song, "Wuthering Heights", written and performed by Kate Bush for the album The Kick Inside, from 1978, and later re-recorded by the band Angra, on their album Angels Cry, from 1993.

In 1801, Mr. Lockwood, the new tenant of the Granja da Cruz dos Tordos estate, located in Yorkshire, visits Heathcliff, his landlord, at his remote property on the moor: the Morro dos Ventos Uivantes. During his visit, he meets the reserved Cathy Linton, the servant Joseph, and Hareton, an illiterate young man who appears to be another servant. Lockwood describes them all as taciturn people and the setting as inhospitable. Trapped at the property by the storm, Lockwood reads the diary of the former occupant of the room he is staying in, Catherine Earnshaw, and has a nightmare in which Catherine's ghost begs to be let in through the window. Heathcliff wakes to Lockwood's screams, which leave him distraught.

Lockwood chooses to brave the snow to return to the Granja da Cruz dos Tordos, falls ill and finds himself confined to bed. During his recovery, the housekeeper Ellen "Nelly" Dean narrates the family's story.

Thirty years before Lockwood's tenancy, the Earnshaw couple live at the Morro dos Ventos Uivantes with their two children, Hindley and Catherine, and a housekeeper — Nelly.

title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens
synopsis:
Great Expectations (Great Expectations) is a book written by Charles Dickens, which tells the story of Philip Pirrip. It is divided into three volumes and has been adapted for film and television several times.

It was written during the Victorian era.

The story of Great Expectations takes place between 1812, when the protagonist was 7 years old, and the winter of 1840.

It narrates the life of Pip (Philip Pirip), a boy who is granted a fortune in order to become a gentleman without the hard work or the aristocratic source of income required for such a role. Early in life, he helps a convict, Abel Magwitch, who, after being deported to Australia, repays his young benefactor with large sums of money; as the lawyer involved in the case says nothing when handing over the money, Pip believes it to be the doing of an old lady, Miss Havisham. Magwitch later returns clandestinely to London, where he is poorly received by Pip, since everything about him reeks of delinquency and unpleasantness.

In the end, however, Pip is reconciled with Magwitch and his reality; he comes to acknowledge Magwitch - hunted, imprisoned and mortally ill - as a kind of father, neither denying nor rejecting him, even though Magwitch is in fact unacceptable (at that time), coming from Australia, a penal colony intended for the rehabilitation, but not the repatriation, of banished English criminals.

title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
subjects: British fiction (fictional works by one author)
synopsis:
Frankenstein; ou, O Prometeu Moderno (Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus, in the original English), better known simply as Frankenstein, is a Gothic horror novel inspired by the Romantic movement, written by Mary Shelley, a British writer born in London. The book is often considered the first work of science fiction in history, although this is still an open debate. The novel tells the story of Victor Frankenstein, a student of natural sciences who builds a monster. Mary Shelley wrote the story when she was only 19, between 1816 and 1817, and the work was first published in 1818, with no credit to the author in the first edition. Today the revised version of the book's third edition, published in 1831, is usually regarded as the definitive one.

The novel is narrated through letters written by Captain Robert Walton to his sister while he is in command of a nautical expedition seeking to find a passage to the North Pole. When his ship becomes trapped in the ice, the crew sights Victor Frankenstein's creature traveling on a sled pulled by dogs. Next, the sea grows rough, freeing the ship, and on an ice floe they sight the dying Doctor Victor Frankenstein. On being taken aboard, Frankenstein begins to tell his story to Captain Walton, who reproduces it in the letters to his sister. Captain Walton's story is called a frame narrative (sometimes also a frame story), in which one story contains another.

Victor Frankenstein begins by telling of his childhood in Geneva as the son of a Swiss aristocrat and his adolescence as a dedicated and talented self-taught student. At this point, he introduces Elizabeth, raised as his adoptive sister, and Henry Clerval, his lifelong friend.

title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker
synopsis:
Dracula (in English: Dracula) is a Gothic horror novel published in 1897, written by the Irish author Bram Stoker. As an epistolary novel, the narrative is told through letters, diaries and newspaper articles. It has no single protagonist, but opens with the lawyer Jonathan Harker taking a business trip to stay at the castle of a Transylvanian nobleman, Count Dracula. Harker escapes the castle after discovering that Dracula is a vampire, and the Count moves to England and plagues the seaside town of Whitby. A small group, led by Abraham Van Helsing, hunts Dracula and, in the end, kills him.

Dracula was written mainly in the 1890s. Stoker produced more than a hundred pages of notes for the novel, drawing extensively on the history and culture of Transylvania.

Jonathan Harker, a newly qualified English lawyer, visits Count Dracula at his castle in the Carpathian Mountains to help the Count buy a house near London. Ignoring the Count's warning, Harker wanders through the castle at night and encounters three vampire women; Dracula rescues Harker and gives the women a small child tied up inside a bag. Harker wakes up in bed; soon afterwards, Dracula leaves the castle, abandoning him to the women. Harker escapes with his life and ends up delirious in a Budapest hospital. Dracula takes a ship called the Demeter to England with boxes of earth from his castle. The captain's log recounts the disappearance of the crew until he alone remains, tied to the helm to keep the ship on course. An animal resembling a large dog is seen leaping ashore when the ship runs aground at Whitby.

Lucy Westenra's letter to her best friend, Harker's fiancée Mina Murray, describes her marriage proposals from Dr. John Seward, Quincey Morris, and Arthur Holmwood. Lucy accepts Holmwood, but they all remain friends.

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
author: Oscar Wilde
synopsis:
The Picture of Dorian Gray (in English: The Picture of Dorian Gray) is a philosophical and Gothic horror novel by the Irish writer and playwright Oscar Wilde. It was first published as a serialized story in July 1890 in the monthly Lippincott's Monthly Magazine; the editors feared the story was indecent and, without Wilde's knowledge, removed five hundred words before publication. Despite the censorship, The Picture of Dorian Gray still offended the moral sensibilities of British literary critics, some of whom said that Oscar Wilde deserved to be prosecuted for violating the laws protecting public morality. In response, Wilde aggressively defended his novel and his art in correspondence with the British press.

The Picture of Dorian Gray opens on a sunny summer day in Victorian-era England, where Lord Henry Wotton, an opinionated man, watches the sensitive artist Basil Hallward painting the portrait of Dorian Gray, his host, and a handsome young man who is Basil's ultimate muse. After hearing Lord Henry's hedonistic worldview, Dorian begins to think that beauty is the only aspect of life worth pursuing, and wishes that Basil's portrait would grow old in his place.

Under Lord Henry's hedonistic influence, Dorian fully explores his sensuality. He discovers the actress Sibyl Vane, who performs in Shakespeare plays in a dingy working-class theater. Dorian approaches and courts her, and soon proposes marriage. The enamored Sibyl calls him "Prince Charming", and swoons with the happiness of being loved, but her protective brother, James, a sailor, warns that if her "Prince Charming" were to hurt her, he would kill him.

Dorian invites Basil and Lord Henry to see Sibyl perform in a play.

title: Mrs. Dalloway
author: Virginia Woolf
synopsis:
Mrs. Dalloway is a historical novel by Virginia Woolf published on 14 May 1925 that narrates a day in the life of Clarissa Dalloway, a fictional socialite living in post-First World War England. It is one of Woolf's most famous novels.

Created from two short stories, Mrs. Dalloway in Bond Streed and the unfinished The Prime Minister, the novel shows Clarissa's preparations for a party she will host that evening. With an interior perspective, the story moves through the future and the past in time and in and out of the characters' minds to build a picture of Clarissa's life and of her interwar social structure. It was included in The Guardian's list of the 100 best books of all time in May 2002 and in Time's October 2005 list of the 100 best English-language books written since 1923.

Clarissa Dalloway walks through London during the morning, getting ready to host a party that evening. The day's fine weather reminds her of her youth spent in the countryside, at Bourton, and makes her question her choice of husband; she married the reliable Richard Dalloway, rather than the enigmatic and demanding Peter Walsh, without having had "the option" of being with Sally Seton. Peter rekindles these conflicts by paying a visit that morning.

Septimus Warren Smith, a First World War veteran suffering from shell shock, spends his day in the park with his Italian wife Lucrezia, where Peter Walsh observes them. Septimus has frequent visitations and indecipherable hallucinations, most of them related to his great friend Evans, who died in the war.

Later that day, after being recommended for involuntary commitment to a psychiatric hospital, he commits suicide by jumping out of the window.

Clarissa's party that evening is a slow success. It is attended by most of the characters she has met in the book, including people from her past.

title: The Waves
author: Virginia Woolf
synopsis:
The Waves is a novel by Virginia Woolf published in 1931. It is Woolf's most experimental work, consisting of soliloquies spoken by the book's six characters: Bernard, Susan, Rhoda, Neville, Jinny and Louis. Percival, the seventh character, is also important, even though the reader never hears him speak for himself. The soliloquies that span the characters' lives are broken up by nine brief third-person interludes detailing a coastal scene at varying stages of a day, from sunrise to sunset.

As the six characters or "voices" speak in turn, Woolf explores the concepts of individuality, self and community. Each character is distinct, although together they compose a form around the central silence of consciousness. Bernard is a storyteller, always in search of an elusive and apt phrase (some critics see Woolf's friend E. M. Forster as an inspiration); Louis is an outsider, who seeks acceptance and success (some critics see T. S. Eliot, whom Woolf knew well, in Louis); Neville (who was probably partly based on another of Woolf's friends, Lytton Strachey) desires love, pursuing a series of men, each of whom becomes the present object of his transcendent love; Jinny is a socialite, whose understanding of the world corresponds to the beauty of her body; Susan flees the city in favor of the countryside, where she grapples with the emotions and doubts of motherhood; and Rhoda is marked by insecurity and anxiety, always rejecting and indicting human compromise, always seeking solitude (to that end, Rhoda quotes Percy Bysshe Shelley's poem The Ques

title: A Room of One's Own
author: Virginia Woolf
synopsis:
A Room of One's Own (Brazil: A Room of One's Own / Portugal: Um Quarto Só para Si) is an essay by Virginia Woolf published on October 24, 1929. The essay was based on a series of lectures delivered in October 1928 at Newnham College and Girton College, two women's colleges at Cambridge University.

Although the essay makes explicit use of a fictional narrator and a narrative to explore both women writers and fictional characters, the initial manuscript, titled Woman and Fiction and published by The Forum in March 1929, and later its final version, are considered non-fiction. The essay is generally seen as a feminist text, and the construction of its argument makes explicit the demand for a literal and figurative space for women writers within a literary tradition dominated by patriarchy.

The essay's title comes from Woolf's opinion that "a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction". Woolf argues that women have been prevented from writing because of their poverty, and that economic freedom would bring women the freedom to write; "In the first place, to have a room of her own... was out of the question, unless her parents were exceptionally rich or very noble". The title also refers to any author's need for poetic license and personal freedom in order to create art.

The essay examines whether women were capable of producing – and more: whether they were capable of producing work of the quality of William Shakespeare's – given the limitations imposed on women writers both in the past and in the present.

Woolf's father, Sir Leslie Stephen, in keeping with the thinking of the time, believed that only the boys of the family should be sent to school. Woolf offered herself as an example, since, as her father did not believe in investing in his daughters' education, she was left without any experience of formal schooling.

title: Ulysses
author: James Joyce
synopsis:
Ulysses (Ulysses in the original) is a novel by the Irish writer James Joyce. It was composed between 1914 and 1921 in Trieste, Zurich and Paris, and published the following year in the last of these cities. Because it describes, at various points, aspects of human physiology then considered unpublishable, the book was censored in several countries, such as the United States and the United Kingdom.

Ulysses adapts Homer's Odisseia by condensing the adventurous voyage of Odysseus across the Hellenic world, on his return from the Trojan War to the island of which he was king, Ithaca, where his wife, Queen Penelope, had remained, into 18 hours of the "voyage" through Dublin of the advertising agent Leopold Bloom on June 16, 1904 and the early hours of the following day. It is James Joyce's masterpiece.

Joyce divided Ulysses into 18 episodes. At first sight, much of the book may seem unstructured and chaotic; Joyce once said that he had "put into it so many enigmas and puzzles that they will keep the professors busy for centuries arguing over what I meant", which would lead to the novel's immortality. The two analytical schemas that Stuart Gilbert and Herbert Gorman published after the release of Ulysses to clear Joyce of the charges of obscenity made the links to the Odisseia clear, and also explained the work's internal structure.

Each episode of Ulysses has a theme, a technique and a correspondence between its characters and those of the Odisseia. The original text did not have these episode titles, and the correspondences with the text of the Odisseia resulted from the analytical schemas of Linati and Gilbert. These schematic tables for interpreting Ulysses were originally owed to Joyce himself, with later additions by Gilbert, Gorman and Linati, analyzing the entire structure of the work.

title: The Great Gatsby
author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
synopsis:
The Great Gatsby (The Great Gatsby) is a novel written by the American author F. Scott Fitzgerald. First published on April 10, 1925, the story takes place in New York and in the town of Long Island during the summer of 1922, and is a critique of the "American Dream".

The novel recounts the chaos of the First World War. American society experiences an unprecedented level of prosperity during the 1920s, as does its economy. At the same time, the ban on the production and consumption of alcoholic beverages, ordered by the 18th Amendment, made a great number of millionaires outside the regular circuit of the sale of goods and brought about a rise in organized crime. Although Fitzgerald, like Nick Carraway in his novel, idolizes the rich and the glamour of the era, he could not come to terms with the boundless materialism and the lack of morals, which brought with them a certain decadence.

Nick Carraway, a young trader from the Midwest, becomes friends with his neighbor Jay Gatsby, a billionaire known for the lively parties he threw at his mansion on Long Island. Gatsby's fortune is the subject of rumors; none of the guests Nick meets at Gatsby's party knows very much about the host's past. Nick also visits Tom Buchanan, a wealthy former college athlete, and his wife Daisy, who is Nick's cousin.

Gatsby is famous for the parties held at his mansion in West Egg. Every Saturday, hundreds of people head to Gatsby's house for the cheerful parties. Nick soon finds himself part of the party scene, although he claims to utterly despise uncultured entertainments. Later, Nick discovers that the millionaire only kept up these parties in the hope that Daisy, his former love, would come to one of them by chance. Over the course of the book we are introduced to the green beacon that stood on the other side of the dock, where Gatsby would stand admiring that greenish light, symbolizing the hope of meeting Daisy again and of the two reliving together the glory years they had shared.

title: The Old Man and the Sea
author: Ernest Hemingway
synopsis:
The Old Man and the Sea (in English: The Old Man and the Sea) is a novella written by the American author Ernest Hemingway and published in 1952. Considered one of the most important works of twentieth-century literature, the narrative follows Santiago, an old Cuban fisherman who faces a long streak of bad luck at sea and sets out alone in search of a great catch. The work explores themes such as human endurance, dignity in the face of defeat, the relationship between man and nature, and perseverance in the face of hardship.

Set in the sea off the coast of Cuba, the story was inspired by Hemingway's experiences with deep-sea fishing during the period when he lived in the country. The simple, direct style of the narrative, associated with the so-called "iceberg theory", became one of the main characteristics of the work and of the author's writing.

The story takes place in a small fishing village in Cuba and follows Santiago, an old fisherman who faces a long streak of bad luck, going 84 days without managing to catch a single fish. Despite the bad spell, Santiago remains hopeful and decides to set out to sea alone in search of a great catch.

On the 85th day, the fisherman manages to hook an enormous marlin, considered the largest fish he had ever encountered. The fish, however, shows tremendous strength and drags Santiago's boat for several days on the open sea. During the struggle, the old fisherman suffers from exhaustion, hunger and pain in his hands, but remains determined to overcome the challenge.

After an intense battle of three days and three nights, Santiago manages to kill the marlin using a harpoon and ties the fish alongside the boat to return to shore. On the way back, however, sharks are drawn by the fish's blood and begin to attack it. Santiago tries to drive them off using harpoons, oars and improvised knives, but cannot prevent the animals from devouring almost all of the marlin's flesh.

title: For Whom the Bell Tolls
author: Ernest Hemingway
synopsis:
For Whom the Bell Tolls is a novel by Ernest Hemingway published in 1940. It tells the story of Robert Jordan, a young American volunteer attached to a Republican guerrilla unit during the Spanish Civil War. As a demolitions expert, he is assigned to blow up a bridge during the Segovia Offensive.

It was published shortly after the end of the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939), which had been widely covered by the international media at the time. The writer assumes that his audience knows the war was fought between the leftist government of the Second Spanish Republic, which many foreigners went to Spain to help, and the Nationalist faction, which was supported by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy. In 1940, the year the book was published, the United States had not yet entered the Second World War.

Robert Jordan is an American, a former Spanish-language instructor at the University of Montana. He had lived in pre-war Spain and fights as an irregular soldier for the Republic against the fascist forces of Francisco Franco. An experienced demolitions expert, he is ordered by a Soviet general to travel behind enemy lines and destroy a bridge with the help of a band of local antifascist guerrillas, in order to prevent enemy troops from responding to an imminent offensive. On his mission, Jordan meets the rebel Anselmo, the "old man", who takes him to a guerrilla camp hidden in the Sierra de Guadarrama, between Madrid and Segovia. Anselmo initially acts as an intermediary between Jordan and the other guerrillas. They include Agustín, Primitivo, Fernando, the brothers Andrés and Eladio, and Rafael, often referred to pejoratively as "the gypsy".

At the camp, Jordan meets María, a young Spanish woman whose life was destroyed by the execution of her parents and by her rape at the hands of the Falangists (part of the fascist coalition) at the beginning of the war.

title: The Sound and the Fury
author: William Faulkner
synopsis:
The Sound and the Fury (in Portuguese, The Sound and the Fury) is a novel by the American writer William Faulkner, in which several types of narrative are used, including the technique known as stream of consciousness, of which Faulkner was one of the pioneers in the 20th century, alongside European writers such as James Joyce and Virginia Woolf. Published in 1929, The Sound and the Fury was his fourth novel, but it was not an immediate success. In 1931, however, when he published his sixth novel, Sanctuary – a more sensationalist novel that Faulkner later confessed to having written for financial reasons – The Sound and the Fury also achieved commercial success, and Faulkner began to receive critical attention. It is consistently regarded by critics and the public as one of the best and most important literary works of the 20th century.

The story of The Sound and the Fury takes place in the fictional Yoknapatawpha County, and has as its central theme the story of an old aristocratic family of the American South, descended from the hero of the American Civil War, General Compson. The general outline of the story is the confrontation with the decline and dissolution of the Compson family's reputation, and the novel is divided into 4 distinct sections.

The first part, on April 7, 1928, is written from the perspective of Benjamin "Benjy" Compson, a 33-year-old mentally disabled man, and the narrative is characterized by a highly disjointed style, with frequent chronological leaps.

The second part, on June 2, 1910, presents Quentin Compson, Benjy's older brother.

The third part, on April 6, 1928, is written from the point of view of Jason, Quentin's cynical younger brother.

title: Of Mice and Men
author: John Steinbeck
synopsis:
Of Mice and Men ("Sobre Of Mice and Men", in Portuguese) is a book written by John Steinbeck and published in 1937, which tells the tragic story of George and Lennie, two farm workers in California during the Great Depression (1929-1939). The story takes place on a ranch a few miles from Soledad in the Salinas Valley.

They make an odd pair: George is small and clever; Lennie a hulking brute with the mind of a child. The pair wander the countryside looking for a farm to work on, always with the plan of buying an acre of land and building their own farm on it.

Buying land was very difficult at the time; it demanded great effort at work and thrift, all the more so for two poorly paid farm workers. The greatest difficulty for the two was job stability, since Lennie almost always got into fights in the places where they arrived to work, which forced them to flee.

At the start of the book, George and Lennie have just fled a farm; the owners wanted to lynch Lennie because he had disrespected a woman. The big man, unaware of his actions, liked to take in his hands everything he found pretty and pleasant. After walking for some time, they decide to camp. They are on their way to another farm, where there is the promise of jobs. George notices that Lennie is hiding something, and soon discovers that it is a dead little mouse.

title: The Catcher in the Rye
editionTitle: O Apanhador no Campo de Centeio
author: J. D. Salinger
synopsis:
The Catcher in the Rye (Brazil: The Catcher in the Rye / Portugal: À Espera no Centeio or Uma Agulha no Palheiro) is a story by J. D. Salinger, partially published in serial form in 1945-1946 and as a novel in 1951. A classic novel originally published for adults, it has since become popular among teenage readers for its themes of angst and alienation and as a critique of the superficiality of society. It has been translated into almost all of the world's major languages.

Around one million copies are sold each year, with total sales of more than 65 million books. The novel's protagonist, Holden Caulfield, has become an icon of teenage rebellion. The novel also deals with complex issues of innocence, identity, belonging, loss and connection.

The book recounts a weekend in the life of Holden Caulfield, a seventeen-year-old from a wealthy New York family. Holden, a student at a reputable boarding school for boys, Pencey, goes home early in the winter, after receiving poor grades in almost every subject and being expelled from the school. On the way home, he decides to take a roundabout journey, thereby postponing the confrontation with his family. Holden reflects on his short life, going back over his peculiar view of the world and trying to set some direction for his future. Before facing his parents, he seeks out a few people who are important to him, such as a teacher, an old girlfriend and his little sister, and, with them, he tries to explain and even understand the confusion going through his head.

The novel is set in December 1949. The story begins with Holden Caulfield describing encounters he had with the students and teachers of Pencey Prep, in Angerstown, Pennsylvania. He criticizes them for being superficial, or, as he would say, "phony".

title: Moby Dick
author: Herman Melville
synopsis:
Moby-Dick; or, The Whale (in Portuguese: Moby Dick, ou, A baleia) is a novel published in 1851 by the American writer Herman Melville. In the book, Ishmael narrates the obsessive quest of Ahab, captain of the whaling ship Pequod, for Moby Dick, the giant white sperm whale that, on the ship's previous voyage, had torn off part of the captain's leg.
