A contribution to the literature of the "American Renaissance", Moby Dick received mixed reviews and was a commercial failure, to the point of no longer even being in print at the time of the author's death, in 1891. Its reputation as a "Great American Novel" was established only in the 20th century, after the centenary of the author's birth. William Faulkner said that he wished he had written the book himself, and D. H. Lawrence called it "one of the strangest and most wonderful books in the world" and "the greatest book of the sea ever written".

At the beginning of the book Ishmael travels from the island of Manhattan to New Bedford, Massachusetts, with plans to sign up for a whaling voyage. The inn is overcrowded, so he must share a bed with the tattooed Polynesian cannibal Queequeg, a harpooner whose father was king of the fictional island of Kokovoko. The next morning, Ishmael and Queequeg attend a sermon and set off for Nantucket, where Ishmael signs up for the voyage of the whaling ship Pequod. One of the ship's owners describes Captain Ahab: "He is a great man, he is not religious, he seems like a god" who, nevertheless, "keeps his human side". They hire Queequeg the following morning. A man named Elias prophesies a terrible fate should Ishmael and Queequeg join Ahab. While the provisions are being loaded, shadowy figures board the ship. On a cold Christmas Day, the Pequod leaves port.

Ishmael discusses cetology and describes the members of the crew.

title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
synopsis:
The Scarlet Letter (The Scarlet Letter, or A Letra Encarnada) is a book by Nathaniel Hawthorne published in the United States in 1850. The story takes place in 17th-century Salem (Massachusetts), settled by Puritans who had come from England.

For Fernando Pessoa, who translated it, "A Letra Encarnada is the most famous and, in the opinion of the great majority of critics, the greatest of North American novels." Henry James called it "the most distinctive piece of prose fiction that American soil has produced". Pessoa quotes another critic who remarked that "It is a sinister tragedy in which the consequences of sin are painted with a simplicity, a steady movement and a pitilessness worthy of the tragedies of Euripides".

A crowd watches Hester Prynne being escorted from the prison to the pillory, carrying a baby in her arms and with the scarlet letter "A" embroidered on her chest. From up high, she sees a man accompanied by an Indian. She follows the man with her gaze for a long time, to the point of forgetting the rest of the world. Afterwards, she is questioned by the town's clergy, who urge her to name the man with whom she had her daughter. Hester refuses to say and is taken back to prison.

In the prison, the man reappears, telling the jailer that he is a practitioner of medicine and that he could help Hester calm down. They are left alone, and it is revealed that the man is, in fact, Hester's husband. He too asks her to say who the child's father is, and she again refuses to tell. He then says that he will find out one way or another and asks her not to tell anyone that he is her husband; let the whole town think that he is dead. He introduces himself to the town under the name Roger Chillingworth.

title: Don Quixote
author: Miguel de Cervantes
synopsis:
Don Quixote, whose full title is O Engenhoso Fidalgo Don Quixote da Mancha, is a Spanish novel by Miguel de Cervantes. Originally published in two parts, in 1605 and 1615, the novel is considered a founding work of Western literature and the first modern novel. The novel has been ranked by many well-known authors as the "best novel of all time" and the "best and most central work in world literature". Don Quixote is also one of the most translated books in the world and one of the best-selling novels of all time. The novel is a satire of chivalric romances and of the literary conventions of the time.

For Cervantes and the readers of his time, Don Quixote was a single-volume book published in 1605, divided internally into four parts, not the first part of a two-part set. The mention in the 1605 book of further adventures yet to be told was entirely conventional, did not indicate any authorial plans for a continuation and was not taken seriously by the book's first readers.

Cervantes, in a metafictional narrative, writes that the first chapters were taken from the "archives of La Mancha", and the rest was translated from an Arabic text by the Moorish historian Cide Hamete Benengeli.

Alonso Quijano is a hidalgo of nearly 50 years of age who lives in a deliberately unspecified region of La Mancha with his niece and housekeeper. Although he leads a frugal life, he is full of fantasies about chivalry stemming from his obsession with books of chivalric romance. Eventually, his obsession becomes reality when he decides to be a knight-errant, donning an old suit of armor.

title: The Divine Comedy
author: Dante Alighieri
synopsis:
The Divine Comedy (in Italian: La Divina Commedia, originally Comedìa and later called Divina Comédia by Giovanni Boccaccio) is an allegorical-didactic and eschatological poem, epic and theological in bent, of Italian and world literature, about the foundations of the Christian faith, written by Dante Alighieri in the fourteenth century and divided into three parts: the Inferno, the Purgatório and the Paraíso. It is written in interlocking tercets of hendecasyllables (later called Dante's tercets par excellence) in the Florentine vernacular.

The original title, by which the author himself designates his poem, was Comedia (probably pronounced with the stress on the i), and this is also the title of the editio princeps of 1472. The adjective "Divina" was given to it by Boccaccio in the Trattatello in laude di Dante, written between 1357 and 1362 and printed in 1477.

Each of the three parts of the poem (Inferno, Purgatório and Paraíso) is divided into 33 cantos, with one more by way of introduction, so the work totals 100 cantos, a number that is said to signify the perfection of perfection. Besides Dante himself, there are three main characters: Virgil, guide in hell and purgatory, Beatrice, guide in the earthly paradise, and Saint Bernard, guide in the celestial spheres. The work also totals 14,233 lines in what have since been called "Dantean tercets".

title: The Odyssey
author: Homero
synopsis:
The Odyssey (Classical Greek: Οδύσσεια; romanized: Odýsseia) is one of the two major epics of ancient Greek literature attributed to Homero. It is one of the oldest surviving works of literature and remains popular with modern audiences. Like the Ilíada, the Odyssey is divided into 24 books. It follows the hero king of Ithaca, Odisseu, also known by the Latin variant Ulisses, and his journey home after the Trojan War, which lasted ten years. His voyage from Troy to Ithaca takes another ten years, during which he encounters many dangers and all his crewmates are killed. In Odisseu's long absence, he is presumed dead, leaving his wife Penélope and his son Telêmaco to deal with a group of unruly suitors competing for Penélope's hand in marriage.

Ten years after the Achaeans (Greeks) won the Trojan War, Odisseu, king of Ithaca, has still not returned home from Troy. In his absence, 108 boorish suitors court his wife Penélope. Penélope tells them she will remarry when she finishes weaving a shroud for Odisseu's elderly father, Laertes; however, she secretly unravels the cloth every night.

The goddess Atena, disguised first as Mentes and then as Mentor, tells Odisseu's son, Telêmaco, to seek news of his father. The two leave Ithaca and visit Nestor, who tells them that Agamemnon, the commander of the Greek army at Troy, was murdered shortly after the war. Telêmaco travels to Sparta to meet Agamemnon's brother, Menelau, who in turn describes his encounter with the shape-shifting god known as the Old Man of the Sea. Menelau says he learned from the Old Man of the Sea that Odisseu is alive but held captive by the nymph Calipso.

Atena implores Zeus to rescue Odisseu, and Zeus sends Hermes to negotiate his release.

title: Hamlet
author: William Shakespeare
synopsis:
A tragédia de Hamlet, príncipe da Dinamarca (The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke in the first edition in English), usually shortened simply to Hamlet, is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, written between 1599 and 1601. The play, set in Denmark, retells the story of how Prince Hamlet tries to avenge the death of his father, Hamlet, the king, killed by Cláudio, his brother, who poisoned him and then took the throne by marrying the queen. The play charts the course of life in real madness and in feigned madness — from overwhelming grief to seething rage — and explores themes such as betrayal, revenge, incest, corruption and morality.

Despite the enormous amount of research done on the text, the exact year in which Shakespeare wrote it remains under debate.

The protagonist of Hamlet is Prince Hamlet of Denmark, son of the recently deceased King Hamlet and nephew of King Cláudio, his father's brother and successor. After King Hamlet's death, Cláudio hastily marries the then widow Gertrudes, the prince's mother. In the historical setting, Denmark is in dispute with neighboring Norway, and there is the expectation of a supposed invasion led by the Norwegian prince Fórtinbras.

The play opens on a cold night at Elsinore Castle, the Danish Royal Castle. The sentries try to convince Horácio, Prince Hamlet's friend, that they have seen the ghost of the dead king, when it appears again. After Horácio's encounter with the Ghost, Hamlet resolves to see it with his own eyes. At night, the Ghost appears to Hamlet. The specter tells Hamlet that it is the spirit of his dead father, and reveals that Cláudio killed him with a vial of poison, pouring the liquid into his ear. The Ghost asks Hamlet to avenge his death; Hamlet agrees, pitying the specter, deciding to feign madness so as not to arouse suspicion.

title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad
synopsis:
Heart of Darkness (O Heart of Darkness) is a novel written by Joseph Conrad. Before its publication in 1902, it appeared as a three-part serial in 1899 in Blackwood's Magazine. It is widely regarded as an important work of English literature and part of the Western canon. The novel tells of Charles Marlow, an Englishman who obtained work with a Belgian trading company as captain of a steamboat on an African river. Although Conrad does not identify the river, in the Congo Free State, the location of the great and important Congo River was at the time a colony privately owned by King Leopoldo II of Belgium. Marlow is hired to transport ivory downriver. However, his most urgent task is to return Kurtz, a famous ivory trader, to civilization.

Aboard the Nellie, anchored on the Thames, near Gravesend, England, Charles Marlow recounts to his fellow sailors the events that led him to become captain of a steamboat, in the service of an ivory trading company.

Marlow begins his narrative by telling how he had obtained the post in the company, through the help and influence of his aunt, who knew the wife of a senior official in the Administration. He thus becomes commander of a steamer, and is assigned the mission of rescuing the head of a trading post, known as Mr. Kurtz. In narrating his adventures up to the point of finding his vessel, in the Congo, Conrad criticizes the lack of connectivity between the regions, slavery, the bureaucratic and detached attitude of the commanders, as well as their lack of information. In the process, Marlow comes to hear much praise for Mr. Kurtz, considered an excellent station chief, very intelligent, a brilliant fellow. Marlow states, at a certain point in the narrative, that, when thinking of Kurtz, he saw only a name and was unable to see the person behind the legend.

author: George Orwell
synopsis:
Mil novecentos e oitenta e quatro (in English: Nineteen Eighty-Four; also published as 1984) is a dystopian novel by the English writer George Orwell. It was published on June 8, 1949 by Secker & Warburg as Orwell's ninth and final book completed in his lifetime. Thematically, it centers on the consequences of totalitarianism, mass surveillance and brainwashing in society. Orwell, a democratic socialist, modeled the authoritarian state described in the novel on the Stalinist Soviet Union and Nazi Germany. More broadly, the novel examines the role of truth and facts in societies and the ways in which they can be manipulated.

The story takes place in an imagined future in an unspecified year believed to be 1984, when much of the world is in a state of perpetual war.

In 1984, global civilization has been devastated by world war, civil conflicts and revolutions. Airstrip One (formerly known as Great Britain) is one of the provinces of Oceania, one of the three totalitarian superstates that rule the planet, and it is governed by the "Party" under the ideology of "Ingsoc" (an abbreviation of "English Socialism" in Newspeak) and by the mysterious leader Big Brother, who has an intense cult of personality. The Party brutally purges anyone who does not fully conform to its regime, using the Thought Police and constant surveillance through telescreens (two-way televisions), concealed cameras and hidden microphones. Those who fall out of favor with the Party become "unpersons" and disappear, with all evidence of their existence destroyed.

In London, Winston Smith is a member of the Outer Party and works at the Ministry of Truth, where he rewrites historical records to fit the state's version, which is constantly changing.

title: Animal Farm
author: George Orwell
subjects: For National Curriculum Key Stage 4 & GCSE
synopsis:
Animal Farm (Brazil: Animal Farm/A Fazenda dos Animais/A Fazenda dos Bichos / Portugal: O Porco Triunfante/O Triunfo dos Porcos/A Quinta dos Animais) is a satirical novel by the English writer George Orwell, published in the United Kingdom on 17 August 1945 and included by the American magazine Time in its list of the 100 best English-language novels. The book's satire of the communist Soviet Union earned 31st place on the list of the best novels of the twentieth century compiled by the Modern Library List.

The book tells a story of corruption and betrayal and uses animal figures to portray human weaknesses and demolish the "communist paradise" put forward by the Soviet Union in Stalin's time. The revolt of the farm animals against the humans is led by the pigs Bola-de-Neve (Snowball) and Napoleão (Napoleon).

Feeling his time approaching, Major, an old pig, gathers the animals of the farm Granja do Solar (Manor Farm) to share a dream: that they, the animals, should govern themselves, free from submission to and exploitation by man. He taught them an old song, Bichos da Inglaterra (Beasts of England), which sums up the philosophy of Animalism, exalting equality among them and the prosperous times that were to come, leaving the other animals in ecstasy at the possibilities.

The elderly Major (also known as Casca Grossa) died three days later, and the lead was taken by the shrewd young pigs Bola-de-Neve and Napoleão, who began to meet in secret in order to map out the strategies of the revolution. One day, Mr. Jones, then the owner of the farm, was careless about feeding the animals, and this became the last straw for those creatures.

title: Brave New World
author: Aldous Huxley
synopsis:
Brave New World (Brave New World in the original English-language version) is a novel written by Aldous Huxley and published in 1932. The story takes place in London in the year 2540 (632 AF - "After Ford" - in the book), and the novel anticipates developments in reproductive technology, hypnopaedia, psychological manipulation and classical conditioning, which combine to profoundly change society.

Together with 1984 (Nineteen Eighty-Four) by George Orwell and Fahrenheit 451 by Ray Bradbury, they are considered the three great literary dystopias of the twentieth century. Huxley responded to this book with a reassessment in an essay, Regresso ao Brave New World (1958), and A Ilha (1962). The title has its origin in Act V of the play A tempestade by William Shakespeare, when Miranda delivers her speech.

The character Bernard Marx feels dissatisfied with the world in which he lives, in part because he is physically different from the members of his caste. In a stronghold where people live along the lines of the past, a kind of "historical reserve" — similar to today's indigenous reserves — where the "savage" customs of the past (which corresponds to the time when the book was written) are preserved, Bernard meets a woman originally from civilization, Linda, and her son, John. Bernard sees a chance to win social respect by presenting John to civilized society as a specimen of the savages.

For civilized society, having a child was an obscene and unthinkable act, and holding a religious belief was an act of ignorance and of disrespect toward society. Linda, on arriving in civilization, was rejected by society.

title: Fahrenheit 451
author: Ray Bradbury
synopsis:
Fahrenheit 451 is a dystopian soft science fiction novel, written by Ray Bradbury (1920-2012) and first published in 1953. The initial concept of the book began in 1947 with the short story "Bright Phoenix" (which would only be published in the magazine The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction in 1963). The original short story was reworked into the novella The Fireman, and published in the February 1951 issue of the magazine Galaxy Science Fiction. The novella also had its chapters published between March and May 1954 in issues of Playboy magazine. Written in the early years of the Cold War, the book is a critique of what Bradbury saw as an increasingly dysfunctional American society.

The novel presents a future in which all books are banned, personal opinions are considered antisocial and hedonistic, and critical thinking is suppressed.

Fahrenheit is set in an unspecified future in a hedonistic and anti-intellectual America that has completely lost control. Anyone caught reading books is, at the very least, confined to an asylum. As for the books, they are considered illegal and, once found in someone's possession, are burned by the "firemen". The illegal books found are mainly famous works such as Whitman, Faulkner and others. The protagonist, Guy Montag, is a fireman who, following the profession of his father and grandfather, is certain that his job (burning books and the houses that shelter them, as well as hunting down the people who keep them) — is the right thing to do. He particularly remembers an occasion from his childhood, when the power went out and his mother lit a candle: in the dark, the candle gave off a strange light, but one in which Montag felt safe and comfortable.

The novel ends on a slightly optimistic note. It is said that the society Montag knew has been almost completely wiped out, and that a new society is rising from its ashes, with a destiny still unknown.

title: Lord of the Flies
author: William Golding
synopsis:
Lord of the Flies (Brazil: Lord of the Flies / Portugal: O Deus das Moscas) is a novel by William Golding, winner of the Nobel Prize in 1983. The book focuses on a group of British boys stranded on an uninhabited island and their disastrous attempt to govern themselves.

The novel was generally well received. It was named one of the "100 best novels of the Modern Library", reaching number 41 on the editor's list and 25 on the reader's list. In 2003, it was listed at number 70 in the BBC's The Big Read survey, and in 2005 Time magazine named it one of the 100 best English-language novels of the period 1923-2005.

In the midst of a wartime evacuation, a British plane crashes on or near an isolated island in a remote region of the Pacific Ocean. The only survivors are preadolescent boys. Two boys — the fair-haired Ralph and an overweight boy with glasses, nicknamed "Piggy" — find a conch, which Ralph uses as a horn to gather all the survivors in one area.

Ralph appears responsible for gathering all the survivors, so he immediately commands some authority over the other boys and is quickly elected their "chief". He does not receive the votes of the members of a group of boys led by the red-headed Jack Merridew, but he allows them to form a separate band of hunters. Ralph establishes three main policies: to have fun, to survive, and to constantly maintain a smoke signal that could alert passing ships to their presence on the island and thus rescue them.

title: Lolita
author: Vladimir Nabokov
synopsis:
Lolita is a 1955 novel written by the Russian-American novelist Vladimir Nabokov that deals with the controversial subject of hebephilia: the protagonist Humbert Humbert, the story's unreliable narrator, is a professor of French literature who is sexually attracted to children. Over the course of the novel, he describes his obsession with Dolores Haze, a 12-year-old girl whom he kidnaps and sexually abuses after becoming her stepfather. He refers to her as a "nymphet" and takes to calling her "Lolita", the Spanish diminutive of the name Dolores. The novel was originally written in English, but fear that it would be censored in the USA (where Nabokov lived) and in England led to its being published first in Paris, on 15 September 1955, by Olympia Press. It was later translated into Russian by Nabokov himself, and published in New York on 18 August 1958.

The story begins with a fictitious foreword written by John Ray, Jr., Ph.D., an editor of psychology books. In it, Ray writes that he is presenting the details of a memoir entitled The Confession of a White Widowed Male written by a literary scholar of mixed European ethnicity who recently died in an American prison of coronary heart disease while awaiting his trial for murder. The author of the memoir uses the pseudonym Humbert Humbert to refer to himself in the manuscript. Humbert begins the memoir with his Parisian childhood and ends it with his incarceration. Ray says that he received the memoir from Humbert's lawyer, C.C. Clark, and adds that he (Ray) has changed the names of the people mentioned in it to protect their identities except for one: "Lolita", the nickname Humbert used to refer to the young girl with whom he was sexually obsessed. Ray notes that Lolita died in 1952 while giving birth to a stillborn girl on Christmas Day while married to Richard Schiller, presumably the father of her daughter.

title: The Unbearable Lightness of Being
author: Milan Kundera
synopsis: The Unbearable Lightness of Being (in Czech: Nesnesitelná lehkost bytí) is a novel by the Czech writer Milan Kundera, originally published in 1984. The work narrates the story of two women, two men and a dog during the Prague Spring, in 1968, a significant period in the history of Czechoslovakia. Although completed in 1982, the book had its first edition in 1984, in a French translation under the title L'insoutenable légèreté de l'être. The original Czech-language version was released the following year. In 2017, Companhia das Letras published the translation into Brazilian Portuguese, done by Teresa Bulhões Carvalho da Fonseca. In Portugal the work has had several publications by Don Quixote since the 1980s.

title: The Name of the Rose
author: Umberto Eco
synopsis:
The Name of the Rose (in Italian: Il nome della rosa it) is the 1980 debut novel by the Italian author Umberto Eco. It is a historical murder mystery set in an Italian monastery in 1327, and an intellectual mystery combining semiotics in fiction, biblical analysis, medieval studies and literary theory. It was translated into English by William Weaver in 1983.

The novel has sold more than 50 million copies worldwide, making it one of the best-selling books of all time. It has received many international awards and honors, such as the Prêmio Strega in 1981 and the Prix Medicis Étranger in 1982, and was ranked 14th on Le Monde's list of the 100 books of the century.

In 1327, the Franciscan friar Guilherme de Baskerville and his assistant Adso de Melk arrive at a Benedictine abbey in Northern Italy to take part in a theological dispute. The abbey is being used as neutral ground in a dispute between Pope John XXII and the Franciscans over the question of apostolic poverty. The monks of the abbey have recently been shaken by the suspicious death of one of their brothers, Adelmo de Otranto, and the abbot asks Guilherme (a former inquisitor) to investigate the incident. During his investigations, Guilherme has a debate with one of the abbey's oldest monks, Jorge de Burgos, about the permissibility of laughter, which Jorge considers a threat to the order established by God.

On the second day, another monk, Venâncio de Salvemec, is found dead in a vat of pig's blood. He has black stains on his tongue and fingers, suggesting poisoning. Guilherme discovers that Adelmo was part of a homosexual love triangle that also involved the librarian, Malaquias de Hildesheim, and Malaquias's assistant, Berengário de Arundel.

title: Invisible Cities
author: Italo Calvino
synopsis:
Invisible Cities is a novel by the Italian writer Italo Calvino, published in 1972. In its 150 pages, the author uses a studied language, which is shaped in a combinatorial game.

The work was written during the period when the author lived in Paris, France, and, at first, took the form of a diary with Calvino's impressions and thoughts around the city.

In this work, the author presents cities and memory, cities and desire, cities and thin cities, cities and trade and other cities. Presented in 150 pages of magic, geometry, geographical concepts that become a complex and inexhaustible symbol of human existence. Cities that are unique for being approached with lightness, multiplicity, exactitude.

The analogy between Marco Polo's travels to the East and his dialogues with the emperor of the Tartars Kublai Khan create a fiction of current and vibrant interpretations. The surprises and ideas contained between the lines make the reading fascinating, characterized by a vision of urban space that is not only geometric and rational, but intensely subjective and reflective. The various cities with feminine names are attended by their essence and by questions pertinent to the various urban functions for human existence.

title: If on a Winter's Night a Traveler
editionTitle: Se um Viajante numa Noite de Inverno
author: Italo Calvino

title: The Baron in the Trees
author: Italo Calvino
synopsis:
Il barone rampante (Brazil: The Baron in the Trees / Portugal: O barão trepador) is a novel written by Ítalo Calvino and published in 1957 in Italy. This is the second book of the trilogy Nossos Ancestrais, which also includes the novels Il visconte dimezzato (1952) and Il cavaliere inesistente (1959).

The inspiration for the novel comes from the story that, one night in 1950, Salvatore Scarpitta tells Italo Calvino at the Osteria Fratelli Menghi at via Flaminia 57 in the city of Rome. The book Il barone rampante was released seven years after this conversation. In 1957 the book received the Premio Letterario Viareggio-Rèpaci in the fiction category.

It tells the story of Cosme, the firstborn son of a baron, who on July 15, 1767 climbs into the trees and never comes down again. The story is narrated by Cosme's brother, Biágio, who recounts the ups and downs of living in the trees and his brother's adventures.

It is a rather quixotic story told with a torrent of countless sensations that only Calvino manages to awaken. In addition, it prompts a series of reflections on the human condition and on the social conditions of the period portrayed in the book, the mid-eighteenth century, a period in which there were paradigm shifts in various fields of knowledge and which the author inserts into his fiction with a rather sarcastic tone, yet with a light, reflective humor that is characteristic and unmistakable, as in all his works.

title: The Leopard
author: Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa
synopsis:
Il gattopardo, translated into Portuguese as The Leopard, is a historical novel, the only one by the writer Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa. The author drew his inspiration from the stories of his old family and, in particular, from the life of an ancestor of his who lived through the crucial years of the Risorgimento, in the reign of Francisco II of the Two Sicilies.

Written between late 1954 and 1957, it was initially submitted to the publishers Einaudi and Mondadori, which turned down its publication, which only came about posthumously through Feltrinelli, with a preface by Giorgio Bassani. In 1959 it received the "Prêmio Strega" and, in 1963, Luchino Visconti adapted the work for his film of the same name: Il gattopardo.

The book opens with the final phrase of the Hail Mary prayer: "Nunc et in hora mortis nostrae. Amen".

Il Gattopardo tells the story of the author's ancestor, Don Fabrizio Corbera, Prince of Salina, and of his family between 1860 and 1910, in Sicily (in Palermo and on the estate of Donnafugata).

Don Fabrizio is the father of seven children and heir to a surname that for centuries "had never managed to do anything more than add up its own expenses and subtract its own debts".

The Prince had a strong inclination for mathematics: he had applied it to astronomy and from this had gained public recognition, as well as delightful private joys. At the beginning of the first chapter it speaks of a corpse found in the gardens of the Salina house, "the corpse of a young soldier of the fifth battalion of chasseurs who had been wounded in the fighting at San Lorenzo".

In May 1860, after Giuseppe Garibaldi's landing in Sicily, Don Fabrizio watches the end of the fighting with detachment and melancholy. The aristocratic class senses that the end of its supremacy is near.

title: If This Is a Man
author: Primo Levi
synopsis:
Se Questo è un Uomo (IPA: Brazil: If This Is a Man / Portugal: Se Isto é um Homem) is a book by the Italian writer Primo Levi. It describes his experiences in the Auschwitz concentration camp during the Second World War.

Se isto é um homem was rejected by Einaudi, the most important publishing house in Levi's native city, Turin. A small publisher brought the book out in November 1947. Only 1500 copies were sold. Levi had to wait until 1958 for the Einaudi house to publish it, in a revised form, which led to its translation into English in 1959 and, later, into many other languages, including Catalan, and to its acceptance as a classic.

Se Isto É um Homem tells the story of Primo Levi, a Jewish Italian citizen with a degree in chemistry, who is taken to Auschwitz. Everything is taken from him and he becomes one more anonymous prisoner of the Nazi concentration camp; even his own name is replaced by a number, calling into question the very notion of identity.

In Auschwitz, he leads an existence full of troubles: the excruciating pain of hunger and thirst, and the arduous labor in the "Lager", which leads to the total exhaustion of human strength and will. Despite a routine that is hard to get through, Levi learns that survival - through cunning and organization - is possible, even for those deprived of any moral right.

Through an objective description of the daily life of an Auschwitz prisoner, Primo Levi exalts human strength and the capacity for endurance above any physical or moral pain, even when dignity itself is called into question.

title: My Brilliant Friend
author: Elena Ferrante
synopsis:
My Brilliant Friend (in Italian: L'amica geniale) is the first volume of a series of novels in four parts known collectively as the Romances Napolitanos, written by the Italian author Elena Ferrante. It is followed by História do Novo Sobrenome, História de Quem Foge e de Quem Fica and História da Menina Perdida.

The novel begins in 2010, when the narrator, Elena Greco (Lenù), receives a phone call from the son of an old friend, saying that his mother has disappeared, leaving no trace of herself in the house. Elena recognizes this behavior as something her friend Raffaela Cerulo (whom she calls Lila) always threatened to do and believes that her disappearance was a conscious decision. In the spirit of their loving but ambivalent relationship, Elena breaks the promise she had made not to write about her friend and begins to put down on paper everything she can remember about Lila, starting in the Naples of the 1950s.

Elena and Lila grow up in a poor neighborhood full of violence and conflict. Few children receive an education beyond elementary school. Elena is diligent and catches the attention of the schoolmistress Oliviero, one of her primary school teachers, who encourages her to escape the life of the poor neighborhood. To everyone's surprise, the rebellious Lila turns out to be a prodigy who taught herself to read and write. She quickly earns the highest grades in the class, seemingly without effort.

title: The Days of Abandonment
author: Elena Ferrante
synopsis:
I Giorni dell'Abbandono is a 2002 Italian novel by Elena Ferrante. It was published in Brazil as The Days of Abandonment, and in Portugal as Os Dias do Abandono. The novel tells the story of a woman whose husband abruptly abandons her after fifteen years together.

In 2005, the novel was adapted into the film I giorni dell'abbandono, directed by Roberto Faenza. HBO Films planned to adapt the novel into a film starring Natalie Portman and written and directed by Maggie Betts, but the production was shelved after Portman left the project.

The story is based on the sudden end of a seemingly solid and happy marriage. Olga, a housewife of almost 30, is told by her husband Mario that he is leaving her and their two children. At first, Olga believes that Mário is not serious, but she soon realizes that he has left her for another woman. The end of the 15-year marriage creates a deep inner crisis for Olga. She has to work again and gets the job of finishing and translating an unfinished novel.

On discovering that the other woman with whom Mário is having an affair is the daughter of one of his colleagues, whom he met when she was fifteen, Olga begins to have a nervous breakdown. She attacks Mario and his new girlfriend Carla when she runs into them in the street. Afterwards, Olga begins a long introspective journey to analyze the years with her husband, to find mistakes and gaps that might have given rise to his desire to leave.

Olga therefore abandons herself completely to her sadness, risking the loss of herself and of her life.

title: The Tin Drum
author: Günter Grass
synopsis:
Die Blechtrommel is a novel of social criticism published in 1959 by the German intellectual and writer Günter Grass (or Günter Graß).

The book tells the whole life story of Oskar, an inmate of an asylum who narrates the story, born in the free city of Danzig, who, being of Kashubian origin, lives through an entire plot that expresses a fierce social critique of the petty bourgeoisie of the time.

Oskar wishes not to grow and in fact lives for many years with the body of a three-year-old boy. Some passages convey strong criticism of society, such as, for example, the glass-killing voice that brought down panes or pierced the surface just enough to make a theft possible and that cannot destroy the stained-glass windows of the Church of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, this perhaps being a way of expressing that at the time the influence of the Church was very great and that no attempt managed to bring it down.

The fast-paced narrative leads the reader into a state of euphoria and eagerness to keep reading, especially in parts where he describes the siege of the headquarters of the Polish post office or the decline in the life of a musician who had changed his life to become an SA man.

title: Perfume
author: Patrick Süskind
synopsis:
Perfume is a novel by the German writer Patrick Süskind, first published in 1985. Fifteen million copies have been sold in forty languages. The original German title is Das Parfum, die Geschichte eines Mörders (literal translation in Portuguese, Perfume, História de um Assassino).

The book tells the story of a man who has an extraordinarily keen sense of smell, which gives him an extremely acute perception of the world, in which he was able to find his way by smells alone.

The story is set in the eighteenth century, in Paris, then in Auvergne, in Montpellier, in Grasse, and finally returns to Paris. The protagonist, Jean-Baptiste Grenouille, came into the world amid fish guts behind a market stall where his mother (executed a few weeks later for infanticides) sold fish. Grenouille has two exceptional characteristics:

he has no odor of his own, which allows him to go completely unnoticed by others, since according to the author "odor is essence, and what has no essence does not exist". Over the course of the story, this absence of smell, which he becomes aware of as an adult, will be compensated for by the creation of perfumes that Grenouille uses according to the circumstances in order to be noticed by others.

he has an extremely developed sense of smell, which allows him to recognize the most imperceptible odors.

title: Norwegian Wood
author: Haruki Murakami
synopsis:
Norwegian Wood (ノルウェイの森, Noruwei no Mori) is a novel by the Japanese writer Haruki Murakami published in 1987. The novel is a nostalgic story of loss. It is told from the first-person perspective of Toru Watanabe, who looks back on his days as a university student living in Tokyo. Through Watanabe's recollections, readers see him develop relationships with two very different women–the beautiful but emotionally troubled Naoko, and the outgoing, lively Midori.

The novel is set in the late 1960s in Tokyo during a period when Japanese students, like those of many other nations, were protesting against the established order. While it serves as the backdrop to the events that unfold, Murakami (through the eyes of Watanabe and Midori) portrays the student movement.

The 37-year-old Toru Watanabe is landing in Hamburg, West Germany, when he hears an orchestral cover of the Beatles song "Norwegian Wood". Suddenly he is overwhelmed by feelings of loss and nostalgia. He thinks back to the 1960s, when so much happened that touched his life.

Watanabe, his classmate Kizuki and Kizuki's girlfriend Naoko are best friends. Kizuki and Naoko are particularly close and feel as if they were soulmates, and Watanabe seems more than happy to be their enforcer. This idyllic existence is shattered by Kizuki's unexpected suicide on his 17th birthday. Kizuki's death deeply affects the two surviving friends; Watanabe feels the influence of death everywhere, while Naoko feels as if an integral part of her has been permanently lost. The two spend more and more time together, taking long walks on Sundays, although their feelings for each other are never clarified during this interval.

title: Kafka on the Shore
author: Haruki Murakami
synopsis:
Kafka on the Shore (海辺のカフカ, Umibe no Kafuka) is a 2002 novel by Haruki Murakami. The book tells the stories of young Kafka Tamura, a 15-year-old teenager with a passion for books who runs away from his Oedipal curse, and of Satoru Nakata, an elderly man with an intellectual disability who has the incredible ability to talk to cats. The work addresses themes such as music as a means of communication, metaphysics, dreams, fate and the subconscious.

Made up of two distinct but interconnected plots, the narrative alternates between the two, addressing each of them in alternating chapters.

The odd-numbered chapters begin with the introduction of the title protagonist, Kafka, who is tormented by a sinister curse placed on him by his father. After consulting his imaginary persona, Corvo, Kafka decides that, on his fifteenth birthday, he will run away from home. While packing, he finds a photo of himself with his older sister at the beach. It is revealed that both Kafka's mother and his older sister abandoned him when he was young, and that he has no memory of their faces or identities. He puts the photograph together with some of his other belongings in a backpack and then leaves Tokyo for Shikoku. On the bus trip, he meets a girl named Sakura, who seems to be about the same age as his sister. Before they part, Sakura, believing that their meeting was fated, gives Kafka her phone number.

title: 1Q84
author: Haruki Murakami
synopsis:
1Q84 (いちきゅうはちよん, Ichi-Kyū-Hachi-Yon, stylized on the Japanese cover as "ichi-kew-hachi-yon") is a novel written by the Japanese writer Haruki Murakami, first published in three volumes in Japan between 2009 and 2010. It covers a fictional year of 1984 in parallel with a "real" one. The novel is the story of how a woman named Aomame begins to notice strange changes taking place in the world. She is quickly caught up in a plot involving Sakigake, a religious cult, and her childhood love, Tengo, and embarks on a journey to discover what is "real".

The novel's first printing sold out on the day it was released, and sales reached one million within a month. The English-language edition of all three volumes, with the first two volumes translated by Jay Rubin and the third by Philip Gabriel, was released in North America and the United Kingdom on October 25, 2011.

Aomame and Tengo, two characters, two parallel stories that take place between April and June 1984. Aomame is a woman close to 30 years old, a martial arts instructor and secretly an assassin. Tengo, a teacher, also in his 30s, who aspires to be a writer. Thus, he gets an opportunity that changes his life completely.

In the second volume, the two parallel stories intersect in a tale full of mystery and surreal events. On one side, Aomame, a professional assassin, suspects she is in a parallel world: 1Q84. On the other, Tengo, the aspiring writer, becomes involved in a project to rewrite a book. With the mysterious name "A Crisálida de Ar", written by the strange teenage girl Fukaeri. At a certain point it becomes clear that Tengo and Aomame met during childhood, having shared a moment that would mark them both for life. A desire to meet again grows, yet neither has heard anything of the other for twenty years.

Book 3 centers the plot on the eventual meeting of Aomame and Tengo. The book brings in a new central character, Ushikawa.

title: The Remains of the Day
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
synopsis:
The Remains of the Day (Os Despojos do Dia (title in Portugal) or The Remains of the Day (title in Brazil)) is a 1989 novel by the Japanese-British writer Kazuo Ishiguro. The work was awarded the Man Booker Prize for Fiction in 1989. The film adaptation of the novel, produced in 1993, directed by James Ivory and with Anthony Hopkins and Emma Thompson in the leading roles, was nominated for eight Oscars.

Kazuo Ishiguro wrote the work in just 4 weeks.

Mr. John Farraday is prepared to travel to the United States, and suggests to Stevens, his butler, that during his absence he could take his Ford automobile and spend a few days away, instead of remaining shut up in the mansion of Darlington Hall, which Mr. Farraday acquired after the death of Lord Darlington, Stevens's former employer.

Now, after the transaction, the household staff consists of four people, far too few for so much work. With the possibility of hiring another person, Stevens decides to make the trip and visit Miss Kenton, who he believes, because of a letter, is eager to return to the mansion, where she worked as housekeeper before getting married, and who now lives elsewhere.

He sets off on the journey, admiring the English landscape, while setting out reflections on his profession, remembering his father, also a butler, and he recalls the time when Miss Kenton worked at Darlington Hall.

title: The Vegetarian
author: Han Kang
synopsis:
The Vegetarian (Korean: 채식주의자; RR: Chaesikjuuija) is a novel by the South Korean writer Han Kang. The book is divided into three acts and was based on the author's 1997 short story, "The Fruit of My Woman". The plot is set in modern-day Seoul and tells the story of Yeonghye, a part-time graphic artist and housewife who, after having a nightmare about human cruelty, decides to radically stop eating, cooking and serving meat, with devastating consequences for her personal and family life.

The Vegetarian was first published in South Korea in 2007. In Brazil, it was published in 2013 by the publisher Devir, in a direct translation from the Korean by Yun Jung Im; and in 2018 by the publisher Todavia, in a direct translation from the Korean by Jae Hyung Woo. In Portugal, it was published by Don Quixote in September 2016.

The Vegetarian tells the story of Yeonghye, a housewife who suddenly decides to stop eating meat after a series of dreams involving images of animal slaughter. This abstention leads her to distance herself from her family and from society. The story is told in three acts: "The Vegetarian", "A Mancha Mongólica" and "Árvores em Chamas". The first part is narrated by Yeonghye's husband, in the first person. The second part is narrated in the third person through the eyes of Yeonghye's brother-in-law, and the third part remains in the third person but focuses on her sister, while speaking sporadically in the present tense.

Cheong considers his wife an ordinary person with no charms, and chose to marry Yeonghye because he thought she would be a good, obedient wife who would fit perfectly into the kind of lifestyle he was looking for. After years of a relatively normal marriage, Cheong wakes up and finds his wife getting rid of all the meat products in the house. He demands an explanation, and Yeonghye replies vaguely that she had had a dream.

title: The Handmaid's Tale
author: Margaret Atwood
synopsis:
The Handmaid's Tale (Brazil: The Handmaid's Tale / Portugal: A História de Uma Serva) is a 1985 dystopian novel by the Canadian author Margaret Atwood. The story is set in the New England of a near future, which is now part of a Christian fundamentalist totalitarian theonomy that has overthrown the government of the United States.

The work explores the themes of the subjugation of women and the various means by which they lose individualism and independence. The novel's title echoes the component parts of Os Contos de Cantuária by Geoffrey Chaucer, which comprises a series of connected stories.

The Handmaid's Tale is set in the República de Gileade, a military Christian theonomy formed within the borders of what was formerly the United States of America.

After a terrorist attack kills the president and most of the United States Congress, a fundamentalist Christian reconstructionist movement calling itself the "Sons of Jacob" launches a coup and suspends the Constitution of the United States under the pretext of "restoring order". They quickly take away women's rights, largely attributed to financial records stored electronically and labelled by sex. The new regime, the República de Gileade, works swiftly to consolidate its power and reorganize American society along a new totalitarian, militarized and hierarchical model of religious and social fanaticism inspired by the Old Testament among its newly created social castes. In this society, human rights are severely limited and women's rights are even more restricted; for example, women are forbidden to read.

title: Americanah
author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
synopsis:
Americanah is a 2013 novel by the Nigerian author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, for which Adichie won the 2013 US National Book Critics Circle Award for fiction. Americanah tells the story of a young Nigerian woman, Ifemelu, who immigrates to the United States to attend university. The novel traces Ifemelu's life in both countries, threaded through by her love story with her schoolmate Obinze. It was Adichie's third novel, published in the US on May 14, 2013 by Alfred A. Knopf. A television miniseries, starring and produced by Lupita Nyong'o, was in development for HBO Max, but was later dropped.

Americanah is about Ifemelu and Obinze who, as teenagers at a secondary school in Lagos, fall in love. Nigeria at the time is under military dictatorship, and people are trying to leave the country. Ifemelu moves to the United States to study, where she faces racism for the first time and the many varieties of racial distinctions: for the first time, Ifemelu discovers what it means to be a "Black Person". Obinze had hoped to join her in the United States, but his visa was denied after September 11, when immigration became more complex. He goes to London, becoming an undocumented immigrant after his visa expires.

Years later, Obinze returns to Nigeria and becomes a wealthy man as a property developer in the newly democratic country. Ifemelu finds success in the United States, where she becomes known for her blog about race and racism in the United States, titled "Raceteenth ou várias observações sobre pretos estadunidenses (aqueles anteriormente conhecidos como negros) por uma preta não estadunidense".

title: Purple Hibiscus
author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
synopsis:
Purple Hibiscus (Purple Hibiscus in Brazil) is a novel written by the Nigerian author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie. It is her debut novel, published by Algonquin Books in 2003.

Purple Hibiscus is set in postcolonial Nigeria, a country plagued by political instability and economic hardship. The central character is Kambili Achike, fifteen years old for much of the period covered by the book, a young girl from a wealthy family in Enugu State, dominated by her devoutly Catholic father, Eugene. Eugene is a religious fanatic and a violent figure in the Achike household, subjecting his wife Beatrice, Kambili herself and her brother Jaja to beatings and psychological cruelty. Beatrice has suffered two miscarriages because of the violence.

The story is told through Kambili's eyes and is essentially about the disintegration of her family unit and her struggle to grow to maturity. A key period is the time Kambili and her brother spend at the home of their father's sister, Ifeoma, and her three children. This household offers a marked contrast to what Kambili and Jaja are used to.

title: Disgrace
author: J. M. Coetzee
synopsis:
Disgrace is a novel by J. M. Coetzee, published in 1999 and winner of that year's Booker Prize. The writer was also awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature four years after its publication.

David Lurie is a South African professor of English who loses everything: his reputation, his job, his peace of mind, his good looks, his dreams of artistic success and, finally, even the ability to protect his own daughter. He has been divorced twice and is dissatisfied with his work as a professor of communications, teaching a class in Romantic literature at a technical university in Cape Town in the post-apartheid era.

His "disgrace" comes when, almost by force, he seduces one of his most vulnerable students. This affair is later revealed at the school, where a committee is convened to judge his actions. David refuses to apologize sincerely and is thus forced to resign from his post.

title: The Road
author: Cormac McCarthy
synopsis:
The Road (2006) (The Road in the original) is a book by the American writer Cormac McCarthy. It is a tale of post-apocalyptic fiction that describes the journey undertaken by a father and his young son over a period of several months across a landscape devastated years earlier by an unnamed cataclysm which destroyed civilization and much of the life on Earth. The novel was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and the 2006 James Tait Black Memorial Prize in the Fiction category, and was chosen for the Oprah's Book Club selection.

In an interview given in 2007 to Oprah Winfrey on The Oprah Winfrey Show, McCarthy said that the inspiration for The Road came during a visit to El Paso, Texas, accompanied by his son, about four years earlier. Imagining what the city might look like in the future, he pictured "fires on the hills" and thought of his son.

title: Atonement
author: Ian McEwan
subjects: National Book Critics Circle Award Winner
synopsis:
Expiação (Portugal)/ Atonement (Brazil) (Atonement, in the original) is a 2001 metafiction novel by the British writer Ian McEwan. Taking place in three time periods - in England in 1935, in England and France in the Second World War and in present-day England (1999), the work starts from a somewhat innocent mistake by an upper-class girl that will ruin lives, follows her adulthood as it unfolds in the shadow of that mistake, and develops a reflection on the nature of writing.

Widely regarded as one of McEwan's best works, Expiação/Atonement was shortlisted for the 2001 Booker Prize for fiction. In 2010, TIME magazine placed Atonement on its list of the 100 best novels in English since 1923.

Briony Tallis, a 13-year-old English girl with a talent for writing, lives on her family's country estate with her parents Jack and Emily Tallis. Her older sister, Cecilia, has recently graduated from the University of Cambridge, as has Robbie Turner, the son of the Tallis family's housekeeper and Cecilia's childhood friend, and the two of them eventually develop a relationship.

In the summer of 1935, Briony's maternal cousins, Lola and the twins Jackson and Pierrot, visit the family while their parents are going through a bitter divorce. Briony's immaturity, and her inability to grasp certain situations that are beyond her understanding, lead her to misinterpret a scene she witnesses of a struggle between Robbie and Cecilia. What she takes to be a moment of sexual tension between Cecilia and Robbie does not correspond to the reality of the situation, and it is the beginning of Briony's fantasies. Misinterpreting this situation, Briony concludes that Robbie is acting aggressively towards Cecilia, owing to their difference in gender and to Briony's idea of men's dominance over women.

title: The Kite Runner
author: Khaled Hosseini
synopsis:
The Kite Runner (in Brazil: The Kite Runner; in Portugal: O Menino de Cabul) is a novel by the Afghan-American writer Khaled Hosseini. Published in 2003, it is the first novel written by Hosseini, and was adapted into a film of the same title in 2007.

In the work, the contrast between the personalities of Amir, the protagonist, and Hassan, his childhood friend, ends up establishing a counterpoint between cowardice and courage, betrayal and loyalty. In addition, the book addresses issues such as: friendship, the father-son relationship, discrimination, eugenics, rape, Afghan culture and history, refugees, the Cold War, pedophilia, the Taliban, etc.

Amir was a boy who grew up in Afghanistan. The boy's mother died giving birth to him. The relationship between him and his father (Baba) is too formal, so that little affection passes from one to the other. Amir comes to think that he is responsible for this coldness, feeling guilty, for example, for his mother's death.

His best friend is Hassan, a Hazara boy with a cleft lip, the son of the family's servant, Ali. This boy lived with his father in a hut in the middle of the garden of Amir's house. Hassan's mother, Sanaubar, had run off with a troupe of traveling singers and dancers, so that he had no contact with a mother figure. Hassan and his father were treated with hostility, because of their ethnicity (Hazara) and religious branch (Shia), by members of the predominant ethnic group in Kabul, the Sunni Pashtuns. Furthermore, Ali's congenital paralysis and a muscular atrophy, resulting from polio, that had also afflicted him were grounds for contempt toward Hassan and his father.

title: The Book Thief
author: Markus Zusak
synopsis:
The Book Thief (in Brazil: The Book Thief /in Portugal: A rapariga que roubava livros) is a drama by the Australian writer Markus Zusak, published in 2005 by the publisher Picador. In Brazil and in Portugal, it was released by Intrínseca and Presença, respectively. The book is about Liesel Meminger, a girl who encounters Death three times during 1939–43 in Nazi Germany.

The Book Thief has as its narrator Death, whose job is to collect the souls of all those who die. During its passage through Germany, in the Second World War, it meets the protagonist, Liesel Meminger, at a train station while her younger brother is being buried nearby. The girl, on noticing that the gravedigger has dropped a book, O manual do coveiro, in the snow, steals it and is then taken to the fictional town of Molching, where her mother intends to hand her over to a family for adoption. On Himmel Street lives the working-class couple formed by Hans and Rosa Hubermann.

There, she lives with her new guardians and goes to school and makes friends with her neighbor, Rudy Steiner. As her mother's helper, she begins a friendship with the mayor's wife, Ilsa Hermann, although she only realizes the extent of this friendship at the end of the story. As the title suggests, she really does steal books. Through her friendship with Ilsa Hermann (also called Frau Hermann), she would enter her house through a window, and steal books.

title: The God of Small Things
author: Arundhati Roy
synopsis:
The God of Small Things (in the original The God of Small Things) is the first book by the Indian writer Arundhati Roy, published in 1997. The book won the distinguished prize for English-language literature, the Booker Prize, of 1998.

The book speaks of castes and touches on taboo subjects. For this reason, the author was taken to court for obscenity.

Two fraternal twins born in 1962 – Estha and Rahel – meet again after many years of separation. Around this reunion there arises a whole series of other small stories of three generations of a family from the region of Kerala, in the south of India, which scatters across the world and comes together again in its homeland. Stories that take in a pickle factory, the death of a child, forbidden loves, repressed desires.

title: Persepolis
author: Marjane Satrapi
synopsis:
Persepolis is an autobiographical French comic book (pt-BR) or graphic album (pt-PT?) by Marjane Satrapi, which portrays her childhood up to her early adult years in Iran, during and after the Islamic Revolution. Persepolis reminds readers of the "precariousness of survival" in political and social situations. The title Persepolis is a reference to the ancient capital of the Persian Empire, Persepolis. Originally published in French, the graphic novel has been translated into many other languages, including English, Spanish, Catalan, Portuguese, Italian, Greek, Swedish, Georgian and others. As of 2018, it has sold more than 2 million copies worldwide. Persepolis 1 was written in 2000 and Persepolis 2 was written in 2004.

The French comics publisher L'Association published the original work in four volumes between 2000 and 2003.

Note: The summary of the English editions of the novel is divided into two sections, one for each book.

Persepolis 1 begins by introducing Marji, the ten-year-old protagonist. Set in 1980, the novel focuses on her experiences of growing up during the Islamic Revolution in Iran. Her story details the impact of war and religious extremism on Iranians, especially women. Belonging to an upper-middle-class family, Marji has access to various educational materials, such as books and a radio, which expose her to Western political thought at a very young age. Upon discovering the ideas of numerous philosophers, Marji reflects on her class privilege and is eager to learn about her family's political past. This inquiry inspires her to take part in popular demonstrations against the Shah's regime, in which people call for his exile as a way of safeguarding their rights. Unfortunately, after the Shah's departure, Marji notices the rise of religious extremism in her society and is unhappy about it.

title: Maus
author: Art Spiegelman
synopsis:
Maus is a graphic novel by the American cartoonist Art Spiegelman, serialized from 1980 to 1991. The comic depicts Spiegelman interviewing his father about the latter's experiences as a Polish Jew and Holocaust survivor. The work uses postmodernist techniques and represents Jews as mice, Germans as cats, and Poles as pigs. Critics have classified Maus as memoir, biography, history, fiction, autobiography and a mixture of genres. In 1992, it became the first graphic novel to win the Pulitzer Prize.

In the story's narrative present, which begins in 1978, in New York City, Spiegelman talks with his father, Vladek, about the latter's experiences of the Holocaust, gathering material for the Maus project he is preparing.

Most of the book alternates between two periods. In the frame narrative of the narrative present, Spiegelman interviews his father, Vladek, in Rego Park, in New York City in 1978–79. The story Vladek tells unfolds in the narrative past, which begins in the mid-1930s and continues until the end of the Holocaust in 1945.

In Rego Park in 1958, a young Art Spiegelman complains to his father that his friends have left him behind. His father replies in broken English, "Friends? Your friends? If you lock them in a room with no food for a week, then you'll see what friends are!"

As an adult, Art visits his father, from whom he has grown distant. Since the suicide in 1968 of Anja, Art's mother, Vladek has remarried, to a woman named Mala. Art asks Vladek to recount his experiences of the Holocaust again. Vladek tells him of his time in the Polish city of Częstochowa and of how he came to marry Anja, enter her wealthy family and move to Sosnowiec to become a textile manufacturer. Vladek begs Art not to include this in his book, and, reluctantly, Art agrees.

title: Kitchen
author: Banana Yoshimoto
synopsis:
Kitchen (（キッチン）) is the first novel written by the Japanese author Banana Yoshimoto, published in 1988. The translation into English came in 1993, by Megan Backus, and the title Kitchen became a worldwide title.

Although there is a certain Western influence in Yoshimoto's style, Kitchen is recognizably an example of contemporary Japanese literature. It received favourable reviews from publications such as The Independent, The Times and The New Yorker.

In Kitchen, a young Japanese woman named Mikage Sakurai struggles to get over the death of her grandmother. Gradually she grows close to one of the deceased's friends, Yuichi, who works in a flower shop, and ends up living with him and his transsexual mother, Eriko.

From Mikage's passion for kitchens to her job as assistant to a cookery teacher and the many scenes in which food is merely presented, Kitchen is a small window onto the life of a Japanese girl and her discoveries about food and love with a tragedy in the background.

In Moonlight Shadow, a woman named Satsuki loses her boyfriend Hitoshi in a car accident and tells us: "On the night he died, my soul fled to some other place and I could not bring it back". She then becomes friends with the dead man's brother, Hiiragi, whose girlfriend died in the same accident. On a sleepless night, out walking, she meets a stranger named Urara, who has also lost someone special. Urara introduces Satsuki to a mystical experience, which makes her find the strength to go on living.

title: Normal People
author: Sally Rooney
synopsis:
Normal People (Normal People) is a novel by the Irish author Sally Rooney published in 2018. It is Rooney's second novel, following Conversas entre Amigos (2017). It was published by Faber & Faber on August 30, 2018. The book became a bestseller in the United States and sold almost 64,000 hardcover copies in its first four months of release.

A television adaptation of the same name, nominated for the Emmy, aired from April 2020 on BBC Three and Hulu. Several newspapers ranked it as one of the best books of the 2010s.

The novel follows the complex relationship of two teenagers, Marianne and Connell, students at the same school in County Sligo, Ireland and, later, at Trinity College Dublin (TCD). It takes place during the post-2008 Irish economic crisis, from 2011 to 2015.

Connell is popular, attractive and highly intelligent; because his mother works as a cleaner at Marianne's house, he begins a relationship with the odd, intimidating, but no less intelligent girl.

Connell imposes secrecy on the affair, out of shame and fear that one of his friends might find out about it. Nevertheless, he ends up attending Trinity, with Marianne, after the summer and their reconciliation. Marianne blossoms at university, becoming beautiful and popular, while Connell struggles, for the first time in his life, to fit in.

The pair weave in and out of each other's lives throughout their university years, developing an intense bond that brings to the surface the traumas and insecurities that make them who they are.

title: Stoner
author: John Williams
synopsis:
Stoner is a novel by the American writer John Williams, first published in 1965. It was later reissued, in 1972 by Pocket Books, in 2003 by Vintage, and in 2006 by New York Review Books Classics with an introduction by John McGahern. In Brazil the work was released in 2015 by the publisher Rádio Londres, in a translation by Marcos Maffei.

Stoner has been categorized as belonging to the academic novel genre. Stoner recounts the life of the eponymous William Stoner, covering his career as a university professor, his marriage to Edith, his relationship with his colleague Katherine, and his love for and pursuit of literature.

William Stoner was born on a small farm in 1891. One day, his father suggests that he should attend the University of Missouri and study agriculture. Stoner agrees, but while attending the compulsory literature course he resolves to devote himself to the field. Without telling his parents, Stoner abandons the agriculture course and goes on to study only the humanities. He completes his master's degree in English and begins teaching. At a college party, Stoner meets and falls in love with a young woman named Edith, whom he marries. Stoner's marriage to Edith has problems from the start. The couple develops a fraught relationship, and the birth of their daughter Grace worsens these conflicts.

Stoner comes to devote himself ever more diligently to his work as a teacher, and grows close to Katherine Driscoll, a younger teacher, and the relationship begins to threaten his career and marriage.

Over the course of Stoner's trajectory the character faces dilemmas regarding the First World War, education grounded in humanist values, and his relationship with death.

title: The Diary of a Young Girl
author: Anne Frank

title: Dune
author: Frank Herbert
synopsis:
Dune (Dune in the original English) is a science fiction novel by the American writer Frank Herbert (1920-1986), originally published by the publisher Chilton Books in the United States in 1965. Winner of the 1966 Hugo award, Dune is considered the best-selling science fiction book of all time. Regardless of its commercial success, Dune is continually singled out as one of the most renowned works of fiction and fantasy ever released, and one of the pillars of modern science fiction. It is the start of the Dune series, and the story contained in the book is expanded in five other books and a short story, all written by Herbert, in addition to inspiring more than a dozen other books, written by the author's son, Brian Herbert, in partnership with fellow American writer Kevin J. Anderson (all of them developed and published after Frank Herbert's death).

About 24,600 years after the present, in which Earth is no longer inhabited and much of its history has already been forgotten, some historical and religious traditions endure. Duke Leto Atreides, ruler of the planet Caladan, receives orders from the Padishah Emperor Shaddam IV to move, along with members of his duchy, to Arrakis, the only source of the spice melange in the known universe. Shaddam IV of House Corrino sees the Atreides as a threat to his throne, owing to Leto's charisma and popularity among the other nobles present in the Landsraad assembly. The Emperor decides that House Atreides must be destroyed. However, there is a convention in the Empire that if the emperor attacks a Great House, all the other Houses must unite to retaliate against the emperor. To get around this obstacle, Shaddam makes use of a millennia-old rivalry between House Atreides and House Harkonnen as a way of covering up his attack, calling on the brilliant and ambitious Baron Vladimir Harkonnen for this purpose in an attempt to eliminate his rival.

title: Neuromancer
author: William Gibson
synopsis:
Neuromancer, by William Gibson, is one of the most famous novels of the cyberpunk genre, and it won the three main science fiction awards: Nebula, Hugo and Philip K. Dick, after its publication in 1984, having been published in Brazil in 1991 by the publisher Aleph. It was Gibson's first book and the beginning of a trilogy.

Neuromancer is a science fiction book that introduced concepts that were new for its time, such as advanced artificial intelligences, a Matrix network and an almost "physical" cyberspace, concepts that were later explored by Masamune Shirow in his manga Ghost in the Shell and in the film Ghost in The Shell (in Brazil, "O Fantasma do Futuro"), directed by Mamoru Oshii, which served as inspiration for the Wachowski sisters in creating the Matrix trilogy.

The novel tells the story of Case, a former hacker (cowboy, as hackers are called in Neuromancer) who was rendered unable to practise his "profession", thanks to a mistake he made when he tried to steal from his employers. They then poisoned Case with a mycotoxin, which damaged his neural system and made it impossible for him to connect to the Matrix. Before that they left a sum of money with him, since he "would need it".

Case then seeks out the clandestine medical clinics of Chiba City, where he spends all his money on tests, without managing to find a cure. Drugged, penniless, unemployed - this is the condition in which Molly finds him and the plot begins, with a cure for Case's damage in sight.

As the reading goes on, several interesting characters are introduced into the plot (Molly, Armitage, Wintermute), and the murky past of each of them is gradually uncovered as the story unfolds, a story that has a surprising ending.

title: The Left Hand of Darkness
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
synopsis:
The Left Hand of Darkness (The Left Hand of Darkness, in the original) is a science fiction novel by the American writer Ursula K. Le Guin, published in 1969. The novel became immensely popular and established Le Guin's status as a major science fiction author.

The novel follows the story of Genly Ai, a native of Earth, who is sent to the planet Gethen as an envoy of the Ekumen, a loose confederation of planets. Ai's mission is to persuade the nations of Gethen to join the Ekumen, but he is hindered by his lack of understanding of Gethenian culture. Individuals on Gethen are "ambisexual", with no fixed sex. This fact has a strong influence on the planet's culture, and creates a barrier of understanding for Ai.

The protagonist of the novel is Genly Ai, a native Terran, who is sent to invite Gethen to join the Ekumen, a coalition of humanoid worlds. Ai travels to the Gethen system in a ship that remains in solar orbit with Ai's companions, who are in stasis. Ai is sent to Gethen alone, as the "First Mobile". Like all envoys of the Ekumen, he can use "mindspeak" — a form of quasi-telepathic speech, of which Gethenians are also capable, but for which they have lost the ability. He lands in the Gethenian kingdom of Karhide, and spends two years trying to persuade the members of its government of the value of joining the Ekumen. Karhide is one of the two great nations on Gethen, the other being Orgoreyn.

The novel begins on the day before an audience that Ai has obtained with Argaven Harge, the king of Karhide. Ai manages this with the help of Estraven, the prime minister, who seems to believe in Ai's mission. However, on the night before the audience, Estraven tells Ai that he can no longer support his cause with the king.

title: The Dispossessed
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
synopsis:
The Dispossessed: An Ambiguous Utopia (The Dispossessed in Brazil or Os Despojados in Portugal) is a utopian science fiction novel by Ursula K. Le Guin written in 1974, winner of the Nebula Award of the same year, as well as the Hugo Award and the Locus Award in 1975. Set in the same universe as The Left Hand of Darkness (1969), the book takes place on two twin planets, Uras and Anarres, with opposing political systems and on the verge of conflict, in an allusion to the Cold War, and deals with themes fundamental to its era, such as the clash between capitalism, Russian communism and anarchism, as well as the concepts of the individual and the collective.

The plot takes place on two twin planets: Urras and Anarres. The first is a world divided into several States and dominated by the two largest, which are rivals. In a clear allusion to the United States and the Soviet Union, one of the States has a strong economy and a patriarchal society, while the other positions itself as proletarian and wishes to stamp its political model on the entire planet. In addition, there is a third country, which, although underdeveloped, is of extreme importance and becomes the target of a political dispute between the two sovereign nations, which begin a disguised war against each other, in an allusion to the Cold War. The planet Anarres, for its part, lives through a very different situation: its anarchist politics, which represents a third way out of Urra's planetary crisis, creates an illusion of a perfect society. That illusion is only broken when a brilliant young physicist, Shevek, discovers the "Theory of Simultaneity", which could end the planet's isolation, as well as favor the wars of its neighbor.

title: Solaris
author: Stanisław Lem
synopsis:
Solaris is a science fiction novel written in 1961 by the Polish author Stanisław Lem.

It narrates the saga of a team of scientists on a research station as they try to understand an extraterrestrial intelligence, which takes the form of a vast ocean on an alien planet called Solaris. The novel, which has a philosophical and existential treatment, is among the best-known works of Stanislaw Lem.

Solaris narrates a failed final attempt at communication with the extraterrestrial life that inhabits a distant alien planet called Solaris. The planet is almost completely covered by a gelatinous ocean that turns out to be a single entity, apparently endowed with intelligence. Terran scientists conjecture that it is a living, sentient being and try to communicate with it. To pursue this scientific project, Kris Kelvin, a psychologist, arrives aboard Solaris Station, a scientific research station hovering near the planet's oceanic surface.

Scientists have already studied this ocean for many decades, but without success. A scientific discipline known as Solaristics has degenerated over the years into simply observing, recording and categorizing the complex phenomena that occur on the ocean's surface. But the scientists have merely compiled an elaborate nomenclature of the phenomena, and still do not understand what such activities really mean.

title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
editionTitle: O Guia do Mochileiro das Galáxias
author: Douglas Adams
synopsis:
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (Brazil: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy; Portugal: O Guia Galáctico do Pendura or À Boleia Pela Galáxia) is a comic science fiction series created by Douglas Adams. Originally broadcast on BBC Radio 4 in 1978, it was later adapted to other formats, and after several years it became an international phenomenon. The adaptations have included stage shows, a "trilogy" of five books published between 1979 and 1992, a sixth novel written by Eoin Colfer, in 2009, a 1981 TV series, a 1984 computer game, and three three-part series of comic book adaptations of the novels published by DC Comics between 1993 and 1996. There were also two towels, produced by Beer-Davies, which are considered by some fans to be an "official version" of the Guia do Mochileiro das Galáxias, since they include the text of the first novel.

The various versions follow practically the same basic plot. However, since Adams substantially rewrote the story for each new adaptation, the characters are often in mutually contradictory places. Throughout all the versions, the series follows the adventures of several characters, the main ones being: Arthur Dent, a hapless Englishman; Ford Prefect, an alien from a small planet somewhere in the vicinity of Betelgeuse and a collector of tourist information for the famous Guia do Mochileiro das Galáxias; Zaphod Beeblebrox, Ford's semi-cousin and the Galactic President; the depressed robot Marvin, the Paranoid Android; and Trillian, formerly known as Tricia McMillan, a woman Arthur had met at a party in Islington.

title: The Hobbit
author: J. R. R. Tolkien
synopsis:
The Hobbit, or There and Back Again (published in Portugal as O Gnomo or The Hobbit and, in Brazil, as The Hobbit ou Lá e de Volta Outra Vez or simply The Hobbit) is a high fantasy book for children and young readers written by the British philologist and professor J. R. R. Tolkien. Originally published on 21 September 1937, it was acclaimed by critics, being nominated for the Carnegie Medal and receiving a prize from the American newspaper New York Herald Tribune for best juvenile fiction. The novel has remained popular over the years and is recognized as a classic of children's literature, having sold more than 190 million copies.

Set in a time "Between the Dawn of Faerie and the Dominion of Men", the book follows the quest of the home-loving hobbit Bilbo Bolseiro to win a share of the treasure guarded by the dragon Smaug.

Gandalf involves Bilbo in a party for Thorin and his band of dwarves, who sing of reclaiming the Montanha Solitária and its vast treasure from the dragon Smaug. When the music ends, Gandalf reveals a map showing a secret door in the mountain and proposes that a dumbfounded Bilbo serve as the expedition's "burglar". The dwarves ridicule the idea, but the hobbit, indignant, joins them in spite of himself.

The group travels towards the wild lands, where Bilbo and Gandalf save the company from a group of trolls. The latter leads them to Rivendell, where Elrond reveals the secrets of the map Thorin holds to the secret entrance of Erebor. Crossing over the Montanhas Sombrias, they are captured by goblins and driven deep underground. Although Gandalf manages to rescue them, Bilbo ends up separated from the others at the moment of escape. Lost in the goblins' tunnels, he comes across a mysterious ring and then meets Gollum, who engages him in a game of riddles.

title: The Lord of the Rings
author: J. R. R. Tolkien
synopsis:
The Lord of the Rings (The Lord of the Rings, in the original) is a high fantasy book written by the British writer J. R. R. Tolkien. Written between 1937 and 1949, with many parts created during the Second World War, the saga is a continuation of The Hobbit (1937). Although Tolkien had planned to produce it as a single volume, the work was originally published in three volumes (The Fellowship of the Ring, The Two Towers and The Return of the King) between 1954 and 1955, with each volume containing two books, and it was in this form, in three volumes, that it became popular.
